CHAPTER 1

Compile, simulate and understand the RTL

Goal: prove the counter’s functional behavior before gates or layout exist.
You start withThe project tree from Chapter 0
You end withrtl/cnt_updown.v, a self-checking testbench, a PASS, a waveform
Toolsirun, ncvlog/ncelab/ncsim, SimVision
Time≈ 45 min
THEORYHow a Verilog simulator thinks≈ 10 min read

T1Design vs testbench

  • The DUT (design under test) is the hardware: only synthesizable constructs.
  • The testbench is a program around it: it makes the clock, drives inputs, and judges outputs. It is never turned into hardware, so it may use delays (#5), loops and $display.
  • A self-checking testbench contains an independent reference model; a checker compares DUT and model every cycle and prints PASS or FAIL.

T2Three phases: analyze → elaborate → simulate

ncvlog: parse each filencelab: connect the hierarchy into a snapshotncsim: run time forward

irun simply runs all three for you. Knowing the phases tells you where an error comes from: syntax errors are analysis; “undefined module” is elaboration; wrong values are simulation (a design bug).

T3Event-driven simulation and why flops use <=

The simulator does not tick every picosecond. It keeps a queue of events (“signal X changes at time t”) and jumps from one to the next. Inside one time step it works in ordered regions:

  1. Active region — run triggered blocks; blocking = assignments update immediately; for non-blocking <= only the right-hand side is evaluated and remembered.
  2. NBA region — all remembered <= updates happen together.
  3. Monitor region — $monitor, waveform dumping see the final values.

That “evaluate everything first, update all together” behaviour is exactly how real flip-flops on one clock work. Compare two flops that should swap values:

Blocking vs non-blocking · Verilog// WRONG for flops: result depends on which always block runs first
always @(posedge clk) a = b;
always @(posedge clk) b = a;     // may copy the NEW a -> both end equal

// RIGHT: both read old values, then both update -> a real swap
always @(posedge clk) a <= b;
always @(posedge clk) b <= a;

Rule of thumb: <= in clocked blocks, = in combinational blocks. Never mix them in one block.

T4Four-valued logic

VALUEMEANINGTYPICAL CAUSE
0 / 1Logic low / high—
xUnknownUninitialized flop, two drivers fighting, missing reset
zHigh impedance (undriven)Unconnected input, tri-state off

== returns x if either side has an x — and an if(x) is treated as false, so a check silently passes. === compares x and z literally and always returns 0 or 1. That is why the checker uses !==.

T5Reading a timing diagram — and avoiding races

  • A race happens when the testbench changes an input in the same time step as the clock edge that samples it — the result depends on event order, not on your design.
  • Changing inputs half a period away from the active edge removes the race and mirrors reality: real inputs arrive well before the clock (that margin is exactly what set_input_delay describes in Chapter 2).
  • The asynchronous reset is the one exception: it acts immediately, between edges.

T6Waveform files

$dumpvars writes a VCD (Value Change Dump): a text log of every change of every recorded signal with its time. SimVision converts it to its faster SST2 format. The same idea — counting changes — is reused for power in Chapter 3, except only toggle counts are kept (TCF).

DEEP DIVE the counter as mathematics

D1A precise specification

Let cn∈{0,…,255}c_n \in \{0,\dots,255\} be the count after the nn-th rising edge, ene_n the enable and unu_n the direction sampled at that edge. The RTL implements exactly

cn+1={0if resetcnif en=0(cn+1) mod 256if en=1, un=1(cn−1) mod 256if en=1, un=0c_{n+1} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if reset} \\ c_n & \text{if } e_n = 0 \\ (c_n + 1) \bmod 256 & \text{if } e_n = 1,\ u_n = 1 \\ (c_n - 1) \bmod 256 & \text{if } e_n = 1,\ u_n = 0 \end{cases}

Compactly, with dn=2un−1∈{−1,+1}d_n = 2u_n - 1 \in \{-1, +1\}:

cn+1=(cn+en dn) mod 28c_{n+1} = \bigl(c_n + e_n\, d_n\bigr) \bmod 2^8

The testbench’s reference model is this equation written in Verilog. The “rollover” you check in Phase 3 is just the  mod 28\bmod 2^8: (0−1) mod 256=255(0 - 1) \bmod 256 = 255.

D2The design is a finite-state machine

The counter has 28=2562^8 = 256 states and 23=82^3 = 8 input combinations, so the full transition table has 256×8=2048256 \times 8 = 2048 entries. Exhaustively checking every transition is cheap here; it becomes impossible for real designs (a 32-bit register alone has 4.3×1094.3\times10^9 states). That is why verification relies on reference models and targeted corner cases (rollover, reset in the middle of a cycle, hold) rather than enumeration.

How long does random stimulus take to reach a rare state? Reaching count = 255 from 0 by counting up needs 255 consecutive enabled “up” edges. If inputs were random with probability 14\tfrac14 per edge of being “enabled up”, the chance of 255 in a row is (1/4)255(1/4)^{255} — effectively never. Directed tests (your Phase 3 counting down through zero) hit the corner in 11 cycles.

D3Try it: step the counter one clock at a time

Toggle the inputs, then press Clock ↑. Watch which bits flip — the pattern is exactly the toggle rule derived in Chapter 2.

D4How a simulator orders events — formally

Think of simulation time as a sequence of time slots t0<t1<…t_0 \lt t_1 \lt \dots. Inside one slot the scheduler repeatedly drains regions until nothing is left:

Active⏟evaluate  →  Inactive⏟#0  →  NBA⏟update ≤  →  Monitor⏟$dump\underbrace{\text{Active}}_{\text{evaluate}} \;\rightarrow\; \underbrace{\text{Inactive}}_{\#0} \;\rightarrow\; \underbrace{\text{NBA}}_{\text{update } \le} \;\rightarrow\; \underbrace{\text{Monitor}}_{\text{\$dump}}

If an NBA update triggers more blocks (it usually does — a flop output feeds logic), those go back into Active in the same time slot; each such pass is called a delta cycle. Delta cycles take zero simulated time but are ordered, which is how zero-delay RTL still produces deterministic results.

Cost model: work per time slot is proportional to the number of signals that change, not the size of the design. That is why event-driven simulation is fast for designs with low activity — and why the activity α\alpha in Chapter 3 also predicts simulation speed.

D5How much has the testbench actually exercised? Coverage metrics

A PASS only says nothing went wrong in the cases you ran. Coverage measures how many cases that was:

METRICDEFINITIONTHIS TESTBENCH
Line / statement#RTL lines executed#lines\dfrac{\#\text{RTL lines executed}}{\#\text{lines}}100 % — every branch of the if runs
Toggle#bits seen going 0→1 and 1→0#bits\dfrac{\#\text{bits seen going } 0\to1 \text{ and } 1\to0}{\#\text{bits}}100 % — the rollover to 255 toggles every count bit
FSM state#states visited28\dfrac{\#\text{states visited}}{2^8}≈ 7 % (0–10, 254, 255): fine for a counter whose logic is identical for every state

Incisive can measure these automatically (irun -coverage all, viewed in IMC). The lesson: choose stimulus so that each distinct behaviour is covered, not every state.

D6Delay models in simulation: transport vs inertial

Real gates cannot respond to arbitrarily short pulses — their internal capacitance must charge first. Simulators model this with two kinds of delay:

MODELRULEUSED FOR
TransportEvery input change appears at the output after δ\delta, however shortWires
InertialA pulse of width w<δw \lt \delta is swallowedGates (Verilog default for assign #δ and gate primitives)

Formally, an inertial element with delay δ\delta outputs

y(t)={x(t−δ)if x was constant on [ t−δ,  t ]y(t−)otherwisey(t) = \begin{cases} x(t-\delta) & \text{if } x \text{ was constant on } [\,t-\delta,\; t\,] \\ y(t^-) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

With SDF annotation (Step 7.2) the cell models use pulse-rejection limits from the SDF. Glitches narrower than a gate delay disappear in gate-level simulation, just as in silicon — and glitches wider than that consume real power (Chapter 3, D8).

Remember
  • Testbench = stimulus + reference model + checker.
  • <= for flops; inputs change away from the active edge.
  • Use ===/!== in checks so x cannot hide a failure.
1.0

Create the counter RTL file

Why this stepThe RTL is the single source of truth that every later stage transforms; it must be correct before anything else.

In the terminal, confirm you are inside the project, then open a text editor. CentOS 6 commonly includes gedit; use vi if it is unavailable (in vi: press i to insert, paste, press Esc, type :wq and Enter to save and quit).

Open the RTL file · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
gedit rtl/cnt_updown.v &
# Alternative terminal editor:
# vi rtl/cnt_updown.v

Paste the module below, save (Ctrl+S), and close the editor. This example has an asynchronous active-high reset, an enable, and an up/down direction control.

rtl/cnt_updown.v · Verilog`timescale 1ns/1ps

module cnt_updown (
  input  wire       clk,
  input  wire       reset,     // asynchronous, active high
  input  wire       enable,    // 1 = count, 0 = hold
  input  wire       up_down,   // 1 = up,    0 = down
  output reg  [7:0] count
);

  always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
    if (reset)
      count <= 8'h00;
    else if (enable) begin
      if (up_down)
        count <= count + 8'h01;
      else
        count <= count - 8'h01;
    end
  end

endmodule

Read the code line by line before moving on:

  • always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) — the block reacts to a rising clock or a rising reset. Listing reset in the sensitivity list is what makes the reset asynchronous: it clears the counter immediately, without waiting for a clock edge.
  • if (reset) … else if (enable) — reset has priority over everything; when enable is 0 none of the assignments run, so count keeps its value (a hold).
  • <= is a non-blocking assignment. Always use it for flip-flops; it models all flops updating together at the clock edge.
  • 8-bit arithmetic wraps: 255 + 1 = 0 and 0 − 1 = 255. Your testbench will check this "rollover".
What hardware this describes

count requires eight flip-flops. The enable and direction behavior becomes an incrementer/decrementer plus a multiplexer feeding their D inputs. The asynchronous reset must map to flops with compatible reset pins (in gsclib045, a DFFR… type) or be restructured by synthesis.

What you should see
  • ls -l rtl/ lists cnt_updown.v with a size of roughly 400–500 bytes.
  • grep -n module rtl/cnt_updown.v shows exactly one module cnt_updown ( and one endmodule.
Checkpointls -l rtl/cnt_updown.v shows a non-empty file, and the module/port names match what the testbench will instantiate.
1.1

Create a self-checking testbench

Why this stepA reference model plus checker turns “looks right” into a provable PASS that you can rerun on every later netlist.

Open the testbench · shellgedit tb/tb_cnt_updown.v &

A testbench is ordinary Verilog that is never turned into hardware. This one does four jobs: it generates a 100 MHz clock, drives the inputs through six phases (reset, count up, hold, count down through zero, asynchronous reset, count up again), keeps an independent reference model of what count should be, and compares the DUT against that model every cycle. It also creates the waveform database expected by the source tutorial.

tb/tb_cnt_updown.v · Verilog`timescale 1ns/1ps

module tb_cnt_updown;
  reg        clk;
  reg        reset;
  reg        enable;
  reg        up_down;
  wire [7:0] count;

  // ---------------- Device under test ----------------
  cnt_updown dut (
    .clk(clk), .reset(reset), .enable(enable),
    .up_down(up_down), .count(count)
  );

  // ---------------- 100 MHz clock (10 ns period) ----------------
  initial clk = 1'b0;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;          // rising edges at 5, 15, 25 ... ns

  // ---------------- Waveform database for SimVision ----------------
  initial begin
    $dumpfile("./updown_counter.dump");
    $dumpvars(0, tb_cnt_updown);
  end

  // ---------------- Optional SDF back-annotation (Chapter 7) ----------------
`ifdef SDF
  initial $sdf_annotate("results/cnt_updown.sdf", dut, , "logs/sdf_annotate.log", "MAXIMUM");
`endif

  // ---------------- Reference model: what count SHOULD be ----------------
  reg [7:0] expected;
  always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
    if (reset)        expected <= 8'h00;
    else if (enable)  expected <= up_down ? expected + 8'h01 : expected - 8'h01;
  end

  // ---------------- Checker: compare on every falling edge ----------------
  integer errors = 0;
  integer checks = 0;
  always @(negedge clk) begin
    if (!reset) begin
      checks = checks + 1;
      if (count !== expected) begin
        errors = errors + 1;
        $display("ERROR  t=%0t ns  count=%0d  expected=%0d  (enable=%b up_down=%b)",
                 $time, count, expected, enable, up_down);
      end
    end
  end

  // ---------------- Stimulus: inputs change only on falling edges ----------------
  initial begin
    reset = 1'b1; enable = 1'b0; up_down = 1'b1;
    #22 reset = 1'b0;                          // release reset between clock edges

    @(negedge clk); enable = 1'b1; up_down = 1'b1;   // Phase 1: count up 10 times
    repeat (10) @(negedge clk);                       //          0 -> 10

    enable = 1'b0;                                    // Phase 2: hold for 3 cycles
    repeat (3) @(negedge clk);

    enable = 1'b1; up_down = 1'b0;                    // Phase 3: count down 12 times
    repeat (12) @(negedge clk);                       //          10 -> 0 -> 255 -> 254

    enable = 1'b0;                                    // Phase 4: hold
    repeat (2) @(negedge clk);

    #2 reset = 1'b1;                                  // Phase 5: asynchronous reset
    #2 reset = 1'b0;                                  //          in the middle of a cycle

    enable = 1'b1; up_down = 1'b1;                    // Phase 6: count up 3 times
    repeat (3) @(negedge clk);                        //          0 -> 3
    enable = 1'b0;
    repeat (2) @(negedge clk);

    if (errors == 0)
      $display("PASS: %0d cycle checks matched, final count = %0d", checks, count);
    else
      $display("FAIL: %0d of %0d cycle checks mismatched", errors, checks);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule

Three design decisions in this file matter more than they look:

  • Inputs change on the falling edge. If the testbench changed enable exactly at a rising edge, the simulator could evaluate the DUT before or after the change (a race). Changing inputs half a period away from the active edge removes the ambiguity — and mimics a real input that arrives well before the clock.
  • Checks also happen on the falling edge, i.e. after the DUT has settled from the previous rising edge.
  • !== instead of != also flags x and z values. A plain != against an unknown value evaluates to unknown and the error would silently be skipped.
PHASEINPUTSEXPECTED COUNT AT THE END
Reset (0–22 ns)reset=10
1 · up ×10enable=1 up_down=110
2 · hold ×3enable=010 (unchanged)
3 · down ×12enable=1 up_down=0254 (passes 0 → 255: rollover)
4 · hold ×2enable=0254
5 · async reset2 ns pulse between edges0 immediately, no clock needed
6 · up ×3enable=1 up_down=13
A waveform is not a complete test. The reference model above is what makes this a self-checking test: you read one PASS/FAIL line instead of trusting your eyes. You will reuse the exact same testbench on the gate-level netlist (Step 2.4) and on the routed netlist with real delays (Step 7.2).
Before you move on Read the testbench once from top to bottom and find its four jobs: the clock generator (one always line), the stimulus phases (the long initial block), the reference model (a second, independent counter), and the checker (the comparison that prints FAIL). A self-checking testbench is only as good as the independence of its model: if the model were copied from the RTL, a shared bug would pass silently.
Checkpointtb/tb_cnt_updown.v is saved and instantiates cnt_updown with the same five port names as the RTL.
1.2

Understand the dump instrumentation

Why this stepThe dump file is what SimVision and later power analysis read; knowing what it records tells you what you can inspect.

The source tutorial expects a dump database containing the full testbench hierarchy. The complete testbench above already contains these calls — this step just explains them.

tb_cnt_updown.v (excerpt) · Veriloginitial begin
  $dumpfile("./updown_counter.dump");
  $dumpvars(0, tb_cnt_updown);
end
  • $dumpfile names the output file. It is a standard VCD (Value Change Dump) text file even though the extension is .dump.
  • $dumpvars(0, tb_cnt_updown) records every signal in tb_cnt_updown and, because the first argument is 0, every level below it (including dut). A 1 would record only the top level.

Physical meaning: none yet. This only records simulator events. Dumping everything is convenient for a tiny counter but can be expensive (gigabytes) for a large SoC.

1.3

Compile and run with Incisive

Why this stepOne command proves the RTL compiles, elaborates and behaves — the first real evidence in the lab.

Return to the terminal. irun performs analysis, elaboration and simulation in one command. Use full debug access while learning. (Your VM runs the 32-bit build of Incisive 10.20-s100, so the banner reads irun: rather than irun(64):.)

Unified run · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
irun -v2001 -access +rwc \
  -logfile logs/irun.log \
  rtl/cnt_updown.v tb/tb_cnt_updown.v
OPTIONMEANING
-v2001Parse the files as Verilog-2001 (ANSI port lists, integer x = 0 initializers).
-access +rwcGive read/write/connectivity access to every signal so SimVision and Tcl can see them. Slower, but essential while debugging.
-logfile logs/irun.logCopy everything printed on screen into a file you can search later.
\ at line endShell line continuation — the three lines are one command.

The screenshot shows the compiler output. Read it top to bottom: file: … lines (each file parsed), module worklib.cnt_updown:v errors: 0, warnings: 0, then the elaborator building the design hierarchy, and finally the simulator running.

Expected end of the log

PASS: 32 cycle checks matched, final count = 3 followed by Simulation complete via $finish(1) at time 350 NS + 0 — the stimulus ends at the falling edge at 350 ns (the exact check count and time change if you edit the stimulus).

Troubleshooting — errors from irun

*E,…: Instance of undefined module 'cnt_updown' — the RTL file was not on the command line or the module name is misspelled. Both file names must be listed.

*E,EXPSMC: expecting a semicolon — a syntax error; the message gives file and line. Usually the line above is missing a ;.

*W,…: port sizes differ — the testbench declares count with a different width. Make it wire [7:0].

A line starts with ERROR t=… — the DUT disagrees with the reference model. Read enable/up_down in that line and compare with the RTL; then look at the waveform at that time (Step 1.8).

Locked database (*E,…: cannot lock) — another irun is still running. Close it or delete the stale INCA_libs folder and rerun.

ANNOTATED OUTPUTEnd of logs/irun.logillustrative — your exact numbers and names will differ
End of logs/irun.logirun: 10.20-s100: (c) Copyright 1995-2011 Cadence Design Systems, Inc.
file: rtl/cnt_updown.v                                              [1]
        module worklib.cnt_updown:v
                errors: 0, warnings: 0

        module worklib.tb_cnt_updown:v
                errors: 0, warnings: 0

Loading snapshot worklib.tb_cnt_updown:v .................... Done

ncsim> run                                                          [3]

  1. Analysis of each file: look for errors: 0 on every module.
  2. Elaboration: the snapshot name printed here is what you pass to ncsim later.
  3. Simulation starts; irun issues run for you in batch mode.
  4. The checker’s verdict — the single most important line.
  5. Normal end through $finish. A run that ends by time-out or *F fatal message is a failure even if no ERROR was printed.
CheckpointThe run reaches $finish without compile, binding or runtime errors, and prints PASS.
1.4

Inspect what the compiler created

Why this stepRecognising generated files lets you tell a stale result from a fresh one and clean up safely.

Incisive places compiled design units and snapshots in INCA_libs/. The log explains which top was elaborated; the dump database contains activity.

Expected generated files · shellls -la
ls -la INCA_libs
tail -n 40 logs/irun.log
grep -iE "error|warning" logs/irun.log

Compare your listing with the screenshot. You should now see three new things: INCA_libs/ (compiled database), updown_counter.dump (waveforms), and logs/irun.log (plus irun.key/irun.history, which record the command).

Analyze versus elaborate

Analysis checks each HDL unit on its own (syntax, declarations). Elaboration resolves hierarchy, parameters and module bindings into one simulatable snapshot. A file can compile cleanly and still fail elaboration because an instance cannot be resolved — which is why tools report the two stages separately.

What you should see
  • A new INCA_libs/ folder containing irun.lnx86.10.20.nc/ (or similar) with the compiled design.
  • updown_counter.dump of a few kilobytes — open it with head to see the VCD header ($date, $timescale 1ps, $scope module tb_cnt_updown).
  • grep -ciE "error|warning" logs/irun.log prints 0 (or only harmless notes).
1.5

Run the three-step flow and restart the saved snapshot

Why this stepRunning the three phases separately teaches where each kind of error comes from and gives a reusable snapshot for Chapter 3.

irun hides three separate programs. Running them by hand once teaches you what each stage does, and creates a named snapshot you can rerun without recompiling (needed again in Chapter 3). This isolates runtime debugging from compilation.

ACreate the library mapping files

The NC tools look for cds.lib (which library names map to which folders) and hdl.var (which library is the default work library) in the current directory.

Watch the last line printed by ncelab: Writing initial simulation snapshot: worklib.tb_cnt_updown:…. Whatever follows the colon is the snapshot's view name. The historical course snapshot is named worklib.tb_cnt_updown:v; on your run it may be :module. Use exactly what your tool printed whenever this page writes the snapshot name.

Saved snapshot (course form) · shellncsim -messages worklib.tb_cnt_updown:v

Troubleshooting — snapshot not found

*E,SNAPNF / "snapshot not found" — the name after the colon is wrong, or ncsim is running in a different directory than ncelab. Run ls worklib or ncls -snapshot to list the snapshots that exist.

*F,CDSLIB — cds.lib is missing from the current directory. Repeat part A.

Why this stepOpening the database is the gateway to visual debugging.

BAccept the translation

SimVision's native format is SST2. Because a VCD file was selected, a dialog asks whether to convert it. Click OK (or Yes). A .trn/.dsn pair appears beside the dump after conversion.

What you are seeing: SimVision is translating the recorded event database into a browsable hierarchy. This does not rerun the simulation — if you change the RTL, you must rerun Step 1.3 to produce a new dump.

Alternative: start directly with simvision updown_counter.dump & to skip the file dialog.

The tree is empty — the dump was written before $dumpvars ran or the simulation crashed at time 0 — rerun Step 1.3 and check the log.

Add the correct hierarchy to the waveform

Why this stepChoosing the right scope and signals is what makes a waveform readable instead of noise.

  2. Select the signals: click clk, then hold Ctrl and click reset, enable, up_down, count and expected.

1.8

Run, zoom and verify edge-by-edge behavior

Why this stepEdge-by-edge inspection is how you confirm the corner cases the checker tests — and how you debug when it fails.

AShow the full time range

When opened from a dump there is nothing to run; the data is already complete. Use the run control only if you started SimVision from a live simulation (irun -gui). Then click View → Zoom → Full X (or the "zoom to fit" toolbar button) so the whole simulation fits the window.

BChange the bus radix and zoom into edges

  1. Right-click count → Radix/Mnemonic → Unsigned Decimal so values read 0, 1, 2 … instead of hex.
  2. Drag a box on the time ruler around a few clock periods to zoom in. Click in the trace area to place the primary cursor; the value column shows every signal at that time.
  3. Check each item in the list below at the matching time.
WHAT TO VERIFYWHERE TO LOOKCORRECT BEHAVIOR
Reset priority0–22 nscount = 0 even though clk toggles.
Enabled up-count~35–125 ns+1 at each rising edge, never at falling edges.
Disabled hold~135–155 nsValue stays 10 for three edges.
Down-count & rollover~165–275 ns…, 1, 0, 255, 254.
Asynchronous reset~302–304 nsDrops to 0 the instant reset rises — between clock edges.
No unknownsEverywhere after resetNo red x segments on count.

Do not accept “the waveform moves” as a pass. Also confirm that count and expected are identical traces.

CMeasuring time in SimVision

  1. Left-click in the trace area: the primary cursor (a vertical line) jumps there and the value column shows every signal at that instant.
  2. Add a second reference with the Create marker toolbar button (or Edit → Create → Marker) and drag it to another edge.
  3. The time difference between cursor and marker is shown at the top of the waveform — measure the clock period (should read 10 ns) and the reset pulse in Phase 5 (2 ns).
  4. Use the next edge / previous edge toolbar arrows with a signal selected to jump exactly from one transition of that signal to the next.

Why no delay between clk and count? RTL simulation has zero delay: count changes in the same time step as the rising edge. After synthesis with SDF (Step 7.2) you will see a real clock-to-Q delay of a few hundred picoseconds.

Debugging rule

Look immediately before and after the active edge. That separates a DUT bug from a testbench race and exposes unknown values that later resolve. A value that changes exactly on a rising edge together with an input is the classic sign of a race.

What a careful waveform review looks like Pick three moments and check them against the RTL by hand: (1) the first rising edge after reset deasserts — count goes 0 → 1 only if enable = 1; (2) the edge where up_down changes — the next value moves in the new direction immediately; (3) the 0 → 255 rollover while counting down. Use the cursor: values change just after each rising edge (non-blocking assignment), never before it.
CheckpointAll six rows of the table are confirmed visually, and the log says PASS. Close SimVision (File → Exit SimVision).

? Check yourself

Q1Which assignment should a clocked always block use?

Non-blocking updates happen together in the NBA region, matching real flip-flops and avoiding order-dependent races.

Q2Why does the checker use !== instead of !=?

With !=, a comparison against x yields x, which an if treats as false — the error would be silently skipped.

Q3The counter is at 0 and counts down one step. The new value is…

cn+1 = (cn − 1) mod 256 = 255: the rollover tested in Phase 3.

⚠ Common mistakes in this chapter
  • Using = instead of <= in clocked blocks — races between flops.
  • Changing testbench inputs exactly on the active clock edge.
  • Comparing with !=, so x values silently pass.
  • Forgetting to rerun irun after editing RTL — SimVision shows the old dump.
  • Calling the waveform “correct” without the PASS line.

CHAPTER 2

Synthesize RTL with RTL Compiler 12.10

Goal: turn behavior into real standard cells under explicit timing constraints.
You start withVerified RTL and an idea of the target clock
You end withresults/cnt_updown_mapped.v + .sdc, clean lint, positive slack, gate-sim PASS
Toolsrc (RTL Compiler), irun
Time≈ 60 min
THEORYFrom behavior to gates — and how timing is judged≈ 15 min read · the most important theory in the lab

T1What synthesis does

  • Elaborate recognises structures: a clocked always becomes flops, + becomes an adder.
  • Generic optimization simplifies the Boolean logic without knowing the library.
  • Mapping chooses real cells from the Liberty file and sizes them until every path meets the SDC.

T2How RTL constructs become hardware

YOU WRITEYOU GET
always @(posedge clk)One flip-flop per assigned bit
… or posedge resetFlops with an asynchronous reset pin
if / else, ? :Multiplexers
+, -Adder / subtractor (half/full-adder cells)
Combinational always @* missing an elseA latch — the value must be “remembered” in that branch
A signal assigned in two always blocksMultiple drivers — an error

T3Reading cell names

Library cell names are compact descriptions. In gsclib045-style naming:

NAMEREADS AS
NAND2X1NAND, 2 inputs, drive strength ×1
INVX4Inverter, ×4 drive (bigger, faster on heavy loads, more leakage)
DFFRHQX1D flip-flop, Reset, High-speed, Q output only, ×1
SDFFRHQX1The same flop with a Scan mux (Chapter 6)
CLKBUFX4Clock buffer: balanced rise/fall delays, used by CTS

T4Static timing analysis (STA)

STA proves timing without simulation vectors. It breaks the design into timing paths that start at a flop clock pin or an input, and end at a flop data pin or an output — then adds up the delays along every path.

T5Setup and hold — the two rules every flop imposes

  • Setup: data must arrive at D some time tsetup before the capturing clock edge. Too slow → the flop captures garbage.
  • Hold: data must stay stable some time thold after the edge. Too fast → the new value races through and corrupts the capture.
Setup  tcq + tcomb,max + tsetup ≤ T − tuncertainty
Hold   tcq + tcomb,min ≥ thold
Slack  required time − arrival time  (positive = OK)
Worked example (numbers typical of this counter): T = 10 ns, uncertainty 0.2, tcq = 0.25, tcomb = 1.8, tsetup = 0.1.
Arrival = 0.25 + 1.8 = 2.05 ns. Required = 10 − 0.2 − 0.1 = 9.7 ns. Setup slack = 7.65 ns ✓

Key insight: the hold equation has no T in it. Slowing the clock fixes setup violations but never hold violations — those must be fixed by adding delay (buffers) on short paths. That is why hold is repaired after CTS (Chapter 4).

T6How the SDC budgets the boundary

Your block is part of a bigger chip. set_input_delay 1 says “the logic before me already used 1 ns of the cycle”; set_output_delay 1 says “the logic after me needs 1 ns”. So:

PATHTIME LEFT FOR LOGIC INSIDE THIS BLOCK
reg2reg10 − 0.2 = 9.8 ns (minus tcq, tsetup)
in2reg10 − 1 − 0.2 = 8.8 ns
reg2out10 − 1 − 0.2 = 8.8 ns

An object the SDC forgets to constrain is simply not checked — the most dangerous kind of “pass”. That is what the lint report in Step 2.3 hunts for.

T7Why synthesis timing is only an estimate

No wires exist yet. RC guesses each net’s capacitance from its fanout (a wire-load model), and treats the clock as ideal (arriving everywhere at once). Both assumptions are replaced by real data in Chapter 4, which is why timing is checked again there.

DEEP DIVE Boolean derivation, the timing graph, and delay tables

D1Deriving the counter’s gate-level logic

Write the count as bits c7…c0c_7 \dots c_0. Adding 1 to a binary number flips bit ii exactly when all lower bits are 1 (the carry reaches it). Subtracting 1 flips bit ii when all lower bits are 0 (the borrow reaches it). So the toggle condition of bit ii is

Ti=e⋅∏j=0i−1xnor⁡(cj, u)andci+=ci⊕TiT_i = e \cdot \prod_{j=0}^{i-1} \operatorname{xnor}(c_j,\, u) \qquad\text{and}\qquad c_i^{+} = c_i \oplus T_i

Here xnor⁡(cj,u)=¬(cj⊕u)\operatorname{xnor}(c_j,u) = \lnot(c_j \oplus u) is 1 when cj=uc_j = u: all-ones for counting up (u=1u=1), all-zeros for counting down (u=0u=0). The empty product for i=0i = 0 is 1, so c0c_0 toggles on every enabled edge.

Check with numbers: c=0000 01112=7c = 0000\,0111_2 = 7, counting up. T0=T1=T2=T3=1T_0 = T_1 = T_2 = T_3 = 1 (bits 0–2 are all 1), T4=0T_4 = 0 (bit 3 is 0). Flipping bits 0–3 gives 0000 10002=80000\,1000_2 = 8. ✓

This is what RC builds: an XNOR per bit, an AND chain for the product, and an XOR feeding each flop’s D pin.

D2Why the critical path grows with width

Computed naïvely, T7T_7 needs the AND of seven terms through a chain (“ripple”), so the logic depth is O(n)\mathcal{O}(n) for an nn-bit counter:

tcombripple≈n⋅tAND2t_{\text{comb}}^{\text{ripple}} \approx n \cdot t_{\text{AND2}}

A balanced tree of 2-input ANDs computes the same product in ⌈log⁡2n⌉\lceil \log_2 n \rceil levels:

tcombtree≈⌈log⁡2n⌉⋅tAND2t_{\text{comb}}^{\text{tree}} \approx \lceil \log_2 n \rceil \cdot t_{\text{AND2}}

For n=8n = 8: 8 levels vs 3 levels. When the clock is tight, synthesis restructures ripple logic into trees (carry look-ahead) — trading area for speed. At 100 MHz this counter has so much slack that RC keeps the smaller ripple form.

D3How STA actually computes timing: a worked graph

Static timing analysis never simulates. It turns the netlist into a graph and does two sweeps of simple arithmetic over it. Here is the whole procedure on a small example.

Step 1 · Build the timing graph

Every pin becomes a vertex. Every cell arc (input pin → output pin of a gate) and every net (driver → receiver) becomes an edge labelled with its delay. Flip-flops break the graph: a flop’s Q pin is a start point, its D pin an end point. Because every loop in a synchronous design passes through a flop, the resulting graph has no cycles — it is a DAG (directed acyclic graph).

Step 2 · Forward pass: arrival times

The arrival time AT is the latest moment the signal at a pin can still change after the clock edge. Start points get their launch times (flop Q pins: tcq=0.3t_{cq} = 0.3 ns; the input: its input delay, 1.0 ns). Then visit vertices in topological order — every vertex only after all of its inputs — and apply

AT(v)=max⁡u→v[AT(u)+d(u,v)]\text{AT}(v) = \max_{u \to v}\bigl[\text{AT}(u) + d(u,v)\bigr]

We take the maximum because a gate’s output is not final until its last input has arrived.

VERTEXINPUTS (AT + delay)AT
g1 (NAND2)A: 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8 · B: 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.51.5 (B is later)
g2 (INV)C: 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.50.5
g3 (NOR2)g1: 1.5 + 0.6 = 2.1 · g2: 0.5 + 0.6 = 1.12.1
D (end point)g3: 2.1 + 0.12.2
Step 3 · Backward pass: required times

The required time RT is the latest moment the signal may arrive and still be captured correctly. At the end point it comes from the setup inequality: RT(D)=T−u−tsu=10−0.2−0.1=9.7\text{RT}(D) = T - u - t_{su} = 10 - 0.2 - 0.1 = 9.7 ns. Then walk the graph in reverse topological order:

RT(v)=min⁡v→w[RT(w)−d(v,w)]\text{RT}(v) = \min_{v \to w}\bigl[\text{RT}(w) - d(v,w)\bigr]

We take the minimum because a pin that feeds several paths must satisfy the most demanding one.

VERTEXOUTPUTS (RT − delay)RT
g39.7 − 0.19.6
g1, g29.6 − 0.69.0
A, B9.0 − 0.58.5
C9.0 − 0.28.8
Step 4 · Slack and the critical path
slack(v)=RT(v)−AT(v)\text{slack}(v) = \text{RT}(v) - \text{AT}(v)

Slack is how much later the signal could arrive at that pin before the design fails. Every vertex on the worst path has the same, smallest slack — here 7.5 ns along B → g1 → g3 → D. That chain is the critical path, and it is exactly what the timing report in Step 2.3 prints line by line. Paths through A or C have more slack (8.2 and 8.5 ns), so speeding them up would not help.

Step 5 · Why it scales

Each pass touches each edge once, so the work is O(∣V∣+∣E∣)\mathcal{O}(|V| + |E|) — linear in design size. A million-gate design is analysed in seconds, and the answer covers every path, which no amount of simulation could. Hold analysis repeats the same two passes with min⁡\min and max⁡\max swapped (earliest arrival vs earliest allowed time). The price: STA checks timing, not function, and it trusts the constraints completely — the reason Step 2.3 lints them first.

D4The complete setup and hold inequalities, term by term

The simple versions in the theory card assumed the clock reaches every flop at the same instant. In a real chip it does not, so we add the clock’s travel time. Name the pieces:

SYMBOLMEANING
ℓL, ℓC\ell_L,\ \ell_Cclock latency: time for the clock edge to reach the launching flop L and the capturing flop C
δ=ℓC−ℓL\delta = \ell_C - \ell_Lskew between the pair (positive = capture clock arrives later)
tcqt_{cq}clock-to-Q delay of L
tcombmax⁡, tcombmin⁡t_{\text{comb}}^{\max},\ t_{\text{comb}}^{\min}longest and shortest logic delay from L to C
tsu, tht_{su},\ t_hsetup and hold time of C
uuuncertainty (jitter + margin), always subtracted from your budget

Setup. Data launched by edge 0 must arrive before edge 1 at C (minus setup and uncertainty). Edge 0 reaches L at ℓL\ell_L; edge 1 reaches C at T+ℓCT + \ell_C:

ℓL+tcq+tcombmax⁡⏟data arrives+tsu  ≤  T+ℓC⏟next edge at C−u⟺tcq+tcombmax⁡+tsu  ≤  T+δ−u\underbrace{\ell_L + t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\max}}_{\text{data arrives}} + t_{su} \;\le\; \underbrace{T + \ell_C}_{\text{next edge at C}} - u \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\max} + t_{su} \;\le\; T + \delta - u

Hold. The same edge that launches new data at L also captures the old data at C. The new data must not arrive until C has finished capturing, tht_h after that edge:

ℓL+tcq+tcombmin⁡⏟new data arrives  ≥  ℓC+th⏟capture finished+u⟺tcq+tcombmin⁡  ≥  th+δ+u\underbrace{\ell_L + t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\min}}_{\text{new data arrives}} \;\ge\; \underbrace{\ell_C + t_h}_{\text{capture finished}} + u \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\min} \;\ge\; t_h + \delta + u

Solving the setup inequality for TT gives the fastest safe clock:

fmax⁡=1 tcq+tcombmax⁡+tsu−δ+u f_{\max} = \frac{1}{\,t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\max} + t_{su} - \delta + u\,}

Read the two inequalities side by side and three facts jump out:

  1. TT appears only in setup. A slower clock cures setup violations and does nothing for hold.
  2. Skew moves slack from one check to the other. δ\delta sits on the right-hand side of both inequalities: in setup it enlarges the time allowed, in hold it raises the minimum required. 0.1 ns of positive skew gives setup 0.1 ns more room and takes 0.1 ns away from hold.
  3. Hold is about the shortest path. Two flops connected by a bare wire (tcombmin⁡≈0t_{\text{comb}}^{\min} \approx 0) are the classic hold risk. The fix is to add delay — optDesign -hold inserts buffers on such paths.

D5Try it: a setup / hold calculator

Drag the sliders. Make the clock faster until setup fails; then add skew and watch hold fail while setup improves.

D6Where cell delays come from: NLDM tables, with a worked lookup

A gate’s delay depends on two things the logical-effort model simplifies away: how fast its input changes (the input transition or slew ss) and how much capacitance it drives (CC). A Liberty file therefore stores each cell arc as a small 2-D table, measured by the library vendor with SPICE — the Non-Linear Delay Model:

What an NLDM table looks like inside slow.lib (illustrative)cell_rise (delay_template_3x3) {
  index_1 ("0.05, 0.20, 0.80");          /* input transition s (ns) */
  index_2 ("0.001, 0.010, 0.050");       /* output load C (pF)       */
  values ("0.031, 0.058, 0.162", \
          "0.044, 0.071, 0.176", \
          "0.090, 0.121, 0.231");        /* delay (ns)              */
}

Rows are input transitions, columns are loads. When the actual (s,C)(s, C) falls between grid points, the tool interpolates bilinearly: first along one axis, then along the other. With (s1,s2)(s_1, s_2) and (C1,C2)(C_1, C_2) the surrounding grid values:

w1(s)=s2−ss2−s1,w2(s)=1−w1(s),d(s,C)=∑i,j∈{1,2}wi(s) wj(C)  d(si,Cj)w_1(s) = \frac{s_2 - s}{s_2 - s_1},\quad w_2(s) = 1 - w_1(s),\qquad d(s,C) = \sum_{i,j \in\{1,2\}} w_i(s)\,w_j(C)\;d(s_i, C_j)
Worked lookup: s=0.35s = 0.35 ns, C=0.020C = 0.020 pF.
Neighbours: s∈[0.20,0.80]s \in [0.20, 0.80] → w1(s)=(0.80−0.35)/0.60=0.75w_1(s) = (0.80-0.35)/0.60 = 0.75, w2=0.25w_2 = 0.25. C∈[0.010,0.050]C \in [0.010, 0.050] → w1(C)=(0.050−0.020)/0.040=0.75w_1(C) = (0.050-0.020)/0.040 = 0.75, w2=0.25w_2 = 0.25.
d=0.75⋅0.75⋅0.071+0.75⋅0.25⋅0.176+0.25⋅0.75⋅0.121+0.25⋅0.25⋅0.231d = 0.75\cdot0.75\cdot0.071 + 0.75\cdot0.25\cdot0.176 + 0.25\cdot0.75\cdot0.121 + 0.25\cdot0.25\cdot0.231
    =0.0399+0.0330+0.0227+0.0144=0.110\;\;= 0.0399 + 0.0330 + 0.0227 + 0.0144 = 0.110 ns.

A second table (rise_transition) gives the output slew the same way. That output slew becomes the next gate’s input slew, so delays are computed stage by stage along each path — the reason set_input_transition and set_load in your SDC change every number in the report. Each row of the RC timing report (Step 2.3) is one such lookup.

D7The wire-load model, quantified

Before placement a net with fanout kk is given an estimated length and capacitance from a lookup table, roughly linear:

Cwire(k)≈C0+k ΔC,Cnet=Cwire(k)+∑p∈sinksCpin(p)C_{\text{wire}}(k) \approx C_0 + k\,\Delta C, \qquad C_{\text{net}} = C_{\text{wire}}(k) + \sum_{p \in \text{sinks}} C_{\text{pin}}(p)

It is a statistical average, so individual nets can be off by 2× or more — the reason timing changes after placement and routing.

D8Technology mapping is dynamic programming

After generic optimisation RC holds a subject graph made only of NAND2 and inverters. Each library cell is also described as a small pattern of NAND2/INV. Mapping chooses a set of patterns that covers the graph at minimum cost. On a tree this has an exact, linear-time solution (the DAGON algorithm):

cost(v)=min⁡m∈matches(v)[ area(m)+∑u∈inputs(m)cost(u)]\text{cost}(v) = \min_{m \in \text{matches}(v)} \Bigl[\, \text{area}(m) + \sum_{u \in \text{inputs}(m)} \text{cost}(u) \Bigr]

Process the nodes from inputs to outputs; each node stores its best cost and the match achieving it. For delay instead of area, replace the sum with a max of arrival times plus the cell delay.

Tiny example: the subject graph of an AND gate is NAND2 → INV. Matches at the INV output: (a) library INV on top of the best cover of the NAND2 (cost 1 + 2 = 3), or (b) the single library AND2 cell, whose pattern is exactly NAND2 → INV (cost 2.5). DP picks AND2. Real libraries offer hundreds of patterns per node, so the choice is never obvious by hand.

D9Reset strategy: why the async reset is a false path

The reset assertion is asynchronous and needs no timing. Its release must not happen inside a flop’s recovery/removal window (the reset-pin equivalent of setup/hold), or flops come out of reset on different cycles or metastable (primer F6). Real designs use a reset synchroniser: assert asynchronously, release through two flops clocked by clk. The lab’s set_false_path -from reset is acceptable only because the testbench releases reset safely between edges.

D10Two-level minimisation and Karnaugh maps

Any Boolean function can be written as a sum of minterms (rows of its truth table where it is 1). Minimisation finds the fewest, largest prime implicants covering them — on a Karnaugh map, the largest power-of-two rectangles of 1s, where adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable (Gray code), including wrap-around.

The algebra behind a group is the adjacency theorem xy+xyˉ=xxy + x\bar{y} = x:

aˉ b cˉ d+aˉ b c d+a b cˉ d+a b c d=b d (aˉcˉ+aˉc+acˉ+ac)=b d\bar a\, b\, \bar c\, d + \bar a\, b\, c\, d + a\, b\, \bar c\, d + a\, b\, c\, d = b\,d\,(\bar a\bar c + \bar a c + a\bar c + a c) = b\,d

K-maps stop being practical beyond 5–6 variables; the Quine–McCluskey method does the same systematically (generate all primes by repeated merging, then solve a set-cover problem). Exact set cover is NP-hard, so tools like Espresso use heuristics. Modern synthesis works on multi-level logic (factored forms such as f=x(y+z)f = x(y + z)) because two-level forms blow up for functions like parity: nn-input XOR needs 2n−12^{n-1} product terms but only n−1n-1 XOR gates.

D11Shannon expansion and binary decision diagrams

Every Boolean function splits on any variable xx (Shannon’s expansion):

f=x⋅f∣x=1  +  xˉ⋅f∣x=0f = x \cdot f\big|_{x=1} \;+\; \bar x \cdot f\big|_{x=0}

Applying it recursively in a fixed variable order and merging identical sub-graphs gives a reduced ordered BDD:

For a fixed order the ROBDD is canonical: two functions are equal if and only if their ROBDDs are the same graph — equality is a pointer comparison. The catch is order sensitivity: for the comparator f=(a1=b1)∧⋯∧(an=bn)f = (a_1{=}b_1)\wedge\dots\wedge(a_n{=}b_n) the order a1b1a2b2…a_1 b_1 a_2 b_2\dots gives 3n+23n+2 nodes, while a1…anb1…bna_1\dots a_n b_1\dots b_n needs about 3⋅2n3\cdot 2^n.

D12Proving the netlist equals the RTL: equivalence checking

Simulation shows the netlist matches the RTL for the vectors you tried. Logic equivalence checking (LEC — Cadence Conformal, driven by the write_do_lec file from Step 6.3) proves it for all inputs:

  1. Map key points. Pair every flop and primary output in the RTL with its counterpart in the netlist (by name, then by structure).
  2. Build a miter for every pair of next-state functions ff (golden) and gg (revised): M(x)=f(x)⊕g(x)M(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) \oplus g(\mathbf{x}).
  3. Prove unsatisfiability. f≡g  ⟺  ∄ x:M(x)=1f \equiv g \iff \nexists\,\mathbf{x}: M(\mathbf{x}) = 1, decided with BDDs or a SAT solver.

A satisfying x\mathbf{x} is a concrete counter-example. Because flops are matched first, only combinational clouds are compared — that is why scan insertion (which changes flops into scan flops) needs the extra constraints written into the dofile.

D13Pipelining, throughput and latency

Split logic of delay tlogict_{\text{logic}} into NN balanced stages separated by registers with overhead tov=tcq+tsut_{ov} = t_{cq} + t_{su} (plus skew/uncertainty):

TN=tlogicN+tov,throughput=1TN,latency=N TN=tlogic+N tovT_N = \frac{t_{\text{logic}}}{N} + t_{ov}, \qquad \text{throughput} = \frac{1}{T_N}, \qquad \text{latency} = N\,T_N = t_{\text{logic}} + N\,t_{ov}

The speed-up saturates:

S(N)=T1TN=tlogic+tovtlogic/N+tov  →  N→∞    tlogic+tovtovS(N) = \frac{T_1}{T_N} = \frac{t_{\text{logic}} + t_{ov}}{t_{\text{logic}}/N + t_{ov}} \;\xrightarrow{\;N\to\infty\;}\; \frac{t_{\text{logic}} + t_{ov}}{t_{ov}}

For the example the ceiling is 9.5/0.5=19×9.5/0.5 = 19\times, but N=3N = 3 already gives 9.5/3.5=2.7×9.5/3.5 = 2.7\times while latency grows from 9.5 to 10.5 ns. Retiming (Leiserson–Saxe) moves existing registers across logic instead of adding them: give each node a lag r(v)r(v); edge register counts become wr(e)=w(e)+r(v)−r(u)≥0w_r(e) = w(e) + r(v) - r(u) \ge 0. The number of registers around any cycle is invariant, so the circuit’s function is preserved while its critical path changes.

D14Adders: from ripple carry to parallel prefix

The counter is an adder in disguise (it adds 1), and adders are the most studied circuits in VLSI because their carry chain is usually the critical path. For two nn-bit numbers aa, bb, define per bit:

gi=ai bi    (generate),pi=ai⊕bi    (propagate),ci+1=gi+pi ci,si=pi⊕cig_i = a_i\,b_i \;\;\text{(generate)},\qquad p_i = a_i \oplus b_i \;\;\text{(propagate)},\qquad c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i\,c_i,\qquad s_i = p_i \oplus c_i

Generate means “this bit creates a carry by itself” (both inputs 1). Propagate means “this bit passes an incoming carry along” (exactly one input is 1). The sum bit is the propagate bit XOR the incoming carry.

Ripple carry: simple and slow

Evaluating ci+1=gi+picic_{i+1} = g_i + p_i c_i bit after bit lets the carry ripple through all nn positions: delay O(n)\mathcal{O}(n), area O(n)\mathcal{O}(n). For 64 bits that is 64 gate delays.

Carry look-ahead: unroll the recurrence
c2=g1+p1g0+p1p0c0,c3=g2+p2g1+p2p1g0+p2p1p0c0c_2 = g_1 + p_1 g_0 + p_1 p_0 c_0, \qquad c_3 = g_2 + p_2 g_1 + p_2 p_1 g_0 + p_2 p_1 p_0 c_0

Every carry can be computed directly from the ggs and pps in two logic levels — but the expressions grow quickly, so in practice they are applied to groups of 4 bits.

Parallel prefix: the clever generalisation

Treat each bit as a pair (G,P)(G, P) and define a combining operator for two adjacent groups (left = more significant):

(G,P)∘(G′,P′)=(G+P G′,    P P′)(G, P) \circ (G', P') = \bigl(G + P\,G',\;\; P\,P'\bigr)

In words: the combined group generates a carry if the left part generates one, or if the left part propagates a carry generated by the right part; it propagates only if both parts do. The operator is associative, so the nn bits can be combined in a balanced tree of depth ⌈log⁡2n⌉\lceil\log_2 n\rceil instead of a chain:

ARCHITECTURELOGIC DEPTHPREFIX CELLSTRADE-OFF
Ripple carrynnnnsmallest, slowest
Brent–Kung2log⁡2n−12\log_2 n - 1≈2n\approx 2nfew cells, low fan-out
Kogge–Stonelog⁡2n\log_2 nnlog⁡2n−n+1n\log_2 n - n + 1fastest, many wires

Back to the counter. Adding 1 means b=0b = 0 and c0=1c_0 = 1, so gi=0g_i = 0, pi=cip_i = c_i (the counter bit), and the carry into bit ii is ∏j<icj\prod_{j \lt i} c_j — exactly the toggle condition derived in D1. When the clock is tight, synthesis turns the incrementer’s AND chain into a prefix tree; at 100 MHz it has no reason to, so the ripple form (the ADDHX1 chain in the gates report) is kept.

Remember
  • Slack = required − arrival. Negative = violation.
  • Setup depends on the clock period; hold does not.
  • Unconstrained paths are invisible failures — lint first, then trust slack.
2.0

Open RTL Compiler from a fresh Bash terminal

Why this stepRC keeps a live database you can query after the script ends; knowing its prompt and GUI saves time when reports surprise you.

  1. Open Applications → System Tools → Terminal.
  2. Type bash if the prompt is not already Bash.
  3. Go to the lab directory and source the college setup file. You must source it once in every new terminal.
  4. Start the graphical shell. Wait for the rc:/> command prompt in the terminal (RC's command line stays in the terminal; the GUI window is a viewer) before continuing.
Terminal · shellbash
cd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
source setup_cadence.sh
which rc
rc -gui &

Try two commands at the rc:/> prompt to get a feel for the tool. RC stores everything (libraries, designs, settings) in a virtual directory tree you can browse like a file system:

rc:/> prompt · Tclls /
help synthesize

Inside RTL Compiler, File → Source runs a Tcl script interactively. For a repeatable run you will normally use the command shown in Step 2.2 instead. Type exit at the prompt to quit.

Do not use rc -version as a health check on this VM — it crashes with a segmentation fault after identifying itself (Step 0.1 D). rc -gui, rc -nogui and rc -files … are the commands used in this lab. If RC also crashes when it starts normally, use the fallbacks listed in Step 0.1’s troubleshooting box (LANG=C rc …).
If which rc prints nothing, stop here. The environment setup did not load, the path in setup_cadence.sh is wrong, or the tool is not installed. Go back to Step 0.1's troubleshooting box. Do not compensate by hard-coding random executable paths.
What you should see
  • The terminal shows a banner Cadence Encounter(R) RTL Compiler with version v12.10-s012_1 and then the prompt rc:/>.
  • ls / lists designs, libraries, hdl_libraries, messages and others — RC’s virtual directory tree.
2.1

Write constraints before optimizing

Why this stepWithout constraints the synthesis tool has no target and the timing reports are meaningless.

Synthesis without constraints is meaningless: the tool has no target, so it cannot tell a "fast enough" circuit from a broken one. The SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) file is the contract between you and every timing-driven tool that follows — RC, Encounter and signoff all read the same constraints. The clock defines the timing budget. Input/output delays reserve time for logic outside this block. Uncertainty reserves margin for skew and jitter.

Create the file · shellgedit constraints/cnt_updown.sdc &
constraints/cnt_updown.sdc · SDC# ---------- Clock: 10 ns period = 100 MHz, on input port clk ----------
create_clock -name core_clk -period 10.000 [get_ports clk]
set_clock_uncertainty 0.20 [get_clocks core_clk]

# ---------- Inputs: arrive 1 ns after the clock edge (outside logic uses it) ----------
set_input_delay  1.00 -clock core_clk [get_ports {enable up_down reset}]

# ---------- Outputs: must be valid 1 ns before the next edge ----------
set_output_delay 1.00 -clock core_clk [all_outputs]

# ---------- Electrical environment of the boundary ----------
set_input_transition 0.10 [get_ports {enable up_down reset}]
set_load 0.05 [all_outputs]

# ---------- Asynchronous reset is not a timed single-cycle path ----------
set_false_path -from [get_ports reset]
COMMANDWHAT IT TELLS THE TOOLUNITS
create_clockA periodic clock exists on port clk. Every flop clocked by it is checked against this period.ns (from the .lib)
set_clock_uncertaintySubtract 0.2 ns from each cycle for skew/jitter you do not model yet.ns
set_input_delayLogic outside this block already used 1 ns of the cycle, so inside paths get 10 − 1 − 0.2 = 8.8 ns.ns
set_output_delayLogic outside needs 1 ns after this block's output, so internal-to-output paths also get 8.8 ns.ns
set_input_transition / set_loadRealistic slew on inputs and capacitive load on outputs, so boundary cells are sized properly.ns / pF
set_false_pathDo not time paths from reset (it is asynchronous; its release is handled by a reset synchronizer in a real chip).—

Note: the clock port is deliberately not given an input delay — a clock is a reference, not data. That is why the ports are listed explicitly instead of using [all_inputs].

Edit the names. If the RTL uses rst_n rather than reset, change the constraint. A command that matches zero objects often leaves the design silently unconstrained — RC prints a warning such as Could not find port 'rst', which is easy to miss. Step 2.3 shows how to catch this.
What you should see
  • When RC reads the file (Step 2.2) the log shows Statistics for commands executed by read_sdc with every command counted, and no Could not find warnings.
  • report clocks later lists one clock, core_clk, period 10000 ps.
Troubleshooting — constraints that silently do nothing

get_ports clk returns nothing — the port name differs (e.g. clock). RC prints a warning, not an error, and every path becomes unconstrained. After reading the SDC, run report timing -lint (Step 2.3) and look for “unconstrained” endpoints.

Input delay applied to the clock port — the file above lists the data inputs explicitly. If you shorten it to [all_inputs], that collection includes clk itself; keep the explicit list (or use [remove_from_collection [all_inputs] [get_ports clk]]).

Units — RC reads SDC times in ns and capacitances in pF by default for this library; a 10 ps period written as 10 means 10 ns. Check with report clocks.

2.2

Read, elaborate, constrain and map

Why this stepThis converts behaviour into real library cells sized to meet the clock — the netlist every later stage builds on.

The only standard-cell library on your VM is the Encounter example kit GPDK045. Its slow corner — slow.lib, library name gpdk045bc, 1.08 V and 125 °C — gives the longest delays, so it is the right target for setup timing: if the design meets timing there, it meets it everywhere.

Create the script · shellgedit scripts/rtl_rc.tcl &
scripts/rtl_rc.tcl · Tcl# ================= RTL Compiler 12.10 synthesis: cnt_updown =================
set TOP  cnt_updown
set ROOT [file normalize .]
source scripts/lib_paths.tcl

file mkdir reports
file mkdir results

# ---- 1. Tool verbosity and library (slow corner: gpdk045bc, 1.08 V, 125 C) ----
set_attribute information_level 7 /
set_attribute hdl_search_path [list $ROOT/rtl] /
set_attribute library [list $LIB_SLOW] /

# ---- 2. Read and elaborate the RTL ----
read_hdl -v2001 [list rtl/cnt_updown.v]
elaborate $TOP
check_design -unresolved
check_design -all > reports/check_design.rpt

# ---- 3. Apply constraints and lint them ----
read_sdc constraints/cnt_updown.sdc
report timing -lint -verbose > reports/timing_lint.rpt
report clocks                > reports/clocks.rpt

# ---- 4. Synthesize in three passes ----
synthesize -to_generic -effort medium
synthesize -to_mapped  -effort medium
synthesize -incremental

# ---- 5. Reports ----
report gates  > reports/gates.rpt
report area   > reports/area.rpt
report timing > reports/timing.rpt
report power  > reports/power_vectorless.rpt
report qor    > reports/qor.rpt

# ---- 6. Outputs for the next tools ----
write_hdl  > results/cnt_updown_mapped.v
write_sdc  > results/cnt_updown_mapped.sdc
puts "==== RC synthesis of $TOP finished. Type 'exit' to quit. ===="
Check the file · shellwc -l scripts/rtl_rc.tcl        # must print 40
COMMANDWHAT HAPPENS
set_attribute libraryLoads the Liberty file: the menu of legal cells, their delays and power.
read_hdlParses the Verilog (syntax only).
elaborateBuilds the design hierarchy, infers flops, adders and muxes. After this the design is at /designs/cnt_updown.
check_designReports unresolved modules, undriven/multiply-driven nets, unloaded ports.
synthesize -to_genericTechnology-independent optimization (Boolean simplification).
synthesize -to_mappedMaps to real gsclib045 cells and optimizes for your SDC.
synthesize -incrementalExtra clean-up pass: fixes remaining violations, recovers area.
write_hdl / write_sdcGate-level netlist and constraints rewritten for that netlist — the inputs to Encounter.

ARun it

Run · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
rc -files scripts/rtl_rc.tcl -logfile logs/rc_synth.log
# RC stops at the rc:/> prompt when the script ends. Inspect, then:
#   exit

To run the same script and look at the result graphically, start rc -gui -files scripts/rtl_rc.tcl -logfile logs/rc_synth_gui.log &. In the GUI, the HDL Viewer/Schematic tabs show the mapped gates.

What you should see
  • The log ends with ==== RC synthesis of cnt_updown finished ==== and no Error lines.
  • results/cnt_updown_mapped.v contains cell instances such as DFFRHQX1, ADDHX1, XOR2XL, MXI2XL (exact names depend on optimization).
  • reports/gates.rpt lists roughly 25–45 cells including 8 sequential cells.
Troubleshooting — RC errors

Error : Could not find library file — $LIB_SLOW in scripts/lib_paths.tcl is wrong. Run ls on the path; fix it.

Error : The design 'cnt_updown' was not found — elaborate failed earlier; scroll up for the first error (usually a Verilog syntax problem).

Warning : Port ... not found while reading SDC — a name in the SDC does not match the RTL. Fix the SDC; never ignore this warning.

"Cannot check out license" — the license file/server variable in Step 0.1 is wrong.

What changes physically

Operators become gates, muxes and flops. Cell selection creates real area, pin capacitance, leakage and delay. Wires are still estimates (a statistical wire-load model); placement and routing do not exist yet, so timing is optimistic-to-approximate.

  1. Half-adder cells: RC recognised count + 1 and built an incrementer chain (Chapter 2, D1–D2).
  2. Exactly 8 resettable flip-flops — one per bit. Check this number first.
  3. Total cell area in µm² — the areas here are the real GPDK045 footprints from gsclib045.lef (e.g. DFFRHQX1 = 4.8 × 1.71 µm = 8.208 µm²). This is the AcellsA_{\text{cells}} that, divided by utilization, sets the core size in Step 4.5.

2.3

Read the reports as evidence (and fix what they reveal)

Why this stepReports are only trustworthy if every path is constrained and no unintended hardware (latches, loops) was inferred.

Work through the reports in this exact order. Each one guards against a different silent failure.

1Timing lint — is every path actually constrained?

Open the lint report · shellless reports/timing_lint.rpt     # q to quit, / to search
cat  reports/clocks.rpt

The lint report is a list of categories, each followed by a count and the objects in it. A correct run of this lab shows 0 in every category except possibly "inputs with no clocked fanout" for reset (expected — it is a false path). Here is what each category means and exactly how to fix it:

LINT CATEGORYWHAT IT MEANSHOW TO FIX IT
Sequential clock pins without clock waveformFlip-flops whose clock pin is not reached by any create_clock. Their timing is not checked at all.Run report clocks. If it is empty, create_clock failed — usually the port is named differently (CLK, clock). Check with ls /designs/cnt_updown/ports_in in RC and fix the get_ports name in the SDC.
Inputs without clocked external delaysA data input has no set_input_delay, so its paths are untimed.Add the port to the set_input_delay list. Never add one to the clock port itself.
Outputs without clocked external delaysAn output has no set_output_delay.Make sure [all_outputs] is used, or list the bus as [get_ports count*].
Unconstrained / timing exceptions with no effectA set_false_path or similar matched nothing.The object name is wrong; check spelling against the RTL.
Multiple clocks on a pin / generated clocksNot expected in this single-clock design.Remove duplicate create_clock lines.

After editing the SDC, rerun the whole script (Step 2.2) — RC does not reread a changed file automatically. Repeat until the lint report is clean.

2Log scan — did synthesis infer something you did not intend?

Search the log for structural problems · shellgrep -inE "latch|unresolved|multiple driver|combinational loop|undriven|black ?box" logs/rc_synth.log
grep -c  -i  "^Error" logs/rc_synth.log
less reports/check_design.rpt
  • Inferred latch — an if without else or a case without default in a combinational block. Fix the RTL by assigning every output in every branch. (This counter has none.)
  • Unresolved reference — a submodule file was not read. Add it to read_hdl.
  • Multiple drivers — two always blocks assign the same signal. Merge them.
  • Combinational loop — an output feeds back to its own input without a flop. Break it with a register.

3Timing report — does the design meet 100 MHz?

Read the worst path · shellless reports/timing.rpt

The report shows the single worst path: a start point (a flop clock pin or an input), every cell it passes through with its incremental delay, and an end point (a flop D pin or an output). The last lines compare Required Time with Data Arrival. Slack = required − arrival. A positive slack (several ns here) means the path is fast enough; a negative slack (marked VIOLATED) means it is not.

If slack were negative: first confirm the constraints are sensible (a 1 ns period would be unrealistic for this library). Then try synthesize -to_mapped -effort high, or relax the period. Do not "fix" timing by deleting constraints.

4Area, gates and QoR

Open reports/gates.rpt and reports/area.rpt. Count the sequential cells: there must be exactly 8 (one per count bit). Fewer means bits were optimized away (check that outputs are really connected); more means unwanted registers.

5Confirm the cells come from the right library

In the GUI use Tools → Object Browser, expand libraries, and confirm only one library — gpdk045bc, i.e. slow.lib — is loaded and the netlist cells belong to it. From the command line:

rc:/> prompt · Tclls /libraries
report gates -summary

g214/Y              NAND2X1        2  3.1  61    84   365 R
g209/Y              NOR2X1         1  1.9  58    77   442 F
g201/Y              XNOR2X1        1  1.6  49   131   573 R

  1. The library used — gpdk045bc is the library name inside slow.lib (operating condition slow: 1.08 V, 125 °C). It must be the slow corner for setup analysis.
  2. Wires are estimated by a wire-load model (Chapter 2 theory, D7).
  3. Columns: Fanout and Load are what the cell drives; Slew its output transition; Delay this stage; Arrival the running total.
  4. The launching clock edge at time 0 — the start of the path (an Rising edge).
  5. Clock-to-Q of the launching flop: tcqt_{cq} = 281 ps. Each following line adds one gate of tcombt_{\text{comb}}.
  6. The endpoint (<<<): data arrives at 573 ps = tcq+tcombt_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}.
  7. The setup requirement of the capturing flop: 112 ps.
  8. The capturing edge one period later (10 000 ps) minus 200 ps uncertainty → 9 800 ps.
  9. Slack = 9 800 − 112 − 573 = 9 115 ps. Positive → met. Notice it is exactly the setup inequality from the theory card.
CheckpointLint is clean, no latches/unresolved/multi-driver messages, 8 sequential cells, positive slack, and results/cnt_updown_mapped.v plus .sdc exist.
2.4

Re-simulate the mapped netlist (gate-level simulation)

Why this stepProves synthesis preserved function; any mismatch here is far cheaper to fix than after layout.

Synthesis tools are very reliable, but your constraints and RTL style can still produce a netlist that behaves differently (a classic example is an RTL simulation/synthesis mismatch from an incomplete sensitivity list). The rule is simple: the same self-checking testbench must pass on the gates.

AUse the generated cell models

The netlist instantiates library cells; the simulator needs a Verilog model for each one. The GPDK045 kit ships none (Step 0.2), so you generated libs/gsclib045_cells.v from slow.lib in Step 0.5. Check that every cell type in the netlist has a model, then simulate.

Every netlist cell must have a model · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
source setup_cadence.sh
CELL_VLOG=libs/gsclib045_cells.v
ls -l $CELL_VLOG                                    # created in Step 0.5
for c in $(grep -oE "^ *[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+ " results/cnt_updown_mapped.v | sort -u); do
  grep -qE "^module $c[ (;]" $CELL_VLOG || echo "NO MODEL: $c"
done; echo "model check done"
Zero-delay functional gate simulation · shellirun -v2001 -access +rwc -nospecify -notimingchecks \
  -timescale 1ns/1ps \
  -logfile logs/irun_gate.log \
  $CELL_VLOG results/cnt_updown_mapped.v tb/tb_cnt_updown.v

grep -E "PASS|FAIL|ERROR" logs/irun_gate.log
  • -nospecify -notimingchecks ignore the cell delays; this run checks function only. Real delays are added after routing (Step 7.2).
  • -timescale 1ns/1ps supplies a default for the RC netlist, which has no `timescale (the generated model file declares its own).
  • The RTL file is not on the command line: the mapped netlist replaces it (both define module cnt_updown).
Troubleshooting — gate-level simulation

*E,CUVMUR: instance of module/UDP 'DFFRHQX1' is not defined — $CELL_VLOG is empty in this terminal (set it again) or Step 0.5 was skipped. grep -c "^module DFFRHQX1" libs/gsclib045_cells.v must print 1.

All count bits are x — usually a flop without reset in the netlist, or reset not reaching it. Check that the netlist flops have an RN/R pin connected to reset (or its inverse).

"Duplicate module cnt_updown" — you passed both RTL and netlist. Remove the RTL file.

What you should see
  • The model check prints only model check done (no NO MODEL: lines).
  • The log lists libs/gsclib045_cells.v being compiled (hundreds of module worklib.…:v lines), then the netlist, then the testbench.
  • PASS: 32 cycle checks matched, final count = 3 and $finish at 350 NS — identical to the RTL run. (This exact flow — models generated by the script, a mapped netlist, this testbench — was checked before publishing and prints the same PASS line.)
CheckpointEvery sequential element is mapped, timing paths are constrained, and the gate-level simulation prints the same PASS line as the RTL simulation.
