Q1Slowing the clock (larger T) can fix…

T appears only in the setup inequality; hold must be fixed by adding delay to short paths.

Q2A port name in the SDC is misspelt. The most likely effect is…

Commands that match zero objects only warn; the timing-lint report is how you catch it.

Q3STA runs in time linear in the design size because…

AT(v) = max over fan-in of AT(u)+d(u,v) — each edge is visited once per pass.

Q4In the STA forward pass, a gate’s arrival time is the…

For setup, the output is not final until the latest input has arrived.

⚠ Common mistakes in this chapter
  • Port names in the SDC that do not match the RTL — the constraint silently does nothing.
  • Putting set_input_delay on the clock port.
  • Trusting the slack before reading the lint report.
  • Editing the SDC but not rerunning the whole RC script.
  • Simulating the netlist and the RTL together (duplicate module).

CHAPTER 3

Generate activity and estimate early power

Goal: replace guessed toggle rates with behavior from simulation.
You start withThe RTL snapshot and the mapped netlist
You end withactivity/dut.tcf and an activity-annotated power report
Toolsncsim, rc
Time≈ 30 min
THEORYWhere the power goes in CMOS≈ 8 min read

T1Three kinds of power

COMPONENTCAUSEDEPENDS ON
SwitchingCharging and discharging wire + pin capacitanceActivity, C, V², f
Internal (short-circuit)Inside a cell during a transition both transistor stacks conduct briefly; internal nodes switchActivity, input slew
LeakageTransistors never fully turn offCell type, temperature, V — not activity

RC calls switching + internal together dynamic power.

T2Where α·C·V²·f comes from

Pswitching = α · C · VDD² · f
α = fraction of clock cycles in which the net switches (0…1)
Worked example: α = 0.5, C = 2 fF, V = 0.9 V, f = 100 MHz → 0.5 × 2×10⁻¹⁵ × 0.81 × 10⁸ = 8.1×10⁻⁸ W = 81 nW for one net. A chip has millions of nets.

T3Activity is the term you can measure

C comes from the library and layout, V and f from the spec — but α depends on the workload. A counter shows this beautifully: bit 0 toggles every cycle, bit 1 every other cycle, bit 7 almost never.

  • Toggle rate — how many transitions per unit time (or per clock).
  • Static probability — fraction of time the net is 1. Leakage of some cells depends on it.

T4Activity file formats

FORMATCONTENTTYPICAL USE
VCDEvery change with its time (big)Waveforms, time-based (dynamic) power
TCFPer net: toggle count + probability (small)Cadence average power (this lab)
SAIFSame idea as TCFSynopsys tools (Chapter 8)

T5The levers designers pull

LEVEREFFECT
Lower VDDQuadratic saving, but cells get slower
Clock gatingStops α on idle registers (the “Clock Gating Awareness” option in Chapter 4)
Smaller cells / shorter wiresLower C
High-Vt cellsLess leakage, slower — used on non-critical paths
DEEP DIVE deriving the power equation

D1Energy drawn from the supply in one 0→1 transition

While the output charges from 0 to VDDV_{DD}, the supply delivers current i(t)=C dVdti(t) = C\,\frac{dV}{dt} at constant voltage VDDV_{DD}:

Esupply=∫0∞VDD i(t) dt=VDD∫0VDDC dV=C VDD2E_{\text{supply}} = \int_0^{\infty} V_{DD}\, i(t)\,dt = V_{DD}\int_0^{V_{DD}} C\,dV = C\,V_{DD}^2

The energy that ends up stored on the capacitor is

Estored=∫0VDDC V dV=12 C VDD2E_{\text{stored}} = \int_0^{V_{DD}} C\,V\,dV = \tfrac12\,C\,V_{DD}^2

The other 12CVDD2\tfrac12 C V_{DD}^2 is dissipated as heat in the PMOS resistance — independent of how large that resistance is. On the 1→0 transition the stored half is dissipated in the NMOS. Net result: one full charge/discharge cycle costs CVDD2C V_{DD}^2.

D2From energy to average power

If the node makes a 0→1 transition in a fraction α0→1\alpha_{0\to1} of the ff clock cycles per second:

Psw=α0→1 C VDD2 fP_{\text{sw}} = \alpha_{0\to1}\, C\, V_{DD}^2\, f

Watch the convention. Tools often count toggles (both 0→1 and 1→0). With toggle rate τ\tau (toggles per cycle), α0→1=τ/2\alpha_{0\to1} = \tau/2, so Psw=12 τ C VDD2 fP_{\text{sw}} = \tfrac12\,\tau\,C\,V_{DD}^2\,f. Many textbooks write 12αCV2f\tfrac12 \alpha C V^2 f for this reason — both are the same physics.

D3The counter’s total activity — a neat result

While counting continuously, bit ii toggles once every 2i2^i cycles, so τi=2−i\tau_i = 2^{-i}. Summing over all nn bits:

∑i=0n−1τi=∑i=0n−12−i=2(1−2−n)  →  n→∞    2\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \tau_i = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} 2^{-i} = 2\left(1 - 2^{-n}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\;n\to\infty\;}\; 2

An nn-bit binary counter flips on average fewer than two bits per clock, no matter how wide it is — 1.992 for 8 bits. A flat default guess of, say, τ=0.2\tau = 0.2 on every one of the 8 outputs would predict 1.6 toggles per cycle and put them in the wrong places (too many on the high bits, too few on bit 0). That is the quantitative reason the TCF changes the report.

D4Leakage is exponential

Below threshold a transistor still conducts a sub-threshold current:

Isub=I0 eVGS−Vthn vT(1−e−VDS/vT),vT=kTq≈26 mV at 300 KI_{\text{sub}} = I_0\, e^{\frac{V_{GS} - V_{th}}{n\,v_T}}\left(1 - e^{-V_{DS}/v_T}\right), \qquad v_T = \frac{kT}{q} \approx 26\,\text{mV at } 300\,\text{K}

With n≈1.5n \approx 1.5, lowering VthV_{th} by just n vTln⁡10≈90 mVn\,v_T \ln 10 \approx 90\,\text{mV} increases leakage 10×. Temperature raises vTv_T and lowers VthV_{th}, so leakage climbs steeply when the chip is hot. This is why libraries offer high-VthV_{th} cells (slower, far less leaky) and why leakage reports must state the corner.

D5Try it: dynamic power calculator

Notice the V2V^2: dropping from 0.9 V to 0.8 V saves 21 %, more than a 20 % frequency reduction would.

D6Short-circuit power and why slew limits exist

While the input of an inverter ramps between VtV_t and VDD−VtV_{DD} - V_t, both transistors conduct and current flows straight from supply to ground. For a symmetric inverter with input rise/fall time trt_r (Veendrick’s result):

Psc=β12 (VDD−2Vt)3 trT  =  β12 (VDD−2Vt)3 tr fP_{sc} = \frac{\beta}{12}\,(V_{DD} - 2V_t)^3\,\frac{t_r}{T} \;=\; \frac{\beta}{12}\,(V_{DD} - 2V_t)^3\, t_r\, f

Short-circuit power grows linearly with input slew. Slow edges waste energy as well as time — one reason libraries and tools enforce a max_transition design rule (the DRV column in optDesign reports). Note also: if VDD<2VtV_{DD} \lt 2V_t the term vanishes, as both devices can never be on together.

D7Clock power and clock gating

The clock toggles every cycle (τ=2\tau = 2, α0→1=1\alpha_{0\to1} = 1), so the clock network is often 30–50 % of dynamic power:

Pclk=(Ctree+Nff Cck pin) VDD2 fP_{\text{clk}} = \bigl(C_{\text{tree}} + N_{\text{ff}}\,C_{\text{ck pin}}\bigr)\,V_{DD}^2\,f

If a group of registers is idle a fraction gg of the time, an integrated clock-gating cell stops their clock in those cycles, saving roughly gg of their clock-pin and local-tree power (minus the gating cell’s own power). For this counter, enable is exactly such a signal: synthesis could gate the 8 flops’ clock with it instead of using a mux to hold the value.

D8Glitches: activity that does nothing useful

If two inputs of an XOR change at the same clock edge but arrive Δ\Delta apart, the output goes 0 → 1 → 0: two extra transitions, real CV2CV^2 energy, no logical effect. The effective activity is

αeff=αfunctional+αglitch\alpha_{\text{eff}} = \alpha_{\text{functional}} + \alpha_{\text{glitch}}

A glitch survives only if Δ\Delta exceeds the gate’s inertial delay (Chapter 1, D6). Glitch power is worst in deep arithmetic (adders, multipliers) where path depths differ, and is reduced by path balancing or by registering intermediate results. Zero-delay RTL simulation sees no glitches at all — another reason post-layout, delay-annotated activity gives a better power estimate.

D9Energy per operation and the stack effect

For computation, energy per operation matters more than power:

Eop=Pfop=∑nets kαk Ck VDD2  +  PleakfopE_{\text{op}} = \frac{P}{f_{\text{op}}} = \sum_{\text{nets } k} \alpha_k\,C_k\,V_{DD}^2 \;+\; \frac{P_{\text{leak}}}{f_{\text{op}}}

The dynamic part is independent of frequency; the leakage part grows as the clock slows (each operation takes longer while leakage keeps flowing) — so running too slowly also wastes energy. Leakage itself is reduced by the stack effect: two series OFF transistors leak much less than one, because the intermediate node rises a little, making VGSV_{GS} of the upper device negative and reducing its VDSV_{DS} — both enter the leakage equation exponentially (D4).

Remember
  • Dynamic = α·C·V²·f; leakage ignores activity.
  • Simulation gives α; without it, power is a guess.
  • Pre-layout power is for comparison, not signoff.
3.1

Understand the activity path

Why this stepUnderstanding the data flow tells you which file feeds which number in the power report.

The report power you ran in Step 2.2 was vectorless: RC assumed a default toggle rate for every net, so the dynamic-power number is a guess. To make it realistic you record how often each net really toggles while running a representative workload, save it as a TCF (Toggle Count Format) file, and give that to RC. TCF records toggle rate and static probability for each net. RTL Compiler combines activity with cell power tables and the clock definition.

Read the diagram left to right: the testbench drives the design in NCSim, a Tcl command (dumptcf) counts toggles inside the DUT, and RTL Compiler reads the resulting TCF together with the library and constraints to produce the power report.

The core equation

Dynamic power is approximately αCV²f. TCF supplies activity α (how often a net switches per clock); Liberty supplies cell capacitance/power and the supply voltage V; the constraints supply frequency f. Leakage power is independent of activity and comes straight from the Liberty tables.

3.2

Run NCSim and dump the DUT activity

Why this stepReal switching activity replaces a guess, and it must come from the DUT, not the testbench.

AWrite the TCF script

The VT course gives you a script called dumptcf.tcl. Here is a complete version for this testbench. It starts counting toggles inside dut only (not the testbench), runs the simulation to just before $finish (the testbench finishes at 350 ns, so the script stops at 345 ns), and writes the file.

dumptcf.tcl · NCSim Tcl# Count toggles of every net inside the DUT and write them to a TCF file.
# The testbench calls $finish at 350 ns, so stop at 345 ns and close the file first.
dumptcf -scope tb_cnt_updown.dut -output activity/dut.tcf -overwrite
run 345 ns
dumptcf -end
puts "TCF written to activity/dut.tcf"
Save it in the project root · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
gedit dumptcf.tcl &

Why stop at 345 ns? $finish runs at 350 ns and ends the simulator; commands after it in the script would never run, and the TCF would not be closed (a run 370 ns would hit $finish first). Stopping 5 ns earlier captures the whole workload — the last counting edge is at 335 ns.

BOpen NCSim in GUI mode on the snapshot from Step 1.5

NCSim · shellncsim -gui worklib.tb_cnt_updown:v
# use the snapshot name ncelab printed (e.g. :module) if :v is not found

SimVision opens attached to a live simulation, stopped at time 0. The Console window at the bottom has an ncsim> prompt where Tcl commands are typed.

CSource the script in the console

Click in the ncsim> console and type the command below, then press Enter. The script runs reset, idle, up-count, down-count and rollover intervals — all the phases from Step 1.1 — so the activity is representative.

NCSim console · Tclsource dumptcf.tcl

The console prints the TCF message and the current simulation time (345 ns). Close SimVision afterwards, then inspect the file:

Check the TCF · shellls -l activity/dut.tcf
head -40 activity/dut.tcf
What a good TCF looks like

A header with duration, then an instance("tb_cnt_updown.dut") block listing nets such as "count[0]" : "… …" (toggle count and probability). count[0] toggles most; count[7] only a couple of times — exactly what a counter should do.

Troubleshooting — empty or missing TCF

File not created — the simulation ended before dumptcf -end (the console shows Simulation complete via $finish); keep the run time below 350 ns. Also make sure the activity/ folder exists.

Scope not found — the snapshot was elaborated without -access +rwc, or the instance path is different. Type scope -list in the console to see the exact names.

Checkpointactivity/dut.tcf exists and its hierarchy corresponds to the DUT instance—not only the testbench clock generator.
3.3

Annotate activity in RTL Compiler

Why this stepAnnotating activity is what makes the dynamic-power figure meaningful enough to compare design versions.

Rerun synthesis exactly as before, but read the TCF before reporting power. Create a small wrapper script so the original stays untouched:

scripts/rc_power.tcl · Tcl# Re-run the full synthesis script, then annotate real activity and report power
source scripts/rtl_rc.tcl

read_tcf -instance tb_cnt_updown.dut activity/dut.tcf
report power         > reports/power_tcf.rpt
report power -verbose > reports/power_tcf_verbose.rpt
puts "==== Power with simulation activity written to reports/power_tcf.rpt ===="
Run and compare · shellrc -files scripts/rc_power.tcl -logfile logs/rc_power.log
#   (type exit at the rc:/> prompt)
grep -iE "asserted|annotat" logs/rc_power.log
diff reports/power_vectorless.rpt reports/power_tcf.rpt

In the GUI you can see the same result through the power-estimation view: the RC window shows the design with leakage, dynamic (internal + switching) and total power per instance.

How to read the comparison
  • The log reports the percentage of nets whose activity was asserted from the TCF. It should be close to 100 %.
  • Leakage is nearly identical in both reports (it does not depend on activity).
  • Dynamic power changes, because real toggle rates (high bits rarely toggle) replace the default guess.
Troubleshooting — 0 % of nets annotated

The -instance name must match the instance name written inside the TCF. Open the file (head activity/dut.tcf) and copy the exact string after instance(. Try in turn: -instance tb_cnt_updown.dut, -instance tb_cnt_updown/dut, -instance dut. The right one makes the annotation percentage jump.

This is not signoff power. The clock tree, routed capacitance, coupling, actual slew and IR drop do not exist yet. Use the result to compare versions and catch gross mistakes (e.g. a counter that is always enabled).

---------------------------------------------------------

CHAPTER 4

Physical implementation in Encounter 13.10

Goal: create a legal, powered, placed, clocked and routed layout.
You start withMapped netlist + SDC, LEF, Liberty, (QRC)
You end withA placed, clock-tree-built, routed and verified layout saved as cnt_updown_postRoute.enc
Toolsencounter, NanoRoute
Time≈ 2 h the first time
THEORYTurning a netlist into geometry≈ 18 min read · one section per stage, read each before its step

T1Floorplan anatomy → Steps 4.5–4.9

  • Die — the whole piece of silicon. Core — the inner area where standard cells go. Margin — space between them for the ring and pins.
  • Rows — horizontal slots exactly one cell high; each row is divided into sites (the smallest width step).
  • Utilization = total cell area ÷ core area. At 0.72, 28 % of the core stays empty for buffers, clock tree and routing detours.
Example: 40 cells totalling 72 µm² at 0.72 utilization → core area 100 µm² → a 10 µm × 10 µm square (aspect ratio 1).

T2Rows, rails and special cells → Steps 4.9, 4.10, 4.14

CELLWHY IT EXISTS
FillerKeeps the N-well, implant layers and power rails continuous across gaps (a broken well is a DRC error).
Tie-high / tie-lowGives a logic constant through a transistor instead of wiring a gate input straight to VDD/VSS (ESD and reliability).
DecapA capacitor between VDD and VSS that supplies charge locally during switching, reducing dynamic IR drop.

T3The metal stack → Steps 4.7, 4.8, 4.13

  • Alternating preferred directions (horizontal, vertical, …) let the router cross nets without collisions.
  • Lower metals are thin and dense: great for short local wires, but high resistance.
  • Top metals are thick: low resistance — so the power grid and clock use them. That is why the ring and stripes go on the top two layers.

On your VM: the diagram shows a generic ten-layer stack; gsclib045.lef has nine routing layers (Metal1 horizontal … Metal9 horizontal). Its top two layers are therefore Metal9 (horizontal) and Metal8 (vertical) — the layers used in Steps 4.7–4.8.

T4The power grid → Steps 4.6–4.9

pad / pinring (top metal)stripes (top metal)vias downfollow-pin rails (Metal1)cell VDD/VSS pins

Current flows from the supply down this chain. Every piece has resistance, so voltage is lost along the way (IR drop, Chapter 7). More/wider stripes = less drop but fewer tracks left for signals.

T5Placement → Steps 4.10–4.11

  1. Global placement — spreads cells to minimise total wire length, estimated as the half-perimeter of each net’s bounding box (HPWL). Cells that talk a lot end up close.
  2. Legalization — snaps every cell onto a row and site with no overlaps.
  3. Detailed placement — local swaps and shifts to improve further.

Encounter’s placer is timing-driven (pulls critical-path cells together) and congestion-driven (avoids packing too many nets in one area).

T6Clock tree synthesis → Step 4.12

Until now the clock was ideal. In reality one clk pin must drive every flop, through wires and buffers. CTS builds a balanced buffer tree.

  • Latency (insertion delay) — time from clock pin to a flop.
  • Skew — difference in latency between two flops. CTS minimises skew.
  • Skew enters the STA equations: if the capture flop’s clock is late, setup gets easier but hold gets harder — this is why hold is fixed only after CTS.

T7Routing → Step 4.13

  1. Global routing divides the chip into tiles (gcells) and decides which tiles each net passes through, balancing demand against available tracks.
  2. Track assignment picks actual tracks.
  3. Detailed routing draws exact wires and vias that obey every spacing/width rule.

Trial Route = a fast global-only estimate (for checking congestion). NanoRoute = the real global + detailed router.

T8Wires are resistors and capacitors → Steps 4.13, 7.1

  • Wire delay grows roughly with R × C, and both grow with length — so delay grows with length². Long nets get buffers inserted to break them up.
  • Capacitance to a neighbouring wire (Cc) means a switching neighbour can speed up, slow down or glitch your net: signal integrity (SI). “SI driven” routing spaces sensitive nets apart.
  • After routing, extraction computes these R and C values; that is when timing becomes accurate.

T9Why optDesign runs three times

STAGECLOCKWIRESMAINLY FIXES
pre-CTSIdealEstimated (from placement)Setup, max transition/cap/fanout
post-CTSReal treeEstimatedSetup and now hold
post-RouteReal treeExtracted R/CFinal setup/hold, SI
DEEP DIVE the algorithms and physics behind each stage

D1Sizing the die from utilization → Step 4.5

For total cell area AcellsA_{\text{cells}}, utilization UU, aspect ratio 1 and margin mm on each side:

acore=AcellsU,adie=acore+2ma_{\text{core}} = \sqrt{\frac{A_{\text{cells}}}{U}}, \qquad a_{\text{die}} = a_{\text{core}} + 2m
This lab: Acells≈72 μm2A_{\text{cells}} \approx 72\,\mu\text{m}^2, U=0.72U = 0.72 → acore=10 μma_{\text{core}} = 10\,\mu\text{m}. With m=100 μmm = 100\,\mu\text{m}: adie=210 μma_{\text{die}} = 210\,\mu\text{m}. The core is only (10/210)2≈0.2 %(10/210)^2 \approx 0.2\,\% of the die — that is why your floorplan looks like a speck inside a big empty square. Real chips use margins of a few µm around much larger cores.

D2How the placer decides where cells go → Step 4.11

The objective a placer optimises is wirelength. The exact measure for one net ee is the half-perimeter of its bounding box:

HPWL(e)=(max⁡p∈exp−min⁡p∈exp)+(max⁡p∈eyp−min⁡p∈eyp),W=∑eHPWL(e)\text{HPWL}(e) = \Bigl(\max_{p\in e} x_p - \min_{p\in e} x_p\Bigr) + \Bigl(\max_{p\in e} y_p - \min_{p\in e} y_p\Bigr), \qquad W = \sum_{e} \text{HPWL}(e)

HPWL has kinks (max/min), so analytical placers first minimise a smooth quadratic substitute where every two-pin connection i ⁣− ⁣ji\!-\!j acts like a spring of stiffness wijw_{ij}:

Φ(x)=12∑(i,j)wij (xi−xj)2⇒∂Φ∂xi=∑jwij(xi−xj)=0\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12 \sum_{(i,j)} w_{ij}\,(x_i - x_j)^2 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - x_j) = 0

Solving gives each movable cell at the weighted average of its neighbours; for all cells at once it is a sparse linear system Qx=bQ\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} (same for yy).

1-D example: a cell wired to a fixed pin at x=0x=0 (weight 1) and to one at x=10x=10 (weight 3, e.g. a critical net):
1⋅(x−0)+3⋅(x−10)=0⇒x=7.51\cdot(x-0) + 3\cdot(x-10) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 7.5. Raising the weight of timing-critical nets is exactly how “timing-driven” placement pulls critical cells together.

The quadratic solution piles cells in the middle, so the placer then spreads them to respect density, legalizes them onto rows and sites, and refines with local swaps.

D3Wire delay: the Elmore model, explained and worked

After routing, a net is a tree of wire segments, each with some resistance and some capacitance to ground. The Elmore delay is the standard way to turn that tree into one number per receiver. The rule is easy to say:

To find the delay to a node, go along the path from the driver to that node. For every resistor on the path, multiply its resistance by all the capacitance downstream of it (everything it has to charge). Add the products.

τi=∑k ∈ path(i)Rk  Cdown(k)\tau_i = \sum_{k \,\in\, \text{path}(i)} R_k \; C_{\text{down}}(k)

Why it works. Current to charge a capacitor must flow through every resistor between it and the driver, so a capacitor near the far end “sees” the whole path resistance, while one right at the driver sees almost none. Formally, τi\tau_i is the first moment (the mean) of the node’s impulse response — a good estimate of the time constant, and for a single RC it equals RCRC exactly.

Worked example. R1 is on the path to both sinks and has all three capacitors downstream: R1(C1+C2+C3)=100 Ω×45 fF=4.5R_1(C_1+C_2+C_3) = 100\,\Omega \times 45\,\text{fF} = 4.5 ps.
To sink A we also cross R2, which only charges C2: 200 Ω×20 fF=4.0200\,\Omega\times20\,\text{fF} = 4.0 ps → τA=8.5\tau_A = 8.5 ps.
To sink B we cross R3, which only charges C3: 150 Ω×15 fF=2.25150\,\Omega\times15\,\text{fF} = 2.25 ps → τB=6.75\tau_B = 6.75 ps.
Note that C3 slows down sink A too (through R1) even though it sits on the other branch — every load on a net costs every receiver something.
A uniform wire

Now let the tree be one straight wire of length LL with rr ohms and cc farads per unit length. Cut it into tiny slices of length dxdx. The slice at position xx has resistance r dxr\,dx, and everything beyond it — length L−xL - x — is downstream, capacitance c (L−x)c\,(L-x). Summing (integrating) the products:

τwire=∫0Lr c (L−x) dx=r c[Lx−x22]0L=r c L22\tau_{\text{wire}} = \int_0^L r\,c\,(L - x)\,dx = r\,c\left[Lx - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^L = \frac{r\,c\,L^2}{2}

Adding a driver of resistance RdR_d (which charges the whole wire and the receiving pin CLC_L) and the wire’s own charging of CLC_L:

τ=Rd (cL+CL)⏟driver+rcL22⏟wire itself+rL CL⏟wire charging the pin\tau = \underbrace{R_d\,(cL + C_L)}_{\text{driver}} + \underbrace{\frac{rcL^2}{2}}_{\text{wire itself}} + \underbrace{rL\,C_L}_{\text{wire charging the pin}}

The middle term is the important one: doubling a wire’s length quadruples its own delay, because both its resistance and its capacitance double. (For a 50 % delay rather than a time constant, multiply a lumped RC by 0.69 and a distributed wire’s rcL2/2rcL^2/2 by about 0.76, giving 0.38 rcL20.38\,rcL^2.)

D4Why tools insert buffers on long wires

The L2L^2 term means long wires get disproportionately slow. The cure is to cut the wire into kk equal pieces and put a buffer (repeater) in front of each piece. Each buffer costs a fixed delay tbt_b, but each piece is now only L/kL/k long, so its own delay is rc(L/k)2/2rc(L/k)^2/2:

t(k)=k tb⏟buffers+k⋅rc2(Lk)2⏟k short wires=k tb+rcL22kt(k) = \underbrace{k\,t_b}_{\text{buffers}} + \underbrace{k\cdot\frac{r c}{2}\left(\frac{L}{k}\right)^2}_{k\ \text{short wires}} = k\,t_b + \frac{r c L^2}{2k}

More buffers make the first term grow and the second shrink. The best kk is where the curve bottoms out — set the derivative to zero:

dtdk=tb−rcL22k2=0    ⇒    k∗=Lrc2 tb\frac{dt}{dk} = t_b - \frac{r c L^2}{2k^2} = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; k^\ast = L\sqrt{\frac{r c}{2\,t_b}}

Substituting back, both terms become equal (a sign the balance is optimal) and

t(k∗)=2 k∗tb=L2 rc tbt(k^\ast) = 2\,k^\ast t_b = L\sqrt{2\,r c\,t_b}

With optimal buffering, delay grows linearly with length instead of quadratically.

Rule of thumb: the critical length beyond which buffering pays is where rcL2/2≈2tbrcL^2/2 \approx 2t_b. In 45 nm on mid-level metal it is a few hundred microns — this counter has no wire that long, so optDesign adds few or no buffers. A large chip has thousands.

D5IR drop along a rail — and why stripes help → Step 4.8

Model a cell rail of length LL (resistance rr per unit length) drawing uniform current jj per unit length, fed with VDDV_{DD} at both ends. Current conservation and Ohm’s law give

d2Vdropdx2=− r j,Vdrop(0)=Vdrop(L)=0    ⇒    Vdrop(x)=r j2 x (L−x)\frac{d^2 V_{\text{drop}}}{dx^2} = -\,r\,j, \quad V_{\text{drop}}(0) = V_{\text{drop}}(L) = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; V_{\text{drop}}(x) = \frac{r\,j}{2}\,x\,(L - x)

The worst point is the middle: Vdropmax⁡=r j L2/8V_{\text{drop}}^{\max} = r\,j\,L^2/8. Fed from one end only, the worst drop is r j L2/2r\,j\,L^2/2 — four times worse.

D6Clock skew, formally → Step 4.12

With ℓi\ell_i the clock latency to flop ii:

skew=max⁡iℓi−min⁡iℓi,local skew(L ⁣→ ⁣C)=ℓC−ℓL=δ\text{skew} = \max_i \ell_i - \min_i \ell_i, \qquad \text{local skew}(L\!\to\!C) = \ell_C - \ell_L = \delta

Only local skew between flops that talk to each other enters the setup/hold inequalities of Chapter 2. CTS minimises global skew because it bounds every local one. In an ideal H-tree all ℓi\ell_i are equal by symmetry, so skew is zero.

D6bJitter and the clock-uncertainty budget

Skew is a spatial difference — two flops see the same edge at different times. Jitter is a temporal variation — the edges themselves are not perfectly evenly spaced, because of noise in the PLL that generates the clock and supply noise in the clock buffers.

MEASUREDEFINITIONMATTERS FOR
Period jitterTn−TnominalT_n - T_{\text{nominal}}: how much one cycle differs from idealsetup (a short cycle steals time)
Cycle-to-cycle jitterTn+1−TnT_{n+1} - T_nPLL quality specification
Long-term jitterdrift of edge nn from its ideal timeI/O interfaces

For a single-cycle setup check, the danger is the shortest possible cycle, so the effective period is T−tjitT - t_{\text{jit}}. Hold is checked on one edge, and jitter largely cancels (the same edge launches and captures). Independent random jitter sources add in quadrature:

σjit,total=σPLL2+σbuffers2+⋯,tjit≈k σjit,total    (k≈6–7)\sigma_{\text{jit,total}} = \sqrt{\sigma_{\text{PLL}}^2 + \sigma_{\text{buffers}}^2 + \cdots}, \qquad t_{\text{jit}} \approx k\,\sigma_{\text{jit,total}}\;\;(k \approx 6\text{–}7)

This is what set_clock_uncertainty represents. Before CTS it must cover both future skew and jitter (the 0.2 ns in your SDC). After CTS the real skew is computed from the tree, so good practice is to reduce the uncertainty to jitter only — otherwise skew is counted twice and the design is over-constrained.

D7Congestion as a number → Step 4.13

Each gcell edge gg has a capacity cap(g)\text{cap}(g) = number of routing tracks crossing it (tile width ÷ track pitch, summed over the layers in that direction) and a demand dem(g)\text{dem}(g) = nets the global router wants through it. The router minimises

overflow=∑gmax⁡(0, dem(g)−cap(g))\text{overflow} = \sum_{g} \max\bigl(0,\ \text{dem}(g) - \text{cap}(g)\bigr)

Overflow left after global routing becomes detours or DRC violations in detailed routing — the reason Trial Route is used as an early warning.

D8Crosstalk changes delay

A wire with ground capacitance CgC_g and coupling CcC_c to a neighbour behaves as if its capacitance were

Ceff=Cg+k Cc,k={0neighbour switches the same way1neighbour quiet2neighbour switches the opposite way (Miller effect)C_{\text{eff}} = C_g + k\,C_c, \qquad k = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{neighbour switches the same way} \\ 1 & \text{neighbour quiet} \\ 2 & \text{neighbour switches the opposite way (Miller effect)} \end{cases}

So one net’s delay is not a single number but a window. SI-aware timing (the -routeWithSiDriven option) accounts for the worst kk on critical nets and spaces them apart.

D9Rent’s rule: how wiring demand scales

Empirically, a block of GG gates has a number of external connections

T=t G p,0.5≲p≲0.75T = t\,G^{\,p}, \qquad 0.5 \lesssim p \lesssim 0.75

where tt is the average pins per gate and pp the Rent exponent. Donath showed that for p>0.5p \gt 0.5 the average wire length in a good placement grows as G p−0.5G^{\,p-0.5} (in gate pitches). Bigger designs therefore need proportionally more long wires — the reason chips gained ever more metal layers and why top layers are reserved for long global nets.

D10Why utilization should not be pushed to 100 %

Routing demand in a region is roughly proportional to the pins in it. If a region has nn cells with kk pins each and the available tracks per unit area is fixed, raising utilization from U1U_1 to U2U_2 raises the local pin density by U2/U1U_2/U_1 while track supply stays constant. From 0.72 to 0.95 that is +32 % demand on the same tracks — congestion overflow (D7) appears quickly, and there is no room left for the buffers that optDesign inserts. 60–80 % is the usual range for standard-cell regions.

D11Partitioning: the Kernighan–Lin and Fiduccia–Mattheyses idea

Before or during placement the design is cut into halves to keep strongly connected cells together. For a cell aa in part A, let E(a)E(a) = edges to the other part, I(a)I(a) = edges inside its own part, and D(a)=E(a)−I(a)D(a) = E(a) - I(a). Swapping a∈Aa \in A with b∈Bb \in B reduces the cut by

g(a,b)=D(a)+D(b)−2 c(a,b)g(a,b) = D(a) + D(b) - 2\,c(a,b)

(the c(a,b)c(a,b) term corrects for an edge between them, which stays cut). KL repeatedly makes the best swap, locks the moved cells, and keeps the best prefix of the sequence; Fiduccia–Mattheyses moves single cells with bucket lists in linear time per pass. Encounter’s placer uses recursive partitioning and analytical methods built on these ideas.

Example: cell aa has 3 nets to part B and 1 inside A → D(a)=2D(a) = 2. Cell bb has 2 nets to A and 0 inside B → D(b)=2D(b) = 2. They share one net: g=2+2−2=2g = 2 + 2 - 2 = 2. The cut shrinks by 2.

D12Simulated annealing: accepting bad moves on purpose

Greedy improvement gets stuck in local minima. Annealing accepts a move that worsens the cost by ΔC\Delta C with probability

P(accept)=min⁡ ⁣(1,  e−ΔC/Tk),Tk+1=λ Tk(0.8<λ<0.99)P(\text{accept}) = \min\!\left(1,\; e^{-\Delta C / T_k}\right), \qquad T_{k+1} = \lambda\,T_k \quad (0.8 \lt \lambda \lt 0.99)

High “temperature” early on lets the placement escape local minima; as T→0T\to 0 it becomes greedy. It is slow but robust, and was the workhorse of classic placers (TimberWolf); modern tools use it for local refinement.

D13Maze routing (Lee’s algorithm) and Steiner trees

Detailed routing of one connection is a shortest-path search on a grid. Lee’s algorithm expands a breadth-first wavefront from the source, labelling each free cell with its distance, then backtraces from the target along decreasing labels. It always finds a shortest path if one exists, in O(MN)\mathcal{O}(MN) for an M×NM\times N grid. Try it — click cells to add blockages:

S = source, T = target · click a cell to toggle a blockage

A multi-pin net needs a rectilinear Steiner minimum tree (RSMT) — extra “Steiner” points may be added. Useful bounds:

HPWL  ≤  RSMT  ≤  RMST  ≤  32 RSMT\text{HPWL} \;\le\; \text{RSMT} \;\le\; \text{RMST} \;\le\; \tfrac32\,\text{RSMT}

HPWL equals the RSMT for nets of 2 or 3 pins, which is why it is such a good placement estimate; the minimum spanning tree (RMST) is never more than 50 % worse than the optimum (Hwang’s theorem). Finding the exact RSMT is NP-hard, so routers use fast near-optimal constructions.

D14Clock skew scheduling as a system of inequalities

Zero skew is not always best. For every launch–capture pair i→ji \to j with path delays dijmax⁡,dijmin⁡d^{\max}_{ij}, d^{\min}_{ij} (including tcqt_{cq}), the setup and hold conditions of Chapter 2 become constraints on the clock arrival times ℓ\ell:

ℓi−ℓj  ≤  T−dijmax⁡−tsu,ℓj−ℓi  ≤  dijmin⁡−th\ell_i - \ell_j \;\le\; T - d^{\max}_{ij} - t_{su}, \qquad \ell_j - \ell_i \;\le\; d^{\min}_{ij} - t_h

Every inequality has the form xv−xu≤cuvx_v - x_u \le c_{uv} — a difference constraint. Draw an edge u→vu \to v of weight cuvc_{uv} for each; the system is feasible if and only if this constraint graph has no negative cycle, and Bellman–Ford finds a solution (or the cycle) in O(∣V∣∣E∣)\mathcal{O}(|V||E|). Binary-searching on TT gives the minimum clock period achievable with useful skew — which can be shorter than with zero skew when path delays are unbalanced.

D15Wire resistance in practice: sheet resistance

A wire of resistivity ρ\rho, thickness tt, width WW and length LL:

R=ρ LW t=R□ LW,R□=ρt    [Ω/□]R = \frac{\rho\,L}{W\,t} = R_\square\,\frac{L}{W}, \qquad R_\square = \frac{\rho}{t}\;\;[\Omega/\square]

Resistance depends only on the number of “squares” L/WL/W. Thick top metals have small R□R_\square, which is why power stripes live there.

Example: 100 µm of a 0.07 µm-wide Metal1 at R□=0.2 Ω/□R_\square = 0.2\,\Omega/\square: 100/0.07≈1430100/0.07 \approx 1430 squares → 286 Ω. With about 0.2 fF/µm the wire has 20 fF, so its own Elmore delay is 12⋅286⋅20 fF≈2.9\tfrac12\cdot286\cdot20\,\text{fF} \approx 2.9 ps — negligible here, but it grows with L2L^2: at 1 mm it would be ≈ 290 ps.

D16Latch-up, well taps and end caps

A CMOS inverter does not only contain two transistors. The p+ source of the PMOS, the n-well, the p-substrate and the n+ source of the NMOS form a four-layer PNPN stack — two parasitic bipolar transistors wired in a positive-feedback loop (a thyristor):

Normally both are off. But if a disturbance (an I/O overshoot, a radiation strike, a supply glitch) injects current into the substrate or well, it flows through the well or substrate resistance and raises the local potential. If that voltage drop reaches about 0.7 V it forward-biases a base–emitter junction:

Iinj⋅Rwell≳0.7 Vandβnpn βpnp≥1    ⇒    latch-upI_{\text{inj}} \cdot R_{\text{well}} \gtrsim 0.7\,\text{V} \quad\text{and}\quad \beta_{\text{npn}}\,\beta_{\text{pnp}} \ge 1 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{latch-up}

Once triggered, each transistor keeps the other on; a low-resistance path from VDD to VSS forms and stays until power is removed — often destroying the chip.

The cure is to keep RwellR_{\text{well}} and RsubR_{\text{sub}} small, so no realistic current can build up 0.7 V. That is done with frequent well taps (n+ contacts tying the n-well to VDD and p+ contacts tying the substrate to VSS). Since the resistance grows with distance to the nearest tap, the PDK sets a maximum spacing:

Rwell∝dtap⇒dtap≤dmax⁡    (typically 15–60 μm)R_{\text{well}} \propto d_{\text{tap}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad d_{\text{tap}} \le d_{\max}\;\;(\text{typically } 15\text{–}60\,\mu\text{m})

Older libraries put taps inside every cell. Most modern libraries are “tapless”: standalone tap cells must be placed in a regular checkerboard before standard-cell placement (Encounter: addWellTap), and end-cap cells close each row to protect the well edges. Step 4.10 shows how to check whether your library needs them.

Remember
  • Floorplan → power grid → place → CTS → route → optimize, each with more realism.
  • Top metals carry power and clock; Metal1 rails feed the cells.
  • Hold is only meaningful once the real clock tree exists.
ImportFloorplanGlobal netsRingStripesSpecial routePlaceCTSRouteOptimizeFillersSave
4.0

Open Encounter from the project directory

Why this stepLaunching from the project root makes every relative path in the scripts resolve correctly.

  1. Open a new terminal.
  2. Enter Bash, return to the project, and load the same Cadence environment.
  3. Confirm that the mapped netlist, SDC and physical libraries exist.
  4. Launch Encounter in the background so the terminal remains usable.
Terminal · shellbash
cd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
source setup_cadence.sh
ls results/cnt_updown_mapped.v results/cnt_updown_mapped.sdc
which encounter
encounter -log logs/encounter_gui.log &

Two things appear: the Encounter main window (a black layout canvas with menus File, Edit, View, Partition, Floorplan, Power, Place, Optimize, Clock, Route, Timing, Verify, Tools) and, in the terminal, the encounter 1> Tcl prompt. Every GUI action is echoed as its Tcl command in the terminal and in encounter.cmd — a free way to learn the commands used in Chapter 5.

Why launch from the project directory

Relative paths in Tcl, saved design databases and reports resolve from the directory that started Encounter. Starting elsewhere is a common reason a correct script suddenly cannot find its LEF, Liberty or SDC files.

What you should see
  • The Encounter window opens with a black canvas, a menu bar and a layer panel on the right.
  • The terminal shows the banner Encounter v13.10-p003_1 (32bit) and the prompt encounter 1>; every GUI action you take from now on is echoed there.

BEncounter GUI survival kit

Spend two minutes learning the window before importing anything. The canvas responds to single keys when the mouse is over it:

KEY / CONTROLWHAT IT DOES
fFit the whole design in the window
z / ZZoom in / zoom out (or right-drag a box to zoom into it)
Arrow keysPan
qShow the attributes of the selected object (net name, layer, cell, coordinates)
k / KDraw a ruler / clear all rulers — measure widths and spacings
Three view buttons (top right)Floorplan view (blocks and rows), Amoeba view (module areas), Physical view (every cell and wire)
Layer panel (right)Tick boxes to show/hide each layer and object type; toggle All Colors to isolate one metal
Bottom status barCursor coordinates in µm — useful to check margins and the ring position

If the drawing ever looks stale after a command, press f or use View → Redraw.

CheckpointBoth result files are listed, and the encounter 1> prompt is waiting.
4.1

Insert I/O pads and rename pad-side nets (course step — decide whether you need it)

Why this stepDecides whether your chip connects to the outside through pads or plain pins; the rest of the flow depends on it.

A real chip connects its core to the package through I/O pad cells: large cells with ESD protection and strong drivers that sit on the die edge. An input pad receives a package-side signal and drives a distinct core-side net. An output pad receives the core result and drives the package-side pin. The VT course edits the synthesized netlist by hand to add them. The first screenshot is the synthesized module before editing:

The second shows the same module after pad insertion: the top-level ports now connect to pad instances, and new internal nets (for example clk_core) connect each pad to the original logic.

ACheck whether your VM has a pad library

Look for I/O pad cells · shellfind $PDK45 $PDK45_TECH -iname "*pad*" -o -iname "*io*.lef" -o -iname "*io*.lib"
find /home/buet/cadence/EDI/share/FoundationFlows/EXAMPLES -iname "pdkIO*"
  • The first command prints nothing on your VM — the GPDK045 kit used in this lab has no pad cells. Do a core-only implementation: skip pad insertion, keep results/cnt_updown_mapped.v as-is, and Encounter places plain pins on the die boundary. Everything else in this chapter is identical. This is the path every script on this page uses.
  • The second command finds PROTO/…/GPDK045/lef/pdkIO.lef and timing/pdkIO.lib — an I/O library that belongs to Encounter’s separate prototyping example. It is not needed for this lab, and mixing an extra example library into the flow adds pad-ring and power-pad work that the course screenshots do not cover. Leave it alone.
Why rename constraints

After pad insertion, the old top-level port may be on the package side while the timed core endpoint has a new name. Update the SDC so delays attach to the intended boundary — otherwise Encounter reports "port not found" and your input/output delays silently vanish (the same trap as Step 2.3).

4.2

Prepare the MMMC view file, then import the design

Why this stepImport binds logical netlist, physical cells and timing views into one database.

AWrite the view definition (MMMC) file

Encounter 13 imports timing data through an MMMC (multi-mode multi-corner) file — the course calls it viewDefinition.view. It says which Liberty belongs to which corner, which SDC belongs to which mode, and which cap table models the wires. Create it now; the Import dialog loads it in Step 4.3, and the scripted flow in Chapter 5 reuses it. On your VM: setup uses slow.lib (gpdk045bc), hold uses fast.lib (gpdk045wc), and the RC corner uses $PDK45_TECH/capTable.

Create the file · shellgedit scripts/mmmc.tcl &
scripts/mmmc.tcl · MMMC view definition · Tcl# ---------- MMMC view definition for Encounter 13.10 ----------
source scripts/lib_paths.tcl

# Which SDC to time with: RC's functional SDC unless a caller (Step 6.5) chose another
if {![info exists SDC_FILE]} { set SDC_FILE results/cnt_updown_mapped.sdc }

# Library sets: one per corner
create_library_set -name LIB_SLOW -timing [list $LIB_SLOW]
create_library_set -name LIB_FAST -timing [list $LIB_FAST]

# Interconnect (RC) corner: the kit's cap table; the QRC tech file only if you enabled it
if {$QRC_TECH ne ""} {
  create_rc_corner -name RC_TYP -cap_table $CAPTBL -qx_tech_file $QRC_TECH
} else {
  create_rc_corner -name RC_TYP -cap_table $CAPTBL
}

# Delay corners = library set + RC corner
create_delay_corner -name DC_SLOW -library_set LIB_SLOW -rc_corner RC_TYP
create_delay_corner -name DC_FAST -library_set LIB_FAST -rc_corner RC_TYP

# Constraint mode = the SDC written by RTL Compiler
create_constraint_mode -name FUNC -sdc_files [list $SDC_FILE]

# Analysis views: slow corner for setup, fast corner for hold
create_analysis_view -name VIEW_SETUP -constraint_mode FUNC -delay_corner DC_SLOW
create_analysis_view -name VIEW_HOLD  -constraint_mode FUNC -delay_corner DC_FAST
set_analysis_view -setup [list VIEW_SETUP] -hold [list VIEW_HOLD]
Check the file · shellwc -l scripts/mmmc.tcl        # must print 28

BFill in the Basic tab of Import Design

In Encounter choose File → Import Design. On the Basic tab enter:

FIELDVALUENOTES
Verilog Netlist → Filesresults/cnt_updown_mapped.vThe course used its pad netlist cnt_updown_dve.v.
Top CellBy User: cnt_updownOr "Auto Assign" — explicit is safer.
Technology/Physical Libraries → LEF Files/home/buet/cadence/EDI/share/FoundationFlows/EXAMPLES/EDI/DESIGN/GPDK/LIBS/GPDK045/gsclib045.lefThe only LEF: it holds the technology section and all 487 cell macros, so there is no ordering to get wrong. Use the … button or paste the path.
Analysis Configuration → MMMC View Definition Filescripts/mmmc.tclReplaces separate timing-library and SDC fields in 13.x.

In the course screenshot the timing libraries and constraint file (cnt_updown_syn.sdc) are entered here directly; in Encounter 13 the MMMC file supplies the same information, so leave the separate timing fields empty if your dialog shows them.

Troubleshooting — Import Design fails or the design loads empty

“ERROR: Cannot find cell … in LEF” — the LEF field is empty or points somewhere else. It must be exactly …/GPDK045/gsclib045.lef; every cell RC can use is in that one file.

“The view definition file … could not be sourced” — a Tcl error inside scripts/mmmc.tcl. Source it on its own in the Encounter console (source scripts/mmmc.tcl) to see the exact line; the usual cause is an empty $LIB_SLOW because lib_paths.tcl was not sourced first.

Top cell not found — the module name in the netlist differs from the Top Cell field (e.g. the course’s updown_counter). Use grep "^module" results/cnt_updown_mapped.v and type exactly that name.

Timing reports later say “no constrained paths” — the SDC path in create_constraint_mode is wrong or relative to a different directory. Encounter must be started from the project root (Step 4.0).

How the pieces fit The MMMC file is a small dependency tree: library sets (Liberty per corner) + an RC corner → delay corners; the SDC → a constraint mode; mode + delay corner → an analysis view. Setup is then checked in the slow view and hold in the fast view. Every later timing report names one of these views, so knowing the tree lets you read any report header.
CheckpointEvery path in the dialog points to an existing file (no red text, no "file not found" in the terminal when you browse).
4.3

Define power, MMMC and extraction (Advanced tab)

Why this stepPower nets, timing views and extraction models must be declared before any physical or timing step can run.

Still in Import Design, switch to the Advanced tab. It has a list of categories on the left; set three of them.

1Power

Select Power. Set Power Nets = VDD and Ground Nets = VSS. These match the power pins of every gsclib045 macro (the report shows PIN VDD … USE POWER and PIN VSS … USE GROUND on TIEHI, FILL1, INVX1, DFFRHQX1 …; check with grep -m4 "PIN VDD\|PIN VSS" $PDK45/gsclib045.lef).

2MMMC

Select MMMC. If the view-definition field is not already filled from the Basic tab, load scripts/mmmc.tcl here (the course loads viewDefinition.view).

3RC Extraction

Select RC Extraction (if your dialog shows it — with an MMMC file the RC corner already carries the same data). Set the Capacitance Table File to /home/buet/cadence/EDI/share/FoundationFlows/EXAMPLES/EDI/DESIGN/GPDK/TECH/capTable (= $CAPTBL) and leave the QRC Technology File empty (the course points to its TSMC 65 nm qrcTechFile).

Why not the QRC file? $PDK45_TECH/qrcTechFile describes an 11-metal stack (its strings mention Metal10 and Metal11) while gsclib045.lef has nine; it only works together with mapFile and the integrated QRC engine, and it is 201 MB. The cap table is made for this kit and is what Encounter’s native extractor uses (setExtractRCMode -effortLevel low). If you want to experiment later, set QRC_TECH in lib_paths.tcl to $TECH45/qrcTechFile; scripts/mmmc.tcl then adds it to the RC corner.

Three different models

Liberty models cell delay and power. LEF models abstract geometry. QRC models interconnect resistance and capacitance. They must describe the same process and metal stack.

What you should see
  • Each of the three Advanced categories shows your values when you click it again.
  • No red text in the file fields (red = file not found).
4.4

Save the import configuration and inspect the initial floorplan

Why this stepSaving the configuration makes re-imports one click; inspecting the import log catches missing cells early.

  1. At the bottom of the Import Design dialog click Save… and save the settings as default.conf in the project directory. Next time you can click Load… and pick this file instead of retyping everything.
  2. Click OK. Watch the terminal: Encounter reads the LEF, the netlist, the MMMC file and the SDC.
  3. Inspect the loaded rows, pads and core boundary in the main window. Use View → Fit (key F) to fit the design.

The screenshot shows the course design right after import: a default floorplan with the pads around the edge and the unplaced standard cells stacked to the left of the core. In your core-only design you see only the core box with the cells beside it — that is normal; nothing has been placed yet.

Scan the import messages · shellgrep -nE "\*\*ERROR|\*\*WARN" logs/encounter_gui.log | head -40
Troubleshooting — import errors

**ERROR: (ENCVL-…) cell 'XYZ' not defined in LEF — the netlist uses a cell that has no physical view. Either a LEF is missing from the list, or synthesis used a library that does not match the LEF. Both must come from $PDK45.

Cannot find port 'xxx' while reading SDC — the SDC refers to a name not in this netlist. Use results/cnt_updown_mapped.sdc, not the RTL-level SDC.

Layers missing / "no routing layers" — the technology LEF was not first in the list, or was omitted.

  2. The top cell you named — a wrong name here means nothing else will match.
  3. Every netlist instance was matched to a timing cell. Any “unresolved” count must be zero.

CheckpointAll instances exist, pads are visible when used, and the tool reports no missing routing layers.
4.5

Size the core

Why this stepThe floorplan fixes the area every later step works inside; utilization trades wire length against routability.

Choose Floorplan → Specify Floorplan. The course uses a square core, 0.72 utilization, and 100 units of core-to-boundary spacing on all sides. Enter:

FIELDVALUEMEANING
Specify BySize → Core Size by: Aspect RatioLet utilization decide the size.
Ratio (H/W)1.0Square core.
Core Utilization0.7272 % of row area filled by cells; 28 % left for buffers, CTS and routing detours.
Core Margins byCore to IO Boundary—
Core to Left / Right / Top / Bottom100 eachMicrons of empty space around the core for the power ring and pins.
Everything elsedefault—
Equivalent Encounter TclfloorPlan -site CoreSite -r 1.0 0.72 100 100 100 100

Click OK. The die outline grows, the core box appears in the middle with horizontal standard-cell rows, and the I/O pins (or pads) move to the boundary:

Sanity check: hover over the core corners — the bottom-left status bar shows coordinates. The gap between core and die edge should read 100 µm on each side. For this counter (≈124 µm² of cells at 72 %) the core is only about 13–14 µm on a side — about eight rows of 1.71 µm — so the margin dominates the ≈214 µm die; that is fine for a lab.

Physical effect

Higher utilization shortens some wires but removes space for legalization, clock buffers and routing detours. The margin holds power rings and I/O connections.

What you should see
  • The die outline (outer box) and core boundary (inner box) appear with horizontal rows inside the core.
  • The unplaced cells still sit to the left of the die — placement has not happened yet.
  • The terminal echoes floorPlan -site CoreSite -r 1 0.72 100 100 100 100 — CoreSite (0.2 × 1.71 µm) is the only site in gsclib045.lef.
Troubleshooting — floorplan

“site not found” — the LEF did not load (check the import log); the site name must be exactly CoreSite.

Rows overlap the ring area later — the margins are too small for the ring width + spacing + offset; keep margins ≥ 2 × (width + spacing) + offset.

Core looks tiny inside the die — expected for this 28-cell design with 100 µm margins — see Chapter 4, D1.

4.6

Connect global VDD and VSS

Why this stepCells’ power pins are not in the netlist; without this step nothing is powered.

Each standard cell has its own VDD and VSS pins, but the netlist from synthesis does not connect them (logical netlists usually omit power). This step tells Encounter that every cell's VDD pin belongs to the global net VDD, and likewise for ground. Choose Power → Connect Global Nets and add two rules:

  1. Rule 1: select Pins; Pin Name(s) = VDD; Instance Basename = *; To Global Net = VDD. Click Add to List.
  2. Rule 2: Pin Name(s) = VSS; Instance Basename = *; To Global Net = VSS. Click Add to List.
  3. (Recommended) Rule 3/4: select Tie High → To Global Net VDD, Add to List; Tie Low → VSS, Add to List. This connects any constant logic 1/0 in the netlist.
  4. Click Apply, then Check, then Close.

Course dialog version. In the course’s release the dialog has a Pin Name(s) field, an Apply All check box and a To Global Net field: type VDD, tick Apply All (= every instance, the same as *), type VDD, Add to list; repeat for VSS; then Apply, Check, and close with Cancel.

Equivalent Encounter TclglobalNetConnect VDD -type pgpin -pin VDD -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type pgpin -pin VSS -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VDD -type tiehi -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type tielo -inst * -verbose
What "Check" prints

Lines like N pgpin(s) connected to net VDD with N equal to your cell count, and no "pin not found" warnings.

Troubleshooting — global nets

“Pin VDD not found” — your library names its power pins differently. Open one cell in the LEF (grep -A3 "PIN VDD\|PIN VPWR\|PIN vdd" $PDK45/gsclib045.lef | head — on your VM every macro uses VDD/VSS, so this message means a typo) and use those names in the Pin Name(s) field.

The count of connected pins is smaller than the instance count — rule 1 was added but not applied. Click Apply before Check; the list on the left is only a draft until applied.

Later, verifyConnectivity reports unconnected power pins on fillers or tie cells — those cells were added after this step. Rerun the same globalNetConnect lines after addFiller/addTieHiLo (the script in Chapter 5 does this at the end).

CheckpointThe global-net check reports that power and ground pins are attached to the intended nets.
4.7

Build the core power ring

Why this stepThe ring distributes current around the core with low resistance.

Use Power → Power Planning → Add Ring. A ring is a pair of wide metal loops (one VDD, one VSS) around the core.

FIELDCOURSE VALUE (65 nm)VALUE ON YOUR VM (GPDK045)
Net(s)VDD VSS (click … and pick both)
Ring TypeCore ring(s) contouring → Around core boundary
Layer Top / Bottom (horizontal)APMetal9 (= $H_LAYER; the top layer, HORIZONTAL)
Layer Left / Right (vertical)M6Metal8 (= $V_LAYER; the highest VERTICAL layer)
Width (all sides)3 µm
Spacing (all sides)4 µm
Offset → Specify3 µm

The course's AP/M6 do not exist in GPDK045, and the dialog's layer drop-downs only list layers from your LEF: Metal1 … Metal9. Step 0.2 showed Metal9 is horizontal and Metal8 vertical, so use Metal9 for top/bottom and Metal8 for left/right. (There is no Metal10 — an earlier draft of this lab used it, and Encounter would stop with “layer not found”.) Click OK.

Equivalent Encounter Tclsource scripts/lib_paths.tcl
addRing -nets {VDD VSS} -type core_rings -follow core \
  -layer [list top $H_LAYER bottom $H_LAYER left $V_LAYER right $V_LAYER] \
  -width   {top 3 bottom 3 left 3 right 3} \
  -spacing {top 4 bottom 4 left 4 right 4} \
  -offset  {top 3 bottom 3 left 3 right 3}
What you should see

Two concentric rectangles around the core, each 3 µm wide, 4 µm apart, starting 3 µm from the core edge. Click one and press q to see its net name.

Physical effect

The ring spreads current around the core perimeter and gives stripes multiple low-resistance paths to the pads. Wider metal reduces resistance but consumes routing area.

Troubleshooting — the ring

The layer drop-down offers no Metal10 — correct for this LEF; it ends at Metal9. Metal9 = horizontal, Metal8 = vertical (grep -A2 "^LAYER Metal" $PDK45/gsclib045.lef | grep DIRECTION).

“Ring is outside the die” / nothing appears — the offset + 2 × width + spacing (3 + 6 + 4 = 13 µm) must fit inside the 100 µm margin from Step 4.5. With a smaller margin, reduce width and spacing.

Only one ring appears — both nets must be selected in the Net(s) field (VDD VSS), otherwise Encounter builds a single loop.

4.8

Add horizontal and vertical stripes

Why this stepStripes shorten the path from supply to every cell, reducing IR drop.

Stripes are straight power wires crossing the core and connecting to the ring on both ends, so the middle of the core is not far from a supply. Open Power → Power Planning → Add Stripes and run it twice.

The course values (3 µm wide stripes every 15–20 µm) are for a much larger 65 nm core. Your core is ≈13.7 µm wide, so those values give no stripes at all. The YOUR VM column is sized so that two VDD/VSS pairs cross the core in each direction.

AHorizontal stripes

FIELDCOURSE (65 nm)YOUR VM (GPDK045)
Net(s)VDD VSSVDD VSS
Layer / DirectionAP, HorizontalMetal9 (= $H_LAYER), Horizontal
Width / Spacing3 / 51 / 1
Set Pattern → Set-to-set distance206
Stripe BoundaryCore ringCore ring
First/Last Stripe → Start from bottom, relative offset52 (start and stop offset)

Click Apply (not OK — you will reuse the dialog).

BVertical stripes

FIELDCOURSE (65 nm)YOUR VM (GPDK045)
Layer / DirectionM6, VerticalMetal8 (= $V_LAYER), Vertical
Width / Spacing3 / 51 / 1
Set-to-set distance156
Start from left, relative offset3.52 (start and stop offset)

Click OK.

Equivalent Encounter TcladdStripe -nets {VDD VSS} -direction horizontal -layer $H_LAYER \
  -width 1 -spacing 1 -set_to_set_distance 6 \
  -start_from bottom -start_offset 2 -stop_offset 2
addStripe -nets {VDD VSS} -direction vertical -layer $V_LAYER \
  -width 1 -spacing 1 -set_to_set_distance 6 \
  -start_from left -start_offset 2 -stop_offset 2

Are 1 µm stripes legal? Yes: the LEF spacing table for Metal8 asks for at most 0.25 µm between wires up to 1.5 µm wide, and 1 µm spacing is four times that. Width 1 µm is far above the 0.07 µm minimum.

After applying both directions, inspect the mesh rather than trusting the dialog:

Small-core note: with a 6 µm set-to-set distance you get two VDD/VSS pairs per direction (at about 2 µm and 8 µm from the core edge). If your core came out smaller and only one pair appears, that is not an error — the ring alone can feed a core this small. On a larger design the mesh looks like the screenshot.

Physical effect

Smaller stripe pitch shortens current paths and reduces IR drop, but blocks more signal-routing tracks. Power planning is a resistance-versus-congestion tradeoff.

What you should see
  • Straight vertical and horizontal metal lines across the core, connected to the ring at both ends.
  • Clicking a stripe and pressing q shows its net (VDD or VSS) and layer.
Troubleshooting — stripes

No stripes appear — you typed the course values (set-to-set 20 or 15), which are larger than the ≈13.7 µm core. Use 6.

“layer not found” — the layer must be Metal9 or Metal8; AP, M6 and Metal10 do not exist in gsclib045.lef.

Stripes block signal routing later — increase the pitch or move stripes to the top layers only.

4.9

Special-route the power network

Why this stepConnects the grid to each row’s rails — the last link from supply to cell.

So far the ring and stripes float in metal; nothing connects them to the cells. Choose Route → Special Route. This connects pads, rings, stripes, macro pins and standard-cell rails using power-routing rules.

  1. Net(s): VDD VSS.
  2. In SRoute, tick Block pins, Pad pins, Pad rings, Follow pins (the standard-cell rails — the most important one) and Floating stripes.
  3. Leave the other tabs at default and click OK.
Equivalent Encounter Tclsroute -connect {blockPin padPin padRing corePin floatingStripe} \
  -nets {VDD VSS}

Thin horizontal rails now run along every standard-cell row, alternating VDD and VSS, connected to the ring at both ends (and to stripes through vias where they cross).

What you should see
  • Thin horizontal rails appear along every row boundary, alternately connected to VDD and VSS.
  • The terminal reports the number of follow-pin wires created and 0 DRC violations for the special routes.
CheckpointNo standard-cell row is left without a continuous VDD/VSS rail connection. verifyConnectivity -nets {VDD VSS} reports no opens (dangling stripe ends on a tiny core are warnings, not opens).
4.10

Configure placement

Why this stepTells the placer which special cells exist (tie, filler) and how to treat clock gating.

0Before placement — does your library need well taps and end caps?

Modern “tapless” libraries require separate tap cells to prevent latch-up (Chapter 4 theory, D16). Check once:

Look for tap and end-cap cells · shellgrep -iE "^(TAP|WELLTAP|ENDCAP|CAP|FILLTIE)" logs/cell_names.txt logs/lef_macros.txt
grep -i -A3 "MACRO .*TAP" $PDK45/*.lef | head -20
  • Nothing found — this is what your VM prints: gsclib045.lef has no TAP, WELLTAP or ENDCAP macros (the report’s cell groups list only TIE, FILL, CLK*, BUF, INV, DFF/SDFF and ANTENNA). The well taps are built into every cell — skip this part.
  • A tap cell exists: insert a checkerboard of taps before placement, with the spacing from the PDK documentation (typical 20–60 µm):
Only if your library has a tap cell · TcladdEndCap  -preCap ENDCAP -postCap ENDCAP      ;# only if an end-cap cell exists
addWellTap -cell TAPCELL -cellInterval 30 -checkerBoard -prefix WELLTAP
verifyWellTap -cell TAPCELL -rule 15

Choose Place → Place Standard Cell. The Place dialog opens; do not click OK yet. Click its Mode… button to open Mode Setup. You set four tabs of Mode Setup in turn, exactly in the order of the course screenshots.

1Placement tab

Leave the defaults and additionally tick Enable Clock Gating Awareness. This keeps clock-gating cells close to the flops they control, which matters if synthesis inserted any.

2TieHiLo tab

Click Select. In the cell list choose the tie-high cell and click Add, then the tie-low cell and Add. The course library calls them TIEH/TIEL; gsclib045 calls them TIEHI/TIELO (both 0.6 µm wide, output pin Y). When both appear in the Selectable Cell List, click Close.

3Filler tab

Click Select. Add all seven gsclib045 fillers one by one: FILL64, FILL32, FILL16, FILL8, FILL4, FILL2, FILL1 (they exist only in the LEF, which is why they were missing from logs/cell_names.txt; FILL1 is one site, 0.2 µm, so every gap can be closed). Click Close and tick ECO route.

Equivalent Encounter Tcl (placement modes)setPlaceMode -clkGateAware true
setTieHiLoMode -cell $TIE_CELLS -maxFanout 8
setFillerMode -core $FILLERS -corePrefix FILL
Why tie cells exist

They generate safe constant logic values without directly tying a signal pin to the power rail (a gate oxide wired straight to VDD is an ESD/reliability risk). Filler candidates are selected now but inserted after routing (Step 4.14).

What you should see
  • The Mode Setup dialog keeps your choices when reopened (it applies to the whole session).
  • The terminal echoes setPlaceMode, setTieHiLoMode and setFillerMode commands — copy them into your script.
4.11

Configure CTS behavior, then place

Why this stepGives every cell a legal location and fixes timing with estimated wires.

Still in Mode Setup, open the CTS tab. It has sub-tabs; set them to match the three course screenshots.

1CTS → Trace

Controls how the tool traces the clock network from the clock root to the flops (which gates it may pass through and where it stops). Match the check-boxes in the screenshot; the defaults plus the shown options are fine for a single-clock design.

2CTS → Route/EM

Controls how clock nets are routed (clock nets are routed first, with preferred layers and double-width/spacing rules to reduce coupling) and electromigration checks on clock wires. Match the screenshot.

3CTS → Optimization

Controls post-CTS optimization: whether CTS may resize buffers/gates and whether it optimizes skew and insertion delay. Match the screenshot.

4Apply and place

  1. Click OK to apply and close Mode Setup.
  2. Back in the Place dialog, leave Include Pre-Place Optimization on and click OK.
  3. When placement finishes, run Place → Tie Hi/Lo Cell → Add (Tcl addTieHiLo) if the netlist has constants, then Optimize → Optimize Design with Design Stage: Pre-CTS, Optimization Type: Setup, OK.
Core placement · TclplaceDesign
addTieHiLo
checkPlace reports/checkPlace.rpt
optDesign -preCTS -outDir reports/preCTS
What you should see
  • The cells move into the rows inside the core (zoom in with right-drag).
  • optDesign ends with a summary table: WNS (worst negative slack) ≥ 0, TNS 0, violating paths 0, plus DRV counts (max_tran/max_cap/max_fanout) all 0.
  • reports/checkPlace.rpt reports 0 overlapping or unplaced instances.
Troubleshooting — placement

Negative WNS pre-CTS — check that the clock was found (report_clocks), then rerun optDesign -preCTS. For this tiny counter at 100 MHz a violation almost always means a constraint problem, not a hard path.

"Not enough space" — utilization is too high; redo the floorplan at 0.6.

ANNOTATED OUTPUToptDesign -preCTS summary (Encounter)illustrative — your exact numbers and names will differ
optDesign -preCTS summary (Encounter)------------------------------------------------------------
     optDesign Final Summary
------------------------------------------------------------
+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+
|     Setup mode     |   all   | reg2reg | in2reg  | reg2out |  [1]
+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+
|           WNS (ns):|  7.442  |  9.010  |  7.890  |  7.442  |  [2]
|           TNS (ns):|  0.000  |  0.000  |  0.000  |  0.000  |  [3]
|    Violating Paths:|    0    |    0    |    0    |    0    |
|          All Paths:|   24    |    8    |   16    |    8    |
+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+
+----------------+-------------------------------+------------------+
|                |              Real             |       Total      |
|    DRVs        +------------------+------------+------------------|
|                |  Nr nets(terms)  | Worst Vio  |  Nr nets(terms)  |  [4]
+----------------+------------------+------------+------------------+
|   max_cap      |      0 (0)       |   0.000    |      0 (0)       |
|   max_tran     |      0 (0)       |   0.000    |      0 (0)       |

  1. Path groups as in the STA theory: all paths, then by type.
  2. WNS = worst negative slack. Positive means even the worst path meets timing.
  3. TNS = sum of all negative slacks. 0 means no violations at all.
  4. DRVs (design-rule violations): electrical limits on capacitance, transition and fanout from the Liberty file. All must be 0.
  5. Placement density ≈ the utilization you chose in Step 4.5.
  6. Estimated routing overflow from the congestion model — 0 % means routing will be easy.
CheckpointAll standard cells are legal, congestion is acceptable, and pre-CTS timing has no unexplained unconstrained paths.
4.12

Synthesize the clock tree

Why this stepReplaces the ideal clock with a real buffered tree; from here hold timing becomes meaningful.

ACreate the clock-tree specification file

Until now the clock was ideal (it arrived everywhere at once). CTS builds a real buffer tree. It reads a specification file (.ctstch) listing which buffers it may use and the skew/latency targets. The course supplies Clock.ctstch; generate yours from your own library at the encounter> prompt:

Generate constraints/Clock.ctstch · Tclsource scripts/lib_paths.tcl
createClockTreeSpec -bufferList $CTS_BUFS -file constraints/Clock.ctstch
Inspect it · shellless constraints/Clock.ctstch

Inside you will find an AutoCTSRootPin clk section with targets such as MaxSkew, MaxDelay, SinkMaxTran, BufMaxTran and the Buffer list. The generated values are reasonable defaults; leave them for this lab.

BRun CTS from the GUI

Choose Clock → Synthesize Clock Tree. In the dialog click … beside the specification field, select constraints/Clock.ctstch, and click OK.

Afterwards view the tree with Clock → Display → Display Clock Tree. Then fix any timing that CTS disturbed with Optimize → Optimize Design, Design Stage Post-CTS, type Setup — and again with Hold.

Equivalent TclclockDesign -specFile constraints/Clock.ctstch -outDir reports/clock
optDesign -postCTS       -outDir reports/postCTS
optDesign -postCTS -hold -outDir reports/postCTS_hold

COptional — reduce clock uncertainty after CTS

Before CTS the 0.2 ns uncertainty in the SDC covered future skew plus jitter. Now that the real tree exists, its skew is computed exactly, and keeping the full 0.2 ns counts skew twice (Chapter 4 theory, D6b). Production flows lower the uncertainty to the jitter budget only:

Post-CTS uncertainty (MMMC-aware) · Tclset_interactive_constraint_modes [all_constraint_modes -active]
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.05 [all_clocks]
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.02 [all_clocks]
set_interactive_constraint_modes {}
report_clocks

For this lab either choice is fine — the counter has huge slack. Write down which you used, because it changes the WNS numbers you report.

Read the CTS report

reports/clock/ holds the CTS summary. Look for Nr. of Sinks: 8 (the eight flops), the number of buffers inserted, and Max Skew well below the 0.2 ns uncertainty you budgeted in the SDC.

Physical effect

CTS inserts and sizes clock buffers so insertion delay and skew are controlled. This adds cells, power, routing demand and new hold-time behavior — which is why hold is optimized only from this point on.

ANNOTATED OUTPUTCTS summary (reports/clock)illustrative — your exact numbers and names will differ
CTS summary (reports/clock)*** Clock Tree Synthesis summary ***
Clock tree root : clk                                              [1]
Nr. of Subtrees                : 1
Nr. of Sinks                   : 8                                 [2]
Nr. of Buffer                  : 2                                 [3]
Nr. of Level (including gates) : 2
Max trig. edge delay at sink(R): count_reg[3]/CK 214.6(ps)         [4]
Min trig. edge delay at sink(R): count_reg[6]/CK 207.9(ps)
                                 (Actual)        (Required)
Rise Phase Delay               : 207.9~214.6(ps) 0~10000(ps)
Max. Skew                      : 6.7(ps)          300(ps)          [5]
Max. Slew (Sink)               : 48.2(ps)         400(ps)          [6]
  1. Where the tree starts: the clk port.
  2. Sinks = clock pins of flops. It must equal your flop count (8).
  3. Buffers CTS inserted (from the -bufferList you gave).
  4. Latency to the slowest and fastest flop.
  5. Skew = 214.6 − 207.9 = 6.7 ps, far below the target — and below the 200 ps uncertainty budgeted in the SDC.
  6. Clock transition at the flops; slow clock edges increase tcqt_{cq} and short-circuit power.
Troubleshooting — clock tree synthesis

“No clock root found” — the SDC’s create_clock did not reach Encounter; check report_clocks and the MMMC constraint mode.

A buffer name in -bufferList is unknown — use only names from logs/cell_names.txt; the list in lib_paths.tcl (CLKBUFX2 … X12, CLKINVX1 … X8) was checked against your library.

Skew is large — check that all flops are on the same clock net and that no flop was left unplaced.

4.13

Trial-route, NanoRoute and optimize

Why this stepCreates the real wires; timing is now computed from extracted R and C.

  1. Route → Trial Route → OK. A fast, rough routing used only to expose congestion. Open View → Congestion (or the "density" layer toggles) — red hot-spots would mean the floorplan is too tight.
  2. Route → NanoRoute → Route. Leave Global Route and Detail Route ticked, tick Timing Driven and SI Driven, click OK. This produces the real, DRC-correct wires.
  3. Optimize → Optimize Design, choose Design Stage: Post-Route and Optimization Type: Setup and Hold, click OK. Timing is now calculated on extracted wires instead of estimates — Encounter extracts R and C with its native engine using $PDK45_TECH/capTable from the RC corner.
Equivalent TcltrialRoute
setNanoRouteMode -routeWithTimingDriven true -routeWithSiDriven true
routeDesign -globalDetail
setExtractRCMode -engine postRoute -effortLevel low   ;# native extractor + GPDK045 capTable
setAnalysisMode -analysisType onChipVariation
optDesign -postRoute       -outDir reports/postRoute
optDesign -postRoute -hold -outDir reports/postRoute_hold
timeDesign -postRoute       -outDir reports/timing_final
timeDesign -postRoute -hold -outDir reports/timing_final

The final routed layout (as in the screenshot) shows signal wires in several metal colours over the placed cells. Toggle layers on the right-hand Layer Control panel to see each metal separately.

How to read the timeDesign summary
  • Setup mode: WNS ≥ 0.000 and "Violating Paths: 0" for reg2reg, in2reg, reg2out.
  • Hold mode: same, using the fast corner (VIEW_HOLD).
  • DRVs: max_cap, max_tran, max_fanout all 0.
  • NanoRoute log: Total number of DRC violations = 0.
Troubleshooting — routing and post-route timing

DRC violations after NanoRoute — run routeDesign -globalDetail again (it repairs incrementally). Persistent violations near the ring usually mean the ring offset is too small.

Hold violations remain — hold needs the hold view to be active (check set_analysis_view in mmmc.tcl) and delay cells/buffers in the library — gsclib045 has DLY1X1 … DLY4X4 and BUFX2 … BUFX20.

setExtractRCMode rejects -effortLevel — drop the option; the default post-route engine uses the same cap table.

Unrouted nets — verifyConnectivity lists them; most often a pin is blocked by a power stripe. Delete the stripes over the core and rerun from Step 4.8 with a larger pitch.

timeDesign -postRoute -hold summary+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+
|     Hold mode      |   all   | reg2reg | in2reg  | reg2out |  [1]
+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+
|           WNS (ns):|  0.071  |  0.071  |  0.188  |   N/A   |  [2]
|           TNS (ns):|  0.000  |  0.000  |  0.000  |   N/A   |
|    Violating Paths:|    0    |    0    |    0    |   N/A   |
+--------------------+---------+---------+---------+---------+

  1. Hold uses the minimum-delay paths (min⁡\min in the STA recurrences).
  2. Small positive hold slack is normal: hold only needs to be ≥ 0, extra margin buys nothing.
  3. Must be the fast corner view — if it says VIEW_SETUP, hold is being checked at the wrong corner.
  4. Density grew slightly because CTS buffers and hold-fix cells were added.
CheckpointNo signal net is unrouted; setup and hold are checked against extracted post-route parasitics and both show WNS ≥ 0.
4.14

Add fillers, verify and save the database

Why this stepFillers make the layout manufacturable; verification and saving make the result reproducible.

AInsert fillers

Choose Place → Physical Cell → Add Filler. The cell list is pre-filled from the Filler tab of Step 4.10; check it, set the prefix to FILL, and click OK. Fillers close row gaps and preserve well/power-rail continuity (an N-well with gaps can fail DRC).

Every empty spot in the rows is now occupied — compare with Step 4.13's screenshot.

BVerify

Run Verify → Verify Connectivity (OK) and Verify → Verify Geometry (OK). Results go to the terminal and to violation markers in the Tools → Violation Browser.

CSave

Choose File → Save Design, Data Type Encounter, File Name results/cnt_updown_postRoute.enc (the course names it updown_counter_postRoute.enc). Encounter writes cnt_updown_postRoute.enc plus a folder cnt_updown_postRoute.enc.dat/; keep both together.

Fill, verify and save · TcladdFiller -cell $FILLERS -prefix FILL
globalNetConnect VDD -type pgpin -pin VDD -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type pgpin -pin VSS -inst * -verbose
verifyConnectivity -type all -error 1000 -warning 50 -report reports/connectivity.rpt
verifyGeometry -report reports/geometry.rpt
saveDesign  results/cnt_updown_postRoute.enc
saveNetlist results/cnt_updown_postRoute.v
What clean results look like

  1. Filler count — any non-zero number is fine; it depends on how many row gaps placement left. Zero means the filler cell names in $FILLERS are wrong.
