? Check yourself

Q1Doubling an unbuffered wire’s length multiplies its intrinsic delay by about…

Elmore delay rcL²/2 is quadratic in L — which is why long wires get repeaters.

Q2Why is hold timing only fixed after clock-tree synthesis?

Skew δ enters the hold inequality directly; with an ideal clock it is zero and the result would be wrong.

Q3Halving the power-stripe pitch reduces the worst rail IR drop by about…

Worst drop rjL²/8 with L = stripe pitch — quadratic.

⚠ Common mistakes in this chapter
  • Starting Encounter outside the project directory — relative paths break.
  • Using layer names from the course (AP, M6) — check the LEF.
  • Skipping Connect Global Nets — cells end up unpowered.
  • Fixing hold before CTS (meaningless with an ideal clock).
  • Adding fillers before routing, then wondering why routing has no space.
  • Forgetting setExtractRCMode -engine postRoute before post-route optimisation.

CHAPTER 5

Turn the GUI flow into reproducible Tcl

Use the GUI to learn; use Tcl to repeat and compare.
You start withThe GUI flow you completed in Chapter 4
You end withOne script that rebuilds the whole layout and exports SPEF/SDF/DEF/GDS
Toolsencounter (batch)
Time≈ 30 min
THEORYTcl in ten minutes — enough to read every script on this page≈ 10 min read

T1Why script at all

Clicking is how you learn; scripts are how you repeat. A script records every value, runs the same way tomorrow, can be diffed between versions, and runs without a display (-nowin). RC, Encounter and NCSim all speak Tcl.

T2The whole language in one table

SYNTAXMEANINGEXAMPLE
set name valueCreate / change a variableset TOP cnt_updown
$nameUse a variable’s valueelaborate $TOP
[command]Run a command, use its result[get_ports clk]
"…"Text; $ and [] inside are substituted"top is $TOP"
{…}Text taken literally — nothing substituted{VDD VSS}
list a b cBuild a list (substitutes inside)[list top $H_LAYER]
#Comment — only at the start of a command (use ;# after code);# ps
\ at line endCommand continues on next linelong addRing
source fileRun another Tcl file heresource scripts/lib_paths.tcl
Tcl warm-up you can type at any tool prompt · Tclset period 10.0
set cells {FILL64 FILL32 FILL16}
puts "Clock period is $period ns"             ;# variables expand inside "..."
puts {Clock period is $period ns}             ;# but NOT inside {...}
puts "Half period = [expr {$period / 2}] ns"  ;# [ ] runs a command
foreach c $cells { puts "filler: $c" }
if {[llength $cells] > 2} { puts "more than two fillers" }
proc banner {msg} { puts "==== $msg ====" }
banner "done"

Why the scripts use [list top $H_LAYER …] instead of {top $H_LAYER …}: braces would pass the literal text $H_LAYER to the tool. This is the #1 Tcl mistake.

T3Learning commands from the GUI

  • Encounter writes every GUI action as a Tcl command into encounter.cmd in the start directory. Click once, copy the command.
  • help addStripe (Encounter) or help define_dft (RC) prints every option your build supports.
  • RC stores the design as a virtual file system: ls /designs/cnt_updown, get_attribute on any object.

T4Debugging a script

  1. Find the first ERROR in the log — later errors are usually consequences.
  2. The tool stays at its prompt after a failure: fix, then paste the remaining lines block by block.
  3. Check variables with puts $VAR; a wrong path in lib_paths.tcl causes most failures.
DEEP DIVE writing your own helpers

D1How Tcl evaluates a line (the one rule)

Tcl reads a command, performs exactly one round of substitution — $var, [cmd], backslashes — except inside {…}, splits it into words, and calls the first word with the rest as arguments. Nothing is re-substituted afterwards. Every “strange” Tcl behaviour follows from this rule. For example, in if {$x > 2} {…} the braces delay substitution so that if itself evaluates the condition each time.

D2A helper that extracts WNS from every run

Comparing experiments (different utilization, different clock) is easier with a small procedure. Paste into scripts/helpers.tcl and source it in Encounter:

scripts/helpers.tcl · Tcl# Print the worst setup and hold slack of the current design state
proc slack_summary {tag} {
  set s [report_timing -late  -max_paths 1 -collection]
  set h [report_timing -early -max_paths 1 -collection]
  set ws [get_property $s slack]
  set wh [get_property $h slack]
  puts [format "%-12s  setup WNS = %8.3f ns   hold WNS = %8.3f ns" $tag $ws $wh]
}

# Count lines that contain a pattern in a report file
proc count_in_file {file pattern} {
  set fh [open $file r]; set n 0
  while {[gets $fh line] >= 0} { if {[regexp -- $pattern $line]} { incr n } }
  close $fh
  return $n
}
Using it at the encounter> prompt · Tclsource scripts/helpers.tcl
slack_summary preCTS
puts "geometry violations: [count_in_file reports/geometry.rpt {Viol}]"

If -collection / get_property are not supported in your build (check with help report_timing), fall back to timeDesign and read reports/*/…summary files with count_in_file.

D3Sweeping a parameter

A loop turns one experiment into a table — e.g. how utilization affects timing:

Utilization sweep sketch (batch Encounter) · Tclforeach util {0.60 0.72 0.85} {
  freeDesign
  source scripts/init_only.tcl            ;# import part of encounter.tcl
  floorPlan -r 1.0 $util 100 100 100 100
  # ... power grid + placeDesign + optDesign -preCTS as in encounter.tcl ...
  slack_summary "util=$util"
}
Remember
  • $ = value, [ ] = run, " " substitutes, { } does not.
  • encounter.cmd turns your clicks into a script.
5.1

Reuse the MMMC view

Why this stepThe same MMMC file in GUI and batch runs guarantees both are timed identically.

You already wrote scripts/mmmc.tcl in Step 4.2. The scripted flow uses the identical file, so the GUI run and the batch run time the design the same way. Re-read it once more and make sure you can answer three questions: which Liberty is used for setup (slow), which for hold (fast), and which SDC (the one written by RC).

scripts/mmmc.tcl (summary of what it defines)# LIB_SLOW / LIB_FAST     -> library sets
# RC_TYP                  -> interconnect model ($PDK45_TECH/capTable)
# DC_SLOW / DC_FAST       -> delay corners
# FUNC                    -> constraint mode (results/cnt_updown_mapped.sdc)
# VIEW_SETUP / VIEW_HOLD  -> analysis views used by optDesign / timeDesign
Why MMMC exists

One physical layout must work across operating modes and PVT corners. This teaching setup uses two corners; a production flow normally has several setup and hold corners and separate functional/test modes (e.g. a scan-shift mode with a slower clock).

5.2

Run the complete Encounter script

Why this stepA script turns two hours of clicking into a repeatable minutes-long run you can compare and archive.

This script is the whole of Chapter 4 in one file, in the same order, with the same values. Every line maps to a GUI step you already did, so you can debug it piece by piece. It ends by exporting everything signoff needs.

Create the script · shellgedit scripts/encounter.tcl &
Open the full Encounter 13.10 script (scripts/encounter.tcl, 111 lines)
scripts/encounter.tcl · Tcl# ================= Encounter 13.10 place-and-route: cnt_updown =================
# VARIANT func (default) implements results/cnt_updown_mapped.v (Chapters 4-5);
# VARIANT scan implements the scan netlist from Chapter 6 (set by encounter_scan.tcl).
if {![info exists VARIANT]} { set VARIANT func }
set TOP cnt_updown
source scripts/lib_paths.tcl
if {$VARIANT eq "scan"} {
  set NETLIST  results/${TOP}_scan.v
  set SDC_FILE results/${TOP}_scan.sdc
  set TAG      ${TOP}_scan
  set R        reports/scan
} else {
  set NETLIST  results/${TOP}_mapped.v
  set SDC_FILE results/${TOP}_mapped.sdc
  set TAG      ${TOP}
  set R        reports
}
file mkdir reports results $R

# ---- 4.2-4.4  Import ----
set init_top_cell  $TOP
set init_verilog   $NETLIST
set init_lef_file  $LEF_FILES
set init_mmmc_file scripts/mmmc.tcl
set init_pwr_net   VDD
set init_gnd_net   VSS
init_design
if {$VARIANT eq "scan"} {
  defIn results/${TOP}_scan.scandef          ;# scan-chain description from RC (Step 6.3)
}

# ---- 4.5  Floorplan: square, 72 % utilisation, 100 um margins, gsclib045 site ----
floorPlan -site CoreSite -r 1.0 0.72 100 100 100 100

# ---- 4.6  Global power connections ----
globalNetConnect VDD -type pgpin -pin VDD -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type pgpin -pin VSS -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VDD -type tiehi -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type tielo -inst * -verbose

# ---- 4.7  Core ring: Metal9 (horizontal) top/bottom, Metal8 (vertical) left/right ----
addRing -nets {VDD VSS} -type core_rings -follow core \
  -layer [list top $H_LAYER bottom $H_LAYER left $V_LAYER right $V_LAYER] \
  -width   {top 3 bottom 3 left 3 right 3} \
  -spacing {top 4 bottom 4 left 4 right 4} \
  -offset  {top 3 bottom 3 left 3 right 3}

# ---- 4.8  Stripes sized for this ~15 um core ----
addStripe -nets {VDD VSS} -direction horizontal -layer $H_LAYER \
  -width 1 -spacing 1 -set_to_set_distance 6 \
  -start_from bottom -start_offset 2 -stop_offset 2
addStripe -nets {VDD VSS} -direction vertical -layer $V_LAYER \
  -width 1 -spacing 1 -set_to_set_distance 6 \
  -start_from left -start_offset 2 -stop_offset 2

# ---- 4.9  Special route (cell rails) ----
sroute -connect {blockPin padPin padRing corePin floatingStripe} -nets {VDD VSS}

# ---- 4.10-4.11  Placement ----
setPlaceMode -clkGateAware true
setTieHiLoMode -cell $TIE_CELLS -maxFanout 8
setFillerMode -core $FILLERS -corePrefix FILL
placeDesign
if {$VARIANT eq "scan"} { catch {scanReorder} }
addTieHiLo
checkPlace $R/checkPlace.rpt
optDesign -preCTS -outDir $R/preCTS

# ---- 4.12  Clock tree ----
createClockTreeSpec -bufferList $CTS_BUFS -file constraints/Clock.ctstch
clockDesign -specFile constraints/Clock.ctstch -outDir $R/clock
optDesign -postCTS       -outDir $R/postCTS
optDesign -postCTS -hold -outDir $R/postCTS_hold

# ---- 4.13  Routing and post-route optimisation (cap-table extraction) ----
trialRoute
setNanoRouteMode -routeWithTimingDriven true -routeWithSiDriven true
routeDesign -globalDetail
if {[catch {setExtractRCMode -engine postRoute -effortLevel low}]} {
  setExtractRCMode -engine postRoute
}
setAnalysisMode -analysisType onChipVariation
optDesign -postRoute       -outDir $R/postRoute
optDesign -postRoute -hold -outDir $R/postRoute_hold

# ---- 4.14  Fillers, checks, save ----
addFiller -cell $FILLERS -prefix FILL
globalNetConnect VDD -type pgpin -pin VDD -inst * -verbose
globalNetConnect VSS -type pgpin -pin VSS -inst * -verbose
verifyConnectivity -type all -error 1000 -warning 50 -report $R/connectivity.rpt
verifyGeometry -report $R/geometry.rpt
timeDesign -postRoute       -outDir $R/timing_final
timeDesign -postRoute -hold -outDir $R/timing_final
saveDesign  results/${TAG}_postRoute.enc
saveNetlist results/${TAG}_postRoute.v

# ---- Exports for signoff (Chapter 7) ----
extractRC
rcOut -spef results/${TAG}.spef -rc_corner RC_TYP
write_sdf -view VIEW_SETUP results/${TAG}.sdf
if {[catch {write_sdc -view VIEW_SETUP results/${TAG}_postRoute.sdc}]} {
  catch {writeTimingCon -sdc -view VIEW_SETUP results/${TAG}_postRoute.sdc}
}
defOut -floorplan -netlist -routing results/${TAG}.def
if {[catch {streamOut results/${TAG}.gds -mapFile $STREAM_MAP -libName DesignLib \
              -structureName $TOP -units $DB_UNITS -mode ALL -outputMacros} msg]} {
  puts "**NOTE: streamOut with -outputMacros failed ($msg) - retrying without it"
  streamOut results/${TAG}.gds -mapFile $STREAM_MAP -libName DesignLib \
    -structureName $TOP -units $DB_UNITS -mode ALL
}
puts "==== Encounter flow for $TAG finished ===="
Check the file · shellwc -l scripts/encounter.tcl        # must print 111

(1) The script has a VARIANT switch: by default it implements results/cnt_updown_mapped.v; Step 6.5 sets VARIANT scan to run the identical flow on the scan netlist. Troubleshooting — the script stops

Cell not found in filler/tie/CTS lists — remove names that are missing from logs/cell_names.txt.

CHAPTER 6

Insert scan with RTL Compiler DFT

This is an added chapter. The VT tutorial does not cover DFT.
You start withThe functional RTL and constraints
You end withA scan-inserted netlist with one 8-flop chain, a scandef, and a passing shift test
Toolspython (Step 0.5 output), rc, irun, encounter
Time≈ 45 min
THEORYWhy chips need built-in test hardware≈ 12 min read

T1Verification vs test

VERIFICATION (Ch 1–2)MANUFACTURING TEST (this chapter)
QuestionIs the design correct?Was this particular chip built correctly?
DoneOnce, in simulationOn every chip, on a tester, in seconds
FindsLogic bugsShorts, opens, bad vias, particles

T2The stuck-at fault model

Real defects are messy, so test tools model them simply: a net is stuck at 0 or stuck at 1. Detecting a fault needs two things:

  1. Activate — drive the net to the opposite value (to find stuck-at-0, try to make it 1).
  2. Propagate — make the difference visible at something the tester can read.

T3Why flops make testing hard

A tester can only touch the chip’s pins. To set a flop deep inside to a particular value you may need many clock cycles of carefully chosen inputs (poor controllability); to see a flop’s value you must wait until it influences an output (poor observability). For millions of flops that is hopeless.

Scan solves both at once: in test mode every flop becomes part of a shift register, so the tester can write and read every flop directly.

T4The scan flip-flop

T5How one scan test runs

test cycles ≈ (L + 1) · N + L
L = longest chain length, N = number of patterns
This lab: L = 8, say N = 20 → 9 × 20 + 8 = 188 cycles. A million-flop chip with one chain would need ~10⁶ cycles per pattern — so real chips use hundreds of parallel chains plus compression.

T6Scan design rules — and the reason behind each

RULEWHY
Clocks controllable from a pinThe tester must pulse the clock exactly when it wants.
Async set/reset inactive in testA reset pulse during shifting would wipe the chain.
No latches / combinational loopsTheir values cannot be predicted by ATPG.
No X sources (undriven nets, black boxes)An unknown reaching a scan flop corrupts the compare.

T7Coverage and ATPG

ATPG (Automatic Test Pattern Generation) computes the patterns. Quality is measured as fault coverage = detected faults ÷ total faults; production targets are typically above 95–99 %. Scan insertion (this chapter) makes high coverage possible; ATPG (a separate tool) achieves it.

DEEP DIVE the mathematics of test

D1When does a pattern detect a fault? Activation, propagation and the Boolean difference

Think of the faulty chip as a second copy of the circuit in which one wire ℓ\ell is permanently stuck at a value vv. A test pattern detects the fault if the good and faulty copies give different outputs for it. Two things must happen:

  1. Activate: the pattern must drive ℓ\ell to the opposite of the stuck value in the good circuit, so the two copies differ at the fault site. To find stuck-at-0, set ℓ=1\ell = 1.
  2. Propagate: that difference must reach an output the tester can observe. Every gate on the way must let it through — its other inputs must be at their non-controlling values (1 for AND/NAND, 0 for OR/NOR).

The Boolean difference captures the propagation condition exactly. Evaluate the output once with ℓ\ell forced to 0 and once with ℓ\ell forced to 1, and XOR the results:

∂f∂ℓ=f∣ℓ=0⊕f∣ℓ=1\frac{\partial f}{\partial \ell} = f\big|_{\ell=0} \oplus f\big|_{\ell=1}

It equals 1 precisely for the input patterns where the output depends on ℓ\ell. Detection of “ℓ\ell stuck-at-vv” therefore needs

ℓ(x)=¬v(activate)and∂f∂ℓ(x)=1(propagate)\ell(\mathbf{x}) = \lnot v \quad\text{(activate)} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial \ell}(\mathbf{x}) = 1 \quad\text{(propagate)}
Example 1 — a single AND gate f=A⋅Bf = A\cdot B: ∂f/∂A=(0⋅B)⊕(1⋅B)=B\partial f/\partial A = (0\cdot B)\oplus(1\cdot B) = B. To see A, B must be 1. So A stuck-at-0 needs A=1,B=1A = 1, B = 1; A stuck-at-1 needs A=0,B=1A = 0, B = 1.
Example 2 — two levels f=(a⋅b)+cf = (a\cdot b) + c, fault on the internal wire ℓ=a⋅b\ell = a\cdot b, stuck-at-0.
Propagate: ∂f/∂ℓ=(0+c)⊕(1+c)=c⊕1=¬c\partial f/\partial \ell = (0 + c) \oplus (1 + c) = c \oplus 1 = \lnot c → we need c=0c = 0 (the OR gate’s other input must not already force the output to 1).
Activate: ℓ=1\ell = 1 → a=1,b=1a = 1, b = 1.
Test pattern: a=1,b=1,c=0a = 1, b = 1, c = 0. Good circuit outputs 1, faulty circuit outputs 0. ✓

ATPG tools solve exactly this — activate and propagate — for every fault in the list, using the D-algorithm of D7 or a SAT solver. With full scan, ff is always a combinational cloud between flops, which keeps the problem tractable.

D2Counting faults

Every line can be stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1, so a circuit with NN lines has 2N2N single stuck-at faults. Many are equivalent (no pattern can tell them apart): for an AND gate, any input stuck-at-0 behaves exactly like the output stuck-at-0. Collapsing reduces a 2-input AND from 66 faults to 44. ATPG works on the collapsed list.

FC=#detected faults#total faults\text{FC} = \frac{\#\text{detected faults}}{\#\text{total faults}}

D3Why 95 % coverage is not enough: yield and defect level

Three numbers decide how many bad chips reach customers:

  • Yield YY — the fraction of manufactured dies that are actually good.
  • Fault coverage FC — the fraction of modelled faults the test can detect.
  • Defect level DL — the fraction of chips that pass the test but are bad. Customers measure it in defective parts per million (ppm).

Yield. If defects land randomly with density D0D_0 per cm², the number on a die of area AA follows a Poisson distribution with mean AD0A D_0. A die is good only if it has zero defects:

Y=P(0 defects)=e−A D0Y = P(\text{0 defects}) = e^{-A\,D_0}

(For AD0=0.22A D_0 = 0.22, e.g. 0.5 cm² at 0.45 defects/cm², Y=0.80Y = 0.80.)

Defect level. Williams and Brown showed that if the test detects a fraction FC of faults, the escaping bad chips are approximately

DL=1−Y 1−FC\text{DL} = 1 - Y^{\,1-\text{FC}}

Check the edge cases: FC = 1 gives DL = 0 (perfect test); FC = 0 gives DL = 1−Y1 - Y (no test, every bad chip ships).

Example with Y=0.8Y = 0.8:
FC = 0.95 → DL =1−0.80.05≈0.0111= 1 - 0.8^{0.05} \approx 0.0111 = 11 100 ppm — about one bad chip in 90 shipped.
FC = 0.99 → 2 200 ppm. FC = 0.999 → 220 ppm.
Automotive customers ask for single-digit ppm, which is why scan, high coverage and at-speed tests are mandatory there.

D4Test time with many chains

With FF scan flops split into kk balanced chains, chain length L=⌈F/k⌉L = \lceil F/k \rceil. For NN patterns at shift frequency fsf_s:

ttest=(L+1) N+Lfst_{\text{test}} = \frac{(L + 1)\,N + L}{f_s}
Example: F=106F = 10^6, k=200k = 200 → L=5000L = 5000. With N=2000N = 2000, fs=50 MHzf_s = 50\,\text{MHz}: (5001⋅2000+5000)/5×107≈0.2 s\bigl(5001\cdot2000 + 5000\bigr)/5\times10^{7} \approx 0.2\,\text{s}. With a single chain it would be ≈ 40 s per chip — 200× more tester cost.

D5Try it: drive the scan chain yourself

The 8 counter flops, chained scan_in → count[0] → … → count[7] → scan_out. Load a value with SE = 1, capture one functional clock with SE = 0 (the counter adds 1), then unload. If the unloaded value is the loaded value + 1, the incrementer logic has been tested.

D6Built-in self-test: LFSRs

Instead of storing patterns on an expensive tester, a chip can generate pseudo-random patterns itself with a linear feedback shift register. For the characteristic polynomial x4+x3+1x^4 + x^3 + 1 the register obeys the recurrence over GF(2):

sn+4=sn+3⊕sns_{n+4} = s_{n+3} \oplus s_{n}

If the polynomial is primitive, the register cycles through all 2n−12^n - 1 non-zero states. Starting from Q1Q2Q3Q4 = 1000:

1000010000101001110001101011010110101101111011110111001100011000 …

15 distinct states, then it repeats. A second LFSR with parallel inputs (a MISR) compresses the circuit’s responses into one signature. The probability that a faulty response produces the correct signature by chance (aliasing) is about

Palias≈2−nP_{\text{alias}} \approx 2^{-n}

— about 2.3×10−102.3\times10^{-10} for a 32-bit MISR. Logic BIST and memory BIST let chips test themselves at power-up and in the field.

D7The D-algorithm: five-valued logic

ATPG reasons about the good and faulty circuit at once using the values {0,1,X,D,Dˉ}\{0, 1, X, D, \bar D\}, where DD means “1 in the good circuit, 0 in the faulty one” and Dˉ\bar D the opposite. Gates are evaluated component-wise:

AND01XDD
000000
101XDD
X0XXXX
D0DXD0
D0DX0D

The algorithm has three phases: activate (place a DD or Dˉ\bar D at the fault site), propagate (drive the DD through gates on the D-frontier by setting their side inputs to non-controlling values — 1 for AND, 0 for OR) and justify (find primary-input values producing all required internal values, backtracking on conflicts). Note D⋅Dˉ=0D \cdot \bar D = 0: two fault effects can cancel. PODEM and FAN refine the search; with full scan every flop is a pseudo-primary input and output, so ATPG only ever solves combinational problems.

D8At-speed test: transition faults

Stuck-at tests are applied slowly; they miss defects that only make a path too slow. The transition-fault model (slow-to-rise, slow-to-fall at each node) needs two patterns: V1V_1 initialises the node, V2V_2 launches the transition, and the response is captured exactly one functional period TT later:

tcapture−tlaunch=T⇒detects any extra delay Δ with dpath+Δ>T−tsut_{\text{capture}} - t_{\text{launch}} = T \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{detects any extra delay } \Delta \text{ with } d_{\text{path}} + \Delta \gt T - t_{su}

Two schemes: launch-on-shift (last shift pulse launches; needs a fast scan-enable) and launch-on-capture (two functional pulses; easier timing, lower coverage). The fast launch–capture pair comes from an on-chip PLL, so at-speed test also verifies the timing you signed off in Chapter 7.

D9How many random patterns are enough?

If a fault is detected by a random pattern with probability pp, the chance of missing it after NN independent patterns is (1−p)N(1-p)^N. For confidence cc:

(1−p)N≤1−c    ⇒    N≥ln⁡(1−c)ln⁡(1−p)≈−ln⁡(1−c)p(1-p)^N \le 1 - c \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; N \ge \frac{\ln(1-c)}{\ln(1-p)} \approx \frac{-\ln(1-c)}{p}
Random-pattern-resistant fault: the output stuck-at-0 of a 16-input AND is detected only by the all-ones input, p=2−16≈1.5×10−5p = 2^{-16} \approx 1.5\times10^{-5}. For 99 % confidence: N≥4.6/1.5×10−5≈3×105N \ge 4.6/1.5\times10^{-5} \approx 3\times10^{5} patterns — for one fault. LBIST therefore adds test points (extra control/observe flops) to raise such probabilities, and deterministic ATPG targets the remaining faults directly.
Remember
  • Test checks manufacturing, not design.
  • Scan = mux + flop, chained; SE switches shift/functional.
  • Chain length sets test time.
6.1

Understand the test mode

Why this stepKnowing the three test modes makes every DFT command and report understandable.

After manufacturing, every chip must be tested for defects (a wire shorted to ground, a broken via). Testing a sequential circuit through its normal inputs alone is nearly impossible: you cannot directly set or read the internal flops. Scan fixes that by giving every flop a second input and chaining them into one long shift register.

scan_inscan flopscan flopscan flopscan_out

With scan_enable=0, each flop captures functional logic. With it asserted, the flops form shift registers. ATPG (Automatic Test Pattern Generation) loads a state by shifting it in, pulses one functional (capture) clock, then shifts the response out and compares it with the expected values.

MODEscan_enableWHAT THE FLOPS DO
Functional0Normal counter behavior.
Shift (load/unload)1Each flop takes its neighbour's value; data moves one position per clock.
Capture0 for one clockFlops capture the combinational logic's response to the loaded state.
Scan is not ATPG

Scan creates controllability and observability. A separate ATPG product generates patterns and measures fault coverage. On your VM the scan insertion commands come with RTL Compiler 12.10; there is no Encounter Test/Modus (no ATPG tool appears in the environment report), so pattern generation and fault coverage are explained in the theory card but not run.

6.2

Expose and constrain test signals

Why this stepScan needs dedicated ports, and the design must obey rules that make every flop controllable.

Scan needs three new ports. Create a separate RTL file so the functional flow of Chapters 1–5 is untouched. The original enable and up_down ports stay; the logic is identical — RC adds the scan muxes, you only add the ports.

Create the scan-ready RTL · shellgedit rtl/cnt_updown_scan.v &
rtl/cnt_updown_scan.v · Verilog`timescale 1ns/1ps

module cnt_updown (
  input  wire       clk,
  input  wire       reset,        // asynchronous, active high (held 0 during test)
  input  wire       enable,
  input  wire       up_down,
  input  wire       scan_enable,  // 1 = shift, 0 = functional/capture
  input  wire       scan_in,      // serial data into the chain
  output wire       scan_out,     // serial data out of the chain (driven by RC)
  output reg  [7:0] count
);
  // Functional logic is unchanged. RC replaces the 8 flops with scan flops
  // and connects scan_in -> flop -> ... -> flop -> scan_out.
  always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) begin
    if (reset)
      count <= 8'h00;
    else if (enable) begin
      if (up_down) count <= count + 8'h01;
      else         count <= count - 8'h01;
    end
  end
endmodule

Before mapping, a design must obey the scan design rules. Check each one for your RTL:

  • Every clock must be controllable from a primary input — clk is a port: ✓. (A clock generated by internal logic would need a test-mode bypass mux.)
  • Asynchronous resets must be held inactive during shift — reset is a port that the tester can hold at 0; you declare that in Step 6.3: ✓.
  • Clock gating must be bypassed in test mode — no clock gating here: ✓.
  • No latches, tri-states, black boxes, combinational feedback or X-sources — none: ✓ (Step 2.3 already checked latches and loops).
What you should see
  • rtl/cnt_updown_scan.v saved; the port list now has eight entries (the original five plus scan_enable, scan_in, scan_out).
  • The functional always block is unchanged — scan muxes are added by RC, not by you.
6.3

Run legacy RC scan insertion

Why this stepRC replaces flops with scan flops and stitches the chain — the hardware that makes manufacturing test possible.

One thing differs from the functional run in Chapter 2: RC reads libs/slow_scan.lib (Step 0.5 C) instead of slow.lib. The timing is identical, but only the patched file tells RC, through its test_cell groups, that SDFFRHQX1 is the scan equivalent of DFFRHQX1 (and SDFFRX1 of DFFRX1, and so on). With the original slow.lib — which has 0 test_cell groups — RC would leave every flop unscanned and the chain would be empty.

scripts/rtl_rc_scan.tcl · Tcl# ================= RTL Compiler 12.10 synthesis + muxed scan insertion =================
set TOP  cnt_updown
set ROOT [file normalize .]
source scripts/lib_paths.tcl
file mkdir reports results

# The scan-aware copy of slow.lib (Step 0.5) - same timing, plus test_cell groups
if {![file exists $LIB_SLOW_SCAN]} {
  puts "**ERROR: $LIB_SLOW_SCAN not found - run Step 0.5 (gpdk045_libtool.py scan) first"
  return
}

set_attribute information_level 7 /
set_attribute hdl_search_path [list $ROOT/rtl] /
set_attribute library [list $LIB_SLOW_SCAN] /

read_hdl -v2001 [list rtl/cnt_updown_scan.v]
elaborate $TOP
read_sdc constraints/cnt_updown.sdc

# ---- 1. Declare the scan style and test signals (before mapping) ----
set_attribute dft_scan_style muxed_scan /
define_dft shift_enable -name SE     -active high [find / -port scan_enable]
define_dft test_mode    -name TM_RST -active low  [find / -port reset]
define_dft test_clock   -name scan_clk -period 100000 [find / -port clk]  ;# ps = 100 ns

# ---- 2. Check the DFT rules on the generic design ----
check_dft_rules      > reports/dft_rules_pre_map.rpt
report dft_registers > reports/dft_registers_pre_map.rpt

# ---- 3. Map: flops that passed the rules become scan flops (SDFF... cells) ----
synthesize -to_generic
synthesize -to_mapped

# ---- 4. Build and connect the chain ----
define_dft scan_chain -name chain0 \
  -sdi [find / -port scan_in] -sdo [find / -port scan_out] -shift_enable SE
connect_scan_chains -chains chain0
synthesize -incremental

# ---- 5. Reports and outputs ----
check_dft_rules       > reports/dft_rules_post.rpt
report dft_setup      > reports/dft_setup.rpt
report dft_chains     > reports/scan_chains.rpt
report dft_registers  > reports/dft_registers.rpt
report gates          > reports/gates_scan.rpt
report timing         > reports/timing_scan.rpt
write_hdl     > results/cnt_updown_scan.v
write_sdc     > results/cnt_updown_scan.sdc
write_scandef > results/cnt_updown_scan.scandef
write_do_lec -revised_design results/cnt_updown_scan.v > results/cnt_updown_scan_lec.do
puts "==== Scan insertion finished ===="

The course runs rc -dft. On your VM plain rc is used: the DFT commands are part of RTL Compiler 12.10 and the -dft option is not needed.

What success looks like
  • dft_rules_post.rpt: 0 DFT violations; 8 registers pass.
  • scan_chains.rpt: one chain chain0, length 8, starting at scan_in, ending at scan_out, listing the 8 count_reg flops in order.
  • The uniq -c line counts 8 scan flops, typically 8 SDFFRHQX1 (or SDFFRX1 — the resettable scan flops of gsclib045; RC picks by timing and area).
  • The netlist ports now include scan_enable, scan_in and scan_out.
Troubleshooting — scan insertion

"invalid command" for a define_dft variant — check the exact syntax in your build with help define_dft at the rc:/> prompt; option names differ slightly between RC releases.

The script stops with …slow_scan.lib not found — Step 0.5 C was skipped. Run python scripts/gpdk045_libtool.py scan $PDK45/timing/slow.lib libs/slow_scan.lib and rerun.

Chain length 0 / “no scan equivalent” messages / flops stay DFFR… — RC read a library without test_cell groups. Check the log: grep -i "library" logs/rc_dft.log | head must show libs/slow_scan.lib, and grep -c test_cell libs/slow_scan.lib must be about 40.

Registers fail the rules because of the reset — the test_mode line did not match the port; confirm with report dft_setup.

scan_out stays unconnected — if RC refuses to use the existing output port, replace the two [find / -port …] arguments of define_dft scan_chain by -create_ports and remove scan_in/scan_out from the RTL port list; RC then creates both ports itself.

License error at define_dft — scan insertion is not licensed on this VM. Record that in the README; the rest of the flow (Chapters 1–5, 7) is unaffected.

One genuine blocker remains possible. The missing Liberty scan data — the blocker the course warned about — is solved by Step 0.5. What can still stop this chapter is a missing RC DFT license. Do not hide it by inventing cells or substituting modern Modus commands; report it honestly.

  scan_out:     scan_out

  2. Its serial input and output ports.
  3. The shift-enable signal and its polarity.
  4. Length 8 = all flops scanned. Fewer means some flops failed the DFT rules.
  5. Physical order of the chain: this is the order the scan testbench and the widget in the theory card assume.
Reading the scan report quickly Three numbers matter: the number of chains (1 here), the chain length (= number of scan flops, 8), and the count of flops not on a chain (must be 0 — anything else is a DFT rule violation listed earlier in the log). Then check that scan_in and scan_out appear as new ports of cnt_updown in the netlist.
6.4

Verify functional, shift and capture modes

Why this stepProves the inserted chain really shifts and that functional behaviour is unchanged.

The testbench below checks both modes on the scanned netlist: first a short functional count with scan_enable=0, then a shift test that pushes a random 16-bit pattern through the 8-flop chain and compares scan_out against a shift-register model.

tb/tb_cnt_updown_scan.v · Verilog`timescale 1ns/1ps
module tb_cnt_updown_scan;
  localparam L = 8;                         // chain length from reports/scan_chains.rpt
  reg clk = 0, reset = 1, enable = 0, up_down = 1, scan_enable = 0, scan_in = 0;
  wire       scan_out;
  wire [7:0] count;
  integer    errors = 0, i;

  cnt_updown dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .enable(enable), .up_down(up_down),
                  .scan_enable(scan_enable), .scan_in(scan_in),
                  .scan_out(scan_out), .count(count));
  always #50 clk = ~clk;                    // 100 ns test clock

  // Reference model of the chain: shifts only when scan_enable = 1
  reg [L-1:0] model;
  always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
    if (reset)            model <= {L{1'b0}};
    else if (scan_enable) model <= {model[L-2:0], scan_in};

  initial begin
    $dumpfile("./scan_test.dump"); $dumpvars(0, tb_cnt_updown_scan);
    #120 reset = 0;

    // ---- Functional mode: count up 5 times ----
    @(negedge clk); enable = 1; up_down = 1;
    repeat (5) @(negedge clk);
    enable = 0;
    if (count !== 8'd5) begin errors = errors + 1; $display("ERROR functional count=%0d (expected 5)", count); end
    else $display("Functional mode OK: count = %0d", count);

    // ---- Shift mode: reset chain, then shift 2L random bits ----
    reset = 1; #10 reset = 0;
    scan_enable = 1;
    for (i = 0; i < 2*L; i = i + 1) begin
      scan_in = $random;
      @(negedge clk);
      if (scan_out !== model[L-1]) begin
        errors = errors + 1;
        $display("ERROR shift %0d: scan_out=%b expected=%b", i, scan_out, model[L-1]);
      end
    end
    scan_enable = 0;

    if (errors == 0) $display("PASS: functional and %0d-bit shift test", 2*L);
    else             $display("FAIL: %0d errors", errors);
    $finish;
  end
endmodule
Simulate the scanned netlist · shellCELL_VLOG=libs/gsclib045_cells.v                   # generated in Step 0.5
irun -v2001 -access +rwc -nospecify -notimingchecks -timescale 1ns/1ps \
  -logfile logs/irun_scan.log \
  $CELL_VLOG results/cnt_updown_scan.v tb/tb_cnt_updown_scan.v
grep -E "PASS|FAIL|ERROR|OK" logs/irun_scan.log
  1. Functional — scan enable low, counter behaves normally (checked above; you can also rerun the full Chapter 1 testbench after adding .scan_enable(1'b0), .scan_in(1'b0), .scan_out() to its instance).
  2. Shift — the pattern appears at scan_out exactly L clocks later. If every bit is inverted, RC used an inverting scan path (QN); flip the comparison and note it.
  3. Capture — load a state, drop scan_enable for one clock with enable=1, raise it again and unload: the unloaded value should be the loaded value +1. (A full capture test is what ATPG automates.)
  4. Conformal LEC is not installed on your VM, so keep results/cnt_updown_scan_lec.do for reference; the functional and shift simulations are your equivalence evidence.
  5. After routing (Step 6.5), repeat this scan smoke test on the post-route scan netlist.
Physical consequence

Scan adds area (a mux per flop), extra fanout on scan_enable, and an arbitrary chain can zig-zag across the floorplan. In Encounter, load results/cnt_updown_scan.scandef with defIn before placement and run scanReorder after placement; then hand the final physical chain order back to ATPG. Step 6.5 does exactly that.

What you should see
  • Functional mode OK: count = 5
  • PASS: functional and 16-bit shift test (this testbench was run against a scan netlist built from the generated models before publishing and passes).
  • No ERROR shift lines.
Troubleshooting — the shift test fails

scan_out is X from the very first shift — the reset pulse before shifting did not clear the scan flops, so the chain holds unknowns while the model holds zeros. Check that reset reaches every SDFFR… instance in the scanned netlist (and that the DFT rules did not tie it off).

Every bit comes out one cycle late or early — the chain length L in the testbench differs from reports/scan_chains.rpt (lock-up latches or an extra flop change it). Copy the length from the report.

The pattern comes out inverted — some flops are connected through their QN output; the report marks them. Invert the model for those positions or compare against the report’s polarity column.

The functional test now fails — scan_enable was left floating (X) in functional mode. Drive it to 0 explicitly.

CheckpointChain length 8, 0 DFT violations, and the scan testbench prints PASS.

The functional results from Chapter 5 are not touched.

defIn reports errors in the scan DEF — open results/cnt_updown_scan.scandef; it must contain a SCANCHAINS 1 ; section naming chain0. Q1To detect input A stuck-at-0 on a 2-input AND gate, apply…

Activate (A=1) and propagate (∂f/∂A = B must be 1).

Q2With fault coverage 0.95 and yield 0.8, the defect level is roughly…

DL = 1 − 0.80.05 ≈ 0.011.

Q3Splitting one scan chain into 10 balanced chains cuts shift time by about…

Test cycles ≈ (L+1)N + L, and L drops by 10×.

⚠ Common mistakes in this chapter
  • Declaring the DFT test signals after mapping instead of before.
  • Using an RC test-clock period in ns — RC expects picoseconds.
  • Leaving reset unconstrained in test mode, so flops fail the scan rules.
  • Assuming the chain order; read it from report dft_chains.
  • Synthesizing the scan design with slow.lib instead of libs/slow_scan.lib — RC then finds no scan equivalents.

CHAPTER 7

Signoff: extraction, timing, power, rail and GDS

Goal: verify the routed implementation, not the idealized netlist.
You start withThe saved post-route database
You end withSPEF, SDF, timing/power/IR evidence, a GDS file and DRC/LVS status
Toolsencounter, irun, virtuoso + Assura
Time≈ 1–2 h
THEORYSignoff — proving the layout will work and can be built≈ 12 min read

T1The signoff checklist

CATEGORYQUESTIONSTEP
TimingDo setup and hold pass with real wires at every corner?7.1, 7.2
FunctionDoes the routed netlist still behave the same, with real delays?7.2
Power integrityIs total power acceptable, and does every cell get enough voltage?7.3–7.5
Physical verificationIs the geometry manufacturable (DRC) and the same circuit (LVS)?7.1, 7.6

T2PVT corners — testing the extremes

Delay depends on Process (how fast the transistors came out), Voltage and Temperature. A chip must work at the worst combination for each check:

CORNERTRANSISTORS · VOLTAGE · TEMPWORST FOR
Slow (SS)slow · low V · hot (or very cold at advanced nodes)Setup
Fast (FF)fast · high V · coldHold
Typical (TT)nominalPower estimates

That is exactly the MMMC setup in scripts/mmmc.tcl: VIEW_SETUP = slow, VIEW_HOLD = fast. On-chip variation (OCV) adds a small pessimism because two flops on the same die are never perfectly identical.

T3What SPEF and SDF contain

SPEF excerpt — extracted parasitics of one net (illustrative)*D_NET count[0] 0.0042          // total capacitance (pF)
*CONN
*I count_reg_0_:Q O
*P count[0] O
*CAP
1 count_reg_0_:Q 0.0011
2 count[0]:1 0.0031
*RES
1 count_reg_0_:Q count[0]:1 12.4  // ohms
*END
SDF excerpt — final delays per cell arc (illustrative)(CELL (CELLTYPE "DFFRHQX1") (INSTANCE count_reg_0_)
  (DELAY (ABSOLUTE
    (IOPATH CK Q (0.182:0.182:0.182) (0.201:0.201:0.201)))))

SPEF = raw R and C of every net (input to timing tools). SDF = computed delays of every cell and wire (input to the simulator for the timing-annotated run in Step 7.2).

T4IR drop and electromigration

  • Static IR drop uses average current (what this lab runs). Dynamic IR drop uses peak current at clock edges — decaps help there.
  • Electromigration (EM): high current density slowly pushes metal atoms along a wire until it opens, years later. Rules cap current per wire width.
  • Typical limit: total drop within ~5 % of VDD — the thresholds you enter in Step 7.4.

T5Physical verification

CHECKWHAT IT PROVES
DRCEvery shape obeys width, spacing, enclosure, density… rules of the foundry
LVSTransistors and connections extracted from the polygons match the netlist
AntennaLong wires connected only to a gate during manufacturing do not collect enough charge to damage it
DensityEach layer has enough (and not too much) metal for even chemical-mechanical polishing

T6What GDSII is

A binary file of hierarchical cells, each a list of polygons on numbered (layer, datatype) pairs — e.g. Metal1 might be (31, 0). The tool database uses names (“Metal1”); the stream map file translates names to numbers. Since Encounter only knows cell abstracts, real cell layouts are merged in from the library GDS during stream-out.

DEEP DIVE variation, voltage and reliability, quantified

D1How much does IR drop slow a gate? The alpha-power law

Saturation current in short-channel transistors follows Ion∝(VDD−Vth)αI_{\text{on}} \propto (V_{DD} - V_{th})^{\alpha} with α≈1.2–1.5\alpha \approx 1.2\text{–}1.5. Delay is charge over current:

td  ∝  C VDDIon  ∝  VDD(VDD−Vth)αt_d \;\propto\; \frac{C\,V_{DD}}{I_{\text{on}}} \;\propto\; \frac{V_{DD}}{(V_{DD} - V_{th})^{\alpha}}
Example: VDD=0.9 VV_{DD} = 0.9\,\text{V}, Vth=0.35 VV_{th} = 0.35\,\text{V}, α=1.3\alpha = 1.3. A 5 % drop to 0.855 V gives
td(0.855)td(0.9)=0.855/0.5051.30.9/0.5501.3≈2.0781.958≈1.061\dfrac{t_d(0.855)}{t_d(0.9)} = \dfrac{0.855/0.505^{1.3}}{0.9/0.550^{1.3}} \approx \dfrac{2.078}{1.958} \approx 1.061 — a 6 % slower gate for a 5 % drop. That is why the rail-analysis threshold and timing margins are linked.

D2On-chip variation and CPPR, with numbers

Two identical buffers on the same die are never exactly identical (local doping, temperature and voltage differ slightly). STA covers this pessimistically with derates: for each check, the paths that make it worse are slowed by a factor 1+ε1+\varepsilon, and the paths that help are sped up by 1−ε1-\varepsilon. For setup the launch clock and data are made late and the capture clock early:

(1+ε)(ℓL+tcq+tcombmax⁡)+tsu  ≤  T+(1−ε) ℓC−u(1+\varepsilon)\bigl(\ell_L + t_{cq} + t_{\text{comb}}^{\max}\bigr) + t_{su} \;\le\; T + (1-\varepsilon)\,\ell_C - u

The problem. The launch and capture clocks usually share most of the clock tree — the common part from the root to where the branches split. A physical buffer in that common part cannot be slow for the launch edge and fast for the capture edge at the same time, yet the derates assume exactly that. The extra pessimism is removed by Common Path Pessimism Removal (CPPR):

CPPR credit=(1+ε) ℓcom−(1−ε) ℓcom=2 ε ℓcom\text{CPPR credit} = (1+\varepsilon)\,\ell_{\text{com}} - (1-\varepsilon)\,\ell_{\text{com}} = 2\,\varepsilon\,\ell_{\text{com}}
Numbers: common clock path 400 ps, then 100 ps on each branch, ε=5 %\varepsilon = 5\,\%.
Derated launch clock: 1.05×500=5251.05 \times 500 = 525 ps. Derated capture clock: 0.95×500=4750.95 \times 500 = 475 ps. Pessimism: 50 ps.
Of that, the shared 400 ps contributes 2×0.05×400=402\times0.05\times400 = 40 ps, which is physically impossible → CPPR gives it back. The remaining 10 ps (from the separate 100 ps branches) is real and stays.

That is what the -analysisType onChipVariation setting in Step 4.13 switches on; Encounter applies CPPR automatically in that mode.

D3Electromigration: Black’s equation

The median time to failure of a wire carrying current density J=I/(w t)J = I/(w\,t) (width × thickness) at temperature TT:

MTTF=A J−n exp⁡ ⁣(Eak T),n≈2\text{MTTF} = A\,J^{-n}\,\exp\!\left(\frac{E_a}{k\,T}\right), \qquad n \approx 2

With n=2n = 2, doubling the current density cuts lifetime by 4×; widening the wire 2× restores it. Power rings and stripes are wide for both reasons — IR drop and EM.

D4Corner arithmetic

With 3 process corners × 3 voltages × 3 temperatures × 2 RC corners there are 3⋅3⋅3⋅2=543\cdot3\cdot3\cdot2 = 54 possible delay corners, multiplied by every mode (functional, scan shift, …). MMMC lets you pick the few dominant ones — here just two (slow for setup, fast for hold) — because a check that passes at the worst corner for that check passes at the others.

D5GDS coordinates are integers

With DATABASE MICRONS 2000 one database unit is 1/2000 μm=0.5 nm1/2000\,\mu\text{m} = 0.5\,\text{nm}. Every vertex is an integer multiple of that grid, which is why streamOut -units 2000 must match the LEF: a mismatch scales the whole layout by a power of ten.

D6Sizing decoupling capacitance for dynamic IR drop

At a clock edge many gates switch together and draw a burst of charge faster than the power grid’s inductance and resistance can deliver. On-chip decap supplies it locally. If a region needs current IpeakI_{\text{peak}} for a time Δt\Delta t and the allowed droop is ΔV\Delta V:

Cdecap  ≥  ΔQΔV=Ipeak ΔtΔVC_{\text{decap}} \;\ge\; \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta V} = \frac{I_{\text{peak}}\,\Delta t}{\Delta V}
Example: 10 mA for 50 ps with 45 mV (5 % of 0.9 V) allowed: C≥0.01×50×10−12/0.045≈11 pFC \ge 0.01 \times 50\times10^{-12} / 0.045 \approx 11\,\text{pF}. Every non-switching gate also contributes some decap through its own capacitances, which is why filler-with-decap cells are placed in empty space.

D7Temperature inversion

Heat lowers carrier mobility (slower) but also lowers VtV_t (faster). In older nodes mobility wins and hot = slow. In advanced low-voltage nodes, where VDD−VtV_{DD} - V_t is small, the VtV_t effect can win so cold becomes the slow corner. That is why modern signoff checks setup at both temperature extremes — a direct consequence of the alpha-power law in D1.

D8Statistical variation: Pelgrom’s law and path averaging

Random dopant fluctuations make two identically drawn transistors differ. The standard deviation of their threshold mismatch follows Pelgrom’s law:

σ(ΔVt)=AVtW L\sigma(\Delta V_t) = \frac{A_{V_t}}{\sqrt{W\,L}}
Example with a typical AVt≈2.5 mV⋅μmA_{V_t} \approx 2.5\,\text{mV}\cdot\mu\text{m} and WL=0.2×0.045 μm2W L = 0.2 \times 0.045\,\mu\text{m}^2: 0.009≈0.095\sqrt{0.009} \approx 0.095 → σ≈26\sigma \approx 26 mV — about 7 % of VtV_t. Smaller devices vary more; bigger ones average out.

A path of NN gates with independent random delays (mean μg\mu_g, deviation σg\sigma_g) has

μpath=Nμg,σpath=N σg    ⇒    σpathμpath=1N σgμg\mu_{\text{path}} = N\mu_g, \qquad \sigma_{\text{path}} = \sqrt{N}\,\sigma_g \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \frac{\sigma_{\text{path}}}{\mu_{\text{path}}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt N}\,\frac{\sigma_g}{\mu_g}

Deep paths are relatively less variable — the basis of depth-dependent derating (AOCV) and statistical STA, which replace the single OCV factor of D2 with numbers that shrink with path depth.

The probability a single path meets timing is Φ((treq−μ)/σ)\Phi\bigl((t_{\text{req}} - \mu)/\sigma\bigr), where Φ\Phi is the standard normal CDF. Try the margin calculator:

D9Crosstalk noise: when a quiet wire glitches

If a victim net is held only weakly and its neighbour (aggressor) switches by VDDV_{DD}, charge sharing through the coupling capacitance gives a peak noise of about

Vnoise≈VDD CcCc+CgV_{\text{noise}} \approx V_{DD}\,\frac{C_c}{C_c + C_g}
Example: Cc=2C_c = 2 fF, Cg=3C_g = 3 fF, VDD=0.9V_{DD} = 0.9 V → Vnoise≈0.36V_{\text{noise}} \approx 0.36 V. That exceeds the 0.28 V noise margin from the primer (F2): the receiving gate may switch falsely. A strong victim driver holding the line reduces the peak (the noise decays with the victim’s RC time constant), which is how SI fixing works: upsize the victim driver, space the wires, or shield with a grounded track.

D10The antenna effect

During manufacturing each metal layer is etched by plasma before the layers above exist. A long wire connected only to a transistor gate collects charge, and the thin gate oxide can be damaged. The rule limits the ratio

antenna ratio=Ametal connected to the gate (this layer)Agate oxide  ≤  Rmax⁡\text{antenna ratio} = \frac{A_{\text{metal connected to the gate (this layer)}}}{A_{\text{gate oxide}}} \;\le\; R_{\max}

with Rmax⁡R_{\max} typically a few hundred. Fixes: break the wire with a jump to a higher layer (so the long piece is not connected to the gate until later), or add a reverse-biased antenna diode that drains the charge. NanoRoute repairs antenna violations automatically when the LEF has antenna data; verifyGeometry reports the remainder.

Remember
  • Setup at slow, hold at fast, power at typical.
  • SPEF = R/C; SDF = delays.
  • Only a matching-PDK DRC/LVS run proves manufacturability.

You can run this step either by typing the commands below at the encounter> prompt, or all at once with encounter -nowin -init scripts/signoff.tcl -log logs/signoff.log (the file is at the end of this step).   1. Verify → Verify Connectivity → OK. Opens, unconnected pins, antennas of dangling wires. Must be 0.

Each window of each metal must contain a minimum and maximum percentage of metal. gsclib045.lef asks for 20–65 % in every 120 × 120 µm window; your ≈14 µm core sits in a ≈214 µm die, so minimum density fails on most layers (the course notes the same, caused by widely spaced pads).   5. Verify → Verify Cut Density → OK. The same idea for vias.
  6. Timing → Report Timing: Design Stage Post-Route, Analysis Type Setup, OK; repeat with Hold.

Troubleshooting — restore and signoff exports

restoreDesign: “cannot find … .dat” — pass the .enc.dat folder, not the .enc file, and give the top-cell name as the second argument.

rcOut: “RC corner RC_TYP not found” — the MMMC file was not reloaded. Restoring from the .dat folder normally brings it back; if you moved the project, re-run source scripts/lib_paths.tcl first because the MMMC file uses those variables.

Metal-density violations only — expected on this tiny design (see the note above). Run addMetalFill and re-verify; geometry and connectivity must still be 0.

Hold violations appear only after extraction — real wire caps changed the clock tree delays slightly. Run optDesign -postRoute -hold and re-export the SPEF/SDF.

7.2

Run extracted static timing and an SDF gate-level simulation

Why this stepChecks timing with real wires and re-proves function with real delays.

AThe course's PrimeTime sequence

The VT course signs off timing in Synopsys PrimeTime with this sequence. pt_setup.tcl sets the target/link libraries (compiled .db files). Positive slack in the max report means no setup violation; positive slack in the min report means no hold violation.

PrimeTime sequence from the mixed course · Tclsource pt_setup.tcl

read_sdc ./cnt_updown_syn_final.sdc
report_timing -nosplit -capacitance -path_type full_clock -significant_digits 4 -delay_type max
report_timing -nosplit -capacitance -path_type full_clock -significant_digits 4 -delay_type min

Your environment report confirms there is no PrimeTime or Tempus on the VM. Treat this as course coverage; use it only on a machine where the named signoff tool is installed. On your VM, the post-route timeDesign reports from Step 7.1 (which use the same extracted parasitics) are your timing evidence — state clearly in your report that they come from the implementation tool, not an independent signoff tool.

BRe-run the testbench with real routed delays

This is the strongest functional check available on your VM: the post-route netlist plus the SDF file (every cell and wire delay) plus the Chapter 1 testbench. The testbench already contains $sdf_annotate inside `ifdef SDF; +define+SDF switches it on.

  • model check done with no NO MODEL: line (clock buffers, tie and filler cells inserted by Encounter all have models).
  • PASS: 32 cycle checks matched, final count = 3.
  • The SDF statistics show the path delays annotated (a high percentage) and the timing checks at 0 %. That is expected: the generated models contain specify delay paths but no $setup/$hold checks, so NC reports warnings such as SDFNET/SDFNCAP for the TIMINGCHECK entries. Setup and hold are proven by Encounter’s static timing (Step 7.1), not by this simulation.
  • Because the testbench changes inputs half a cycle from the clock, real delays of a few hundred picoseconds do not upset it. In SimVision you can now see count change ≈0.3 ns after each rising clock edge (the routed clock-to-Q delay).

7.3

Create the PowerGrid library and run power

Why this stepPost-route power includes the clock tree and real wire capacitance; its current files feed rail analysis.

Post-route power and rail (IR-drop) analysis run inside Encounter's integrated power system (labelled Power & Rail in the course's version; in 13.10 these items live under the Power menu). They may require an extra license on your VM; if a menu item is greyed out, note that in your report.

Rail analysis needs an electrical model of every cell's power pins. Choose Power & Rail → PowerGrid Library → Create PowerGrid Library and enter:

You may instead select dynamic vectorless or vector-based analysis; for vector-based, load the activity file from Chapter 3.

CRun the analysis

Power & Rail → Run Power Analysis: Results Directory report_power. Optionally load the VCD/TCF from the front-end simulation (only if the mode is dynamic vector-based). Click OK.

DView the results

Run the analysis and load power.db to inspect total and instance power: Power & Rail → Power & Rail Results; State Directory ./report_power → Load State; tick Power Database and select ./report_power/power.db; choose a Plot type (e.g. Total Instance Power) and tick Auto Apply so each selection redraws immediately.

If plots stay empty: as the course notes, try work as the state directory — the tool's default location for intermediate results.

Equivalent Tcl pattern (verify each option with help <command> in your build) 
Static power analysis in Encounter 13 · Tclset_power_analysis_mode -reset
set_power_analysis_mode -method static -analysis_view VIEW_SETUP -corner max \
  -create_binary_db true -write_static_currents true
set_power_output_dir -reset
set_power_output_dir report_power
set_default_switching_activity -reset
set_default_switching_activity -input_activity 0.2 -period 10.0
# optional: real activity from Chapter 3
# read_activity_file -format TCF -scope tb_cnt_updown.dut activity/dut.tcf
report_power -rail_analysis_format VS -outfile report_power/cnt_updown.rpt
Why post-route power differs

Clock-tree cells, extracted wire capacitance and actual slew now contribute. Vector-based activity is more realistic only when the workload is representative.

What you should see
  • power_library/ fills with one .cl file per corner (the course’s was fast_allcells.cl).
  • After Run Power Analysis, report_power/ contains power.db, a text report, and *.ptiavg current files.
  • The text report shows total power in the µW range for this design, with internal, switching and leakage columns.
Troubleshooting — power analysis

Menu items greyed out — the integrated power/rail engine may need a separate license on your VM — record that in the README.

“no activity” — set a default switching activity or load the TCF from Chapter 3.

Empty plots — load work as the state directory, as the course suggests.

7.4

Set up and run rail analysis

Why this stepVerifies every cell receives enough voltage under load.

ARail-analysis mode

Choose Power & Rail → Set Rail Analysis Mode. Load the PowerGrid library from power_library, the analysis view (VIEW_SETUP; the course uses its typical view) and temperature 125 °C — the temperature of slow.lib, which that view uses (the course used 25 °C with its typical corner). Use static analysis to match the power run.

BRun domain-based rail analysis

Choose Power & Rail → Run Rail Analysis. Define a domain containing VDD and VSS, and enter the supply voltages and the drop thresholds (the voltage below which a region is flagged):

NETCOURSE (65 nm)YOUR VM
VDD voltage / threshold0.88 V / 0.84 V1.08 V (slow.lib nom_voltage) / 1.026 V (5 % drop)
VSS voltage / threshold0 V / 0.04 V0 V / 0.054 V (5 % of 1.08 V)

Provide the current files written in Step 7.3 (report_power/*.ptiavg) and the package connection (voltage source) locations — for a core-only design, use the ring as the source (tick the option to place sources on the ring/pins). Click OK.

CExactly how the course filled in this dialog

FIELDCOURSE VALUEMEANING
Domain Basedticked; Domain Name allDomainsanalyse VDD and VSS together
Power Net(s) / Voltage / ThresholdVDD / 0.88 V / 0.84 Vflag any point below 0.84 V (≈ 5 % drop)
Ground Net(s) / Voltage / ThresholdVSS / 0 V / 0.04 Vflag ground bounce above 40 mV
Power DataCurrent files, Scale 1use the currents written by power analysis
Power/Current File(s)./report_power/*.ptiavg (select all with Ctrl)one average-current file per net
Voltage Source FilesVDD_wb.ppl → net VDD, VSS_wb.ppl → net VSS (Add each)where the supply enters the grid

A .ppl file lists the supply connection points, one per line, as net x y layer. For a core-only design put a few points on the power ring. Print the real ring coordinates of your design at the encounter> prompt:

Print the ring wires · Tclforeach net {VDD VSS} {
  foreach w [dbGet [dbGet -p top.nets.name $net].sWires] {
    if {[dbGet $w.shape] eq "ring"} { puts "$net [dbGet $w.layer.name] [dbGet $w.box]" }
  }
}

Each line is net layer {llx lly urx ury}. Take the middle of a ring segment: for a horizontal Metal9 segment use x anywhere between its ends and y = (lly + ury)/2; for a vertical Metal8 segment use y anywhere and x = (llx + urx)/2. With the floorplan of Step 4.5 the VDD ring (the inner one, listed first in addRing) runs about 4.5 µm outside the core — roughly x or y ≈ 95.5 on the left/bottom and ≈ 118 on the right/top. If the dbGet lines print nothing, click the ring in the GUI and press q instead.

VDD_wb.ppl (example for your floorplan — replace with the coordinates printed above)VDD  106.8   95.5  Metal9
VDD  106.8  118.1  Metal9
VDD   95.5  106.8  Metal8
VDD  118.1  106.8  Metal8

Write VSS_wb.ppl the same way on the VSS ring. Fewer or farther sources give larger IR drop — try moving them and watch the plot change.

Equivalent Tcl pattern (verify with help) 
Static rail analysis · Tclset_rail_analysis_mode -method static -accuracy xd -analysis_view VIEW_SETUP \
  -power_grid_library [glob power_library/*.cl] -temperature 125
set_pg_nets -net VDD -voltage 1.08 -threshold 1.026
set_pg_nets -net VSS -voltage 0.0  -threshold 0.054
set_rail_analysis_domain -name CORE -pwrnets VDD -gndnets VSS
set_power_data -reset
set_power_data -format current -scale 1 [glob report_power/*.ptiavg]
analyze_rail -type domain -results_directory rail_results CORE
Physical effect

Current through finite metal resistance creates voltage loss. A logically correct cell may slow down or fail if local supply voltage collapses during switching.

What you should see
  • The run log reports the worst IR drop for VDD and the worst ground bounce for VSS, and whether they exceed the thresholds.
  • rail_results/ (or the state directory) contains the result database loaded in Step 7.5.
7.5

Inspect IR drop and stream GDSII

Why this stepVisualises where voltage sags, then writes the GDSII the foundry would manufacture.

ALoad and plot the rail results

Open Power & Rail → Power & Rail Results, select the rail state directory, click Load State, and choose the IR-drop plot.

The layout is coloured by voltage drop: blue near the supply connections, warmer colours where current must travel farthest. Zoom into hot regions and use report_power -instance … on the cells there to relate current demand to voltage loss.

Pass criterion: the worst drop is below the threshold you set. If not: add stripes (smaller pitch), widen the ring, or add decap cells near the hot spot, then rerun Chapter 4 from the stripe step.

BStream out GDSII

GDSII is the polygon file a foundry manufactures from. In a production kit the real cell layouts are merged in from the library GDS during stream-out, and a map file from the PDK translates Encounter layer names to GDS layer numbers. The GPDK045 example kit on your VM has neither (Step 0.2), so you do the next-best complete thing:

  • Map file — write your own, scripts/gds_view.map, in the exact format of the Encounter map that ships with gpdk090 (gpdk090_v4.6/soce/soce_gds.map). The layer names Metal1–Metal9 and Via1–Via8 are identical in both kits, so the file reuses gpdk090’s GDS numbers (Metal1 = 7, Via1 = 8, Metal2 = 9 …). That makes the result viewable in Virtuoso with the gpdk090 technology in Step 7.6.
  • Cells — -outputMacros writes every standard cell as its LEF abstract (pins and obstructions on Metal1, Cont and Poly) instead of an empty reference, so the GDS is self-contained.

diff <(awk '$1~/^(Metal|Via)/{print $1,$(NF-1)}' $GPDK090/soce/soce_gds.map | sort -u) \

B2Write the GDS

Use File → Save → GDS/OASIS (Output file results/cnt_updown.gds, Map File scripts/gds_view.map, Library Name DesignLib, Units 2000, Mode ALL, and tick the option to output the LEF macros), or type:

Stream-out on your VM · Tclsource scripts/lib_paths.tcl
streamOut results/cnt_updown.gds \
  -mapFile $STREAM_MAP \
  -libName DesignLib -structureName cnt_updown \
  -units $DB_UNITS -mode ALL \
  -outputMacros

The course form is streamOut updown_counter.gds -mapFile ./libs/gds2.map -merge {standard_cell_library.gds io_pad_library.gds}. There is no -merge here because no cell GDS exists on your VM. -units must equal the LEF DATABASE MICRONS value: 2000.

Expected

The log ends with a summary of structures and layers written; ls -l results/cnt_updown.gds shows a file of some hundreds of kilobytes (the routed design plus abstracts of every gsclib045 cell). Warnings about layers that are not in the map (implant layers such as Nimp/Pimp inside cell abstracts, if any) are harmless for viewing.

ANNOTATED OUTPUTTail of the streamOut logillustrative — your exact numbers and names will differ
Tail of the streamOut logParse map file...                                                   [1]
Writing GDSII file ...
    ****** db unit per micron = 2000 ******
    ****** output gds2 file unit per micron = 2000 ******            [2]
    ****** unit scaling factor = 1 ******
Output for LEF macros                                               [3]
Stream Out Information Processed for GDS version 5:
Units: 2000 DBU
Object                             Count
----------------------------------------
Instances                            98                             [4]
Ports/Pins                            5
Nets                                  ...
    metal layer Metal1              ...
    via layer Via1                  ...
Done with stream out                                                [5]
  1. Parse map file reads scripts/gds_view.map. A line about an unknown object type would point to a typo in the map.
  2. Unit scaling factor = 1 is the line to check: anything else means -units disagrees with the LEF.
  3. Because of -outputMacros each used gsclib045 cell is written as a structure with its LEF pins and obstructions — no Merging with GDS libraries line, because there is nothing to merge.
  4. Instances ≈ your cell count plus fillers; ports = the five top-level pins of cnt_updown (clk, reset, enable, up_down, count bus).
  5. Done with stream out with no ERROR lines above it = a complete GDS. Next, view it in Virtuoso (Step 7.6).
Troubleshooting — stream-out

-outputMacros is not accepted — run the same command without it. The GDS then contains the routing and empty references to the cells; Virtuoso shows the cells as named boxes only.

“Layer … is not mapped” for Metal* or Via* — a line of scripts/gds_view.map was lost while pasting; compare with the block above (wc -l).

Map-file parse error on LEFPIN/LEFOBS — your build may not know these object types; delete , LEFPIN, LEFOBS from the nine Metal lines (that is exactly the format of $GPDK090/soce/soce_gds.map) and stream out again.

Virtuoso shows the layout 10× too small or too large — -units does not match the LEF DATABASE MICRONS (see the GDS-grid diagram in the signoff theory).

Final checkpointConnectivity, geometry and antenna checks are 0, density results are recorded, setup and hold pass, power and rail results (or the missing-license note) are recorded, and results/cnt_updown.gds was written with unit scaling factor 1.
7.6

View the final GDS in Virtuoso — and what DRC/LVS can prove on this VM

Why this stepSeeing the streamed layout closes the RTL→GDS loop; knowing what Assura can and cannot check here keeps your report honest.

AWhy Assura cannot sign off this layout here

Assura DRC compares polygons with a foundry rule deck, and LVS extracts transistors from the layout and compares them with a netlist. Your VM has Assura decks only for gpdk090 ($GPDK090/assura/drc.rul, extract.rul, compare.rul …), and the 45 nm GDS contains no transistors at all — only routing and LEF abstracts, because the kit has no cell GDS. A 90 nm deck run on 45 nm geometry would flag nearly every wire, and LVS would find nothing to extract. So, on this VM:

QUESTIONEVIDENCE YOU HAVEWHERE
Are the wires legal (width, spacing, shorts, antennas)?Encounter verifyGeometry, verifyProcessAntenna against the rules in gsclib045.lefStep 7.1
Is everything connected, including power?verifyConnectivity (0 opens, 0 unconnected pins)Steps 4.14, 7.1
Does the layout netlist do what the RTL does?Post-route netlist + SDF simulation with the same self-checking testbench (PASS)Step 7.2
Is the scan chain intact after layout?Post-route scan shift test (PASS)Step 6.5
Does it meet timing with real wires?Post-route timeDesign setup + hold with cap-table extractionSteps 4.13, 7.1
Foundry DRC / LVSNot available for GPDK045 on this VM — record exactly thatREADME (Step 7.7)

BStream the GDS into a viewing library

Work in a separate virtuoso/ folder so Virtuoso’s cds.lib does not clash with the NC cds.lib in the project root (Step 1.5). The new cds.lib simply includes your usual /home/buet/cds_work/cds.lib, which already defines gpdk090. strmin creates the library cnt_gds_view, attaches it to the gpdk090 technology, and uses gpdk090’s own layer map — the numbers your gds_view.map wrote.

Stream in for viewing · shellcd /home/buet/cds_work/asic_lab
source setup_cadence.sh
mkdir -p virtuoso && cd virtuoso
echo "SOFTINCLUDE /home/buet/cds_work/cds.lib" > cds.lib
strmin -library cnt_gds_view -strmFile ../results/cnt_updown.gds -topCell cnt_updown \
  -view layout -attachTechFileOfLib gpdk090 \
  -layerMap $GPDK090/libs.oa22/gpdk090/gpdk090.layermap \
  -logFile ../logs/strmin.log
tail -15 ../logs/strmin.log
grep cnt_gds_view cds.lib || echo "DEFINE cnt_gds_view ./cnt_gds_view" >> cds.lib
virtuoso &

The same through the GUI: in the CIW choose File → Import → Stream; Stream File = ../results/cnt_updown.gds, Library = cnt_gds_view, Top Cell = cnt_updown, Attach Technology Library = gpdk090; under Options → Layers load the layer map /home/buet/cadence/gpdk090_v4.6/libs.oa22/gpdk090/gpdk090.layermap; click Translate.

COpen and inspect the layout

  1. In the CIW open Tools → Library Manager, select library cnt_gds_view, cell cnt_updown, view layout, and open it.
  2. Press Shift+F to show all hierarchy levels and f to fit. Your ~/.cdsinit key bindings (scroll-wheel zoom) work here too.
  3. Check what you see against Encounter: the VDD/VSS ring on Metal8/Metal9 around a ≈14 µm core, the two stripe pairs per direction, the Metal1 rails along the eight rows, signal routing on the lower metals, and each standard cell as a sub-cell named after its gsclib045 master, showing its pins.
  4. Use the ruler (k) on the ring: 3 µm wide, 4 µm apart — the values you typed in Step 4.7. A correct scale proves that -units 2000 matched the LEF.
What you should see
  • strmin.log ends with a translation summary and no errors; unmapped-layer warnings should not appear for Metal/Via layers.
  • The layout opens and shows the routed counter in gpdk090’s layer colours. The cells show pins and obstructions, not transistors — expected, because the kit has no cell GDS.
Viewing only. The gpdk090 technology is attached purely so Virtuoso knows how to draw layers 7, 8, 9 …. Do not run Assura DRC/LVS from this view, and do not report any result from it — the geometry is 45 nm and the rules are 90 nm. If you want to practise Assura itself, run it on your own gpdk090 layouts (your mylib2/nand2 cell, for example) — that is the deck’s real purpose.
Troubleshooting — strmin and Virtuoso

strmin: command not found — the setup file was not sourced in this terminal (which strmin must print …/IC615/tools/dfII/bin/strmin).

“Library gpdk090 not found” — the cds.lib in virtuoso/ was not created, or /home/buet/cds_work/cds.lib moved. cat cds.lib must show the SOFTINCLUDE line; grep gpdk090 /home/buet/cds_work/cds.lib must show DEFINE gpdk090 /home/buet/cadence/gpdk090_v4.6/libs.oa22/gpdk090.

“Library cnt_gds_view already exists” on a second run — delete it first: rm -rf cnt_gds_view (inside virtuoso/), then rerun strmin.

The layout is empty — the top cell name must be cnt_updown (it is the -structureName of Step 7.5). strings ../results/cnt_updown.gds | grep -m3 cnt_updown shows it.

Checkpointcnt_gds_view/cnt_updown/layout opens in Virtuoso and shows the ring, stripes, rails and routed cells at the right scale; your README states that foundry DRC/LVS is not available for GPDK045 on this VM and lists the Encounter checks used instead.
7.7

Archive the evidence, not only the GDS

Why this stepA result is only credible if someone (including future you) can reproduce it from the archived inputs.

Keep the exact RTL, testbench, constraints, Tcl scripts, libraries by version, tool logs, reports, scan-chain report, final netlist, SDF/SPEF, DEF, GDS, stream map, DRC/LVS summaries and a short README containing the commands used. A GDS with no reproducible inputs is not a complete lab result.

What you should now have
FILEWHAT IT IS
results/cnt_updown.spef / .sdfParasitics and delays

? Check yourself

Q1Hold is checked at the fast corner because…

Hold fails when new data arrives too early — worst with the fastest transistors.

Q2A 5 % IR drop typically makes gates slower by about…

From the alpha-power law with Vt = 0.35, α = 1.3 the ratio is ≈ 1.06.

Q3Relative delay variation of a path of N independent gates scales as…

σ grows as √N while μ grows as N, so σ/μ ∝ 1/√N — deep paths average out.

⚠ Common mistakes in this chapter
  • Checking hold at the slow corner (it must be the fast corner).
  • Mixing PDKs for DRC/LVS and calling a run “clean”.
  • Streaming out GDS with -units different from the LEF database units.
  • Reporting Encounter verifyGeometry as a foundry DRC pass.
  • Running gpdk090 Assura DRC on the 45 nm GDS that was only streamed into gpdk090 for viewing.
